2003224.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

Most of the WEB_CLIENT signatures detect Javascript type attacks against client software.

2003231.et_name: ACTIVEX Possible Microsoft IE Install Engine Inseng.dll Arbitrary Code Execution
2003231.description:
ActiveX controls are Microsoft Internet Explorer’s native version of plug-ins and can be leveraged by non browse applications as well..  ActiveX provides web application developers a facility to execute code on a client machine through the web browser.  Unfortunately, ActiveX controls have been a significant source of security problems both due to vulnerabilities in the ActiveX control itself, in the browser which can allow the activeX control to bypass security, as well as the fact that it has extensive capabilities to attacker drive code.
ActiveX controls are very powerful and can be used for legitimate and nefarious purposes including monitoring your personal browsing habits, install malware, generate pop-ups, log your keystrokes and passwords, and do other malicious things. ActiveX controls are actually not Internet Explorer-only. They also work in other Microsoft applications, such as Microsoft Office. Other browsers, such as Firefox, Chrome, Safari, and Opera, all use other types of browser plug-ins. ActiveX controls only function in Internet Explorer. A website that requires an ActiveX control is an Internet Explorer-only website.
If you see these ActiveX controls alerts firing, they are unlikely to succeed in exploiting all but legacy windows systems running older versions of IE.  To help validate whether the signature is triggering a valid compromise you should look for other malicious signatures related to the client endpoint which is triggering.  This includes Exploit Kit, Malware, and Command and Control signatures, along with looking to see if the web server is known to be malicious in ET Intelligence.

2003236.et_name: NetrWkstaUserEnum Request with large Preferred Max Len
2003236.description:
This rule detects attempts to exploit a denial of service vulnerability in the Windows Workstation service through SMB protocol on port 445. The attack involves sending a NetrWkstaUserEnum request with an abnormally large Preferred Maximum Length parameter.

The rule specifically looks for:
- TCP traffic from external networks to port 445 on internal networks
- Established connections flowing to the server
- SMB protocol signature ("|ff|SMB")
- Specific byte patterns that identify a NetrWkstaUserEnum request
- A large value in the Preferred Max Length field (verified by byte_test)

This detection addresses CVE-2006-6723, a vulnerability affecting Microsoft Windows 2000 SP4 and XP SP2. The vulnerability allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service condition through memory consumption by specifying an excessively large maxlen value in NetrWkstaUserEnum RPC requests. When exploited, this vulnerability can lead to system resource exhaustion and potential service disruption.

The rule is classified as "attempted-dos" indicating its primary purpose is to detect denial of service attempts against Windows systems. This vulnerability represents a significant risk to older Windows environments where the affected systems might still be in operation, particularly in legacy networks or industrial control systems.

2003237.msg: ET VOIP MultiTech SIP UDP Overflow

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, confidence Medium, signature_severity Informational, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2019_07_26

2003237.description:
This rule detects potential buffer overflow attacks targeting MultiTech VoIP devices through SIP UDP traffic. It monitors for INVITE messages directed to port 5060 (standard SIP port) on internal networks from external sources.

The detection mechanism identifies SIP INVITE requests that contain abnormally structured data - specifically looking for packets where the INVITE message extends beyond 65 bytes without containing a newline character within the first 61 bytes. This pattern matches the exploitation technique used in CVE-2005-4050.

CVE-2005-4050 describes a buffer overflow vulnerability in Multi-Tech Systems MultiVOIP devices with firmware versions prior to x.08. This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code by sending maliciously crafted SIP packets containing an excessively long INVITE field.

The rule classifies this activity as "attempted-user," indicating an attempt to gain user-level access to the affected system. This vulnerability is particularly concerning for organizations using these VoIP devices, as successful exploitation could lead to unauthorized code execution and potential compromise of the voice communication infrastructure.

Network administrators should ensure MultiTech VoIP devices are updated to firmware version x.08 or later to mitigate this vulnerability.

2003238.msg: ET MALWARE W32.Downloader Tibs.jy Reporting to C&C
2003238.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the W32.Downloader Tibs.jy malware communicating with its command and control (C&C) server.

The rule identifies HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations where the malware is sending data to a C&C server. Specifically, it looks for:

- HTTP requests to "/post.php" in the URI
- A distinctive User-Agent string: "Mozilla/3.0b5a (Win95|;| I)" with specific character encoding
- HTTP POST request bodies beginning with "data="

W32.Downloader Tibs is a trojan downloader that establishes communication with remote servers to receive additional malicious payloads. This particular variant (Tibs.jy) uses a specific HTTP-based communication protocol to report system information and receive commands from its operators.

The detection of this traffic is significant as it indicates an active malware infection within the network that is attempting to communicate with external control infrastructure. This communication channel allows threat actors to maintain persistence, exfiltrate data, or deploy additional malware components to the infected system.

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" correctly identifies this as malicious traffic associated with botnet infrastructure rather than initial infection vectors.

2003239.msg: ET MALWARE W32.Downloader Tibs.jy Reporting to C&C (2)
2003239.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the W32.Downloader Tibs.jy malware communicating with its command and control (C2) infrastructure.

The rule specifically monitors HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations, looking for HTTP requests to a specific URI pattern "/rule.php?" that contains multiple parameters: "name=", "b=", and "w=". These parameters are likely used by the malware to transmit system information or receive instructions from the C2 server.

W32.Downloader Tibs is a malware family that functions as a downloader, meaning its primary purpose is to retrieve and install additional malicious payloads onto infected systems. This vulnerability affects Symantec AntiVirus Corporate Edition 8.1, 9.0.x (up to 9.0.3), and Symantec Client Security 1.1, 2.0.x (up to 2.0.3). Unlike local privilege escalation vulnerabilities, this is a remotely exploitable vulnerability that allows attackers to send malicious network traffic to the RTVScan service, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution with SYSTEM privileges on the target machine.

The classification as "attempted-admin" indicates this is a remote attempt to gain administrative access to the affected system. If successful, an attacker could completely compromise the target system, potentially using it as a foothold to move laterally within the network or to deploy additional malware.

# Suricata Rule Analysis: SOCKSv5 Port 25 Inbound Request Detection

This rule detects SOCKSv5 proxy connection attempts targeting port 25 (SMTP) from external networks to internal networks. The rule specifically identifies SOCKSv5 protocol signatures with a specific data size and byte pattern.

## Technical Details

The rule monitors TCP traffic from external networks (ports 1024-5000) to home networks (ports 1024-65535) with the following characteristics:
- Fixed data size of 10 bytes
- Established TCP connections flowing to the server
- Content pattern "|05 01 00 01|" within the first 4 bytes (SOCKSv5 protocol signature)
- Content pattern "|00 19|" at offset 8 (representing port 25 in hex)
- Threshold limiting alerts to once per source IP address within a 15-minute window

## Threat Detection

This rule identifies potential proxy bypass attempts where external actors use SOCKSv5 proxies to relay SMTP traffic into the protected network. This activity may indicate:

1. Proxy circumvention of email security controls
2. Unauthorized mail relay attempts through SOCKSv5 proxies
3. Potential command and control (C2) communications using SMTP over SOCKSv5
4. Attempts to bypass network restrictions on direct SMTP connections

The detection is significant as SOCKSv5 proxies can be used to obfuscate the true origin of connections and bypass security controls. When targeting SMTP services, this could facilitate spam distribution, data exfiltration, or other malicious email-related activities.

## Investigation Guidelines

When this alert triggers, analysts should:
1. Verify if the source IP is associated with known legitimate proxy services
2. Check if the destination host is authorized to receive external SMTP connections
3. Examine session details to determine if actual SMTP commands followed the proxy connection
4. Review logs for successful authentication attempts or failed login attempts
5. Correlate with other alerts from the same source IP for potential scanning or lateral movement

## Response Actions

Consider these response options based on investigation findings:
- Block the source IP at the perimeter if unauthorized proxy activity is confirmed
- Update proxy allow/deny lists if the activity violates organizational policy
- Implement additional monitoring for the affected internal hosts
- Review and strengthen SMTP relay restrictions on internal mail servers
- Document findings for threat intelligence purposes if part of a larger campaign

The rule references multiple RFCs and documentation related to the SOCKSv5 protocol, indicating it's designed to detect specific protocol behaviors rather than a particular vulnerability.

# Suricata Rule Analysis: ET VOIP Centrality IP Phone Session Hijacking

This rule detects attempts to exploit a session hijacking vulnerability in Centrality IP Phones using the PA-168 chipset. The rule specifically identifies HTTP POST requests to a URI path starting with "/g" that contain the parameter "back=++Back++" in the request body.

The detection focuses on traffic from external networks to internal networks, targeting a known vulnerability (CVE-2007-0528) in the admin web console of Centrality Communications PA168 chipset devices. This vulnerability affects firmware version 1.54 and earlier.

The vulnerability exists because the admin web console does not require passwords or authentication tokens when using HTTP. This security flaw allows remote attackers to connect to existing superuser sessions and access sensitive information including passwords and configuration data.

The rule uses several detection techniques:
- Monitors established HTTP connections to internal servers
- Identifies POST requests specifically to URIs beginning with "/g"
- Uses PCRE regex to ensure the path is exactly "/g" or "/g" followed by a query string
- Looks for the specific string "back=++Back++" in the HTTP request body

This vulnerability represents a significant security risk for organizations using affected IP phones, as successful exploitation could lead to unauthorized access to administrative functions and sensitive information. The reference to milw0rm[.]com indicates this vulnerability has been publicly documented with available exploit code.

This high-frequency querying behavior is anomalous for legitimate systems but common for infected hosts attempting to discover mail servers.

The rule uses content matching to identify DNS query packets and specifically looks for MX record type queries (indicated by the hexadecimal pattern "|00 0f 00 01|"). The threshold setting ensures that only sustained, abnormal query patterns trigger alerts, reducing false positives.

2003331.et_name: PHP Generic membreManager.php remote file include
2003331.description:
Remote File Include (RFI) is a technique used to exploit vulnerable "dynamic file include" mechanisms in web applications. When web applications take user input (URL, parameter value, etc.) and pass them into file include commands, the web application might be tricked into including remote files with malicious code. File inclusion is typically used for packaging common code into separate files that are later referenced by main application modules. When a web application references an include file, the code in this file may be executed implicitly or explicitly by calling specific procedures. If the choice of module to load is based on elements from the HTTP request, the web application might be vulnerable to RFI.

PHP is particularly vulnerable to file include attacks due to the extensive use of "file includes" in PHP and due to default server configurations that increase susceptibility to a file include attack. Although most examples point to vulnerable PHP scripts, we should keep in mind that it is also common in other technologies such as JSP, ASP and others.

It is common for attackers to scan for LFI vulnerabilities against hundreds or thousands of servers and launch further, more sophisticated attacks should a server respond in a way that reveals it is vulnerable. You may see hundreds of these alerts in a short period of time indicating you are the target of a scanning campaign, all of which may be FPs. If you see a HTTP 200 response in the web server log files for the request generating the alert, you’ll want to investigate to determine if the attack was successful. Typically, after a successful attack, attackers will wget a trojan from a third party site and execute it, so that the attacker maintains control even if the vulnerable software is patched..

This rule classification is disabled by default, and can be enabled by people wanting to detect attacks against web applications.

2003346.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2003369.et_name: CA BrightStor ARCserve Mobile Backup LGSERVER.EXE Heap Corruption
2003369.description:
This rule detects exploitation attempts targeting a heap corruption vulnerability in CA BrightStor ARCserve Mobile Backup's LGSERVER.EXE component. The alert triggers when external hosts send specific traffic to port 2200 on protected networks.

The rule looks for a specific byte sequence ("|4e 3d 2c 1b|") that must appear within the first 4 bytes of established TCP connections to the server. The depth:4 parameter restricts this content match to only the first 4 bytes of the payload. Additionally, the rule verifies that at least 2891 bytes exist after this signature using the isdataat operator, which is characteristic of the buffer overflow exploit attempt.

This detection targets CVE-2007-0449, which affects multiple buffer overflows in LGSERVER.EXE across several CA BrightStor products including ARCserve Backup for Laptops and Desktops (r11.0-r11.1 SP1), Mobile Backup r4.0, and related protection suites. While the vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via crafted packets sent to both TCP ports 1900 and 2200, this specific rule only monitors traffic on port 2200.

The classification as "attempted-admin" indicates this is a serious attack attempting to gain administrative access to the affected system. Successful exploitation could lead to complete system compromise, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the vulnerable service.

Organizations running affected CA BrightStor products should apply vendor patches or implement network-level protections to mitigate this threat. Network defenders should also consider implementing additional monitoring for similar traffic patterns targeting port 1900, as the same vulnerability affects both ports.

2003371.et_name: PHP Portail Includes.php remote file include
2003371.description:
Remote File Include (RFI) is a technique used to exploit vulnerable "dynamic file include" mechanisms in web applications. When web applications take user input (URL, parameter value, etc.) and pass them into file include commands, the web application might be tricked into including remote files with malicious code. File inclusion is typically used for packaging common code into separate files that are later referenced by main application modules. When a web application references an include file, the code in this file may be executed implicitly or explicitly by calling specific procedures. If the choice of module to load is based on elements from the HTTP request, the web application might be vulnerable to RFI.

PHP is particularly vulnerable to file include attacks due to the extensive use of "file includes" in PHP and due to default server configurations that increase susceptibility to a file include attack. Although most examples point to vulnerable PHP scripts, we should keep in mind that it is also common in other technologies such as JSP, ASP and others.

It is common for attackers to scan for LFI vulnerabilities against hundreds or thousands of servers and launch further, more sophisticated attacks should a server respond in a way that reveals it is vulnerable. You may see hundreds of these alerts in a short period of time indicating you are the target of a scanning campaign, all of which may be FPs. If you see a HTTP 200 response in the web server log files for the request generating the alert, you’ll want to investigate to determine if the attack was successful. Typically, after a successful attack, attackers will wget a trojan from a third party site and execute it, so that the attacker maintains control even if the vulnerable software is patched..

This rule classification is disabled by default, and can be enabled by people wanting to detect attacks against web applications.

The rule triggers when external network traffic sends a specific pattern of four consecutive 0xFF bytes (represented as |ff ff ff ff|) at a specific position (offset 16, with a depth constraint of 4 bytes) within established TCP connections directed to port 2200 on the protected network. The flow:established,to_server parameter ensures that only packets within established TCP sessions flowing from the client to the server are evaluated, filtering out connection attempts and server responses.

This pattern appears to be a signature of an exploit attempt against a vulnerability in the BrightStor ARCserve Backup software. The attack targets the LGServer.exe component, which is responsible for handling backup operations for laptops and desktops. When successfully exploited, this vulnerability could cause the service to crash, resulting in a denial of service condition that would disrupt backup operations and potentially affect business continuity.

The classification as "attempted-dos" confirms that this rule is specifically designed to detect denial of service attempts rather than other types of attacks.

Upon detection, security teams should:

2. Verify if the LGServer.exe process has crashed or is exhibiting unusual behavior
3. Implement temporary network filtering to block external access to port 2200 if immediate patching is not possible
4. Review logs for successful exploitation indicators such as service disruptions or unexpected restarts
5. Apply vendor-provided patches specifically addressing this vulnerability

For long-term mitigation, organizations should:
1. Implement network segmentation to restrict access to backup infrastructure
2. Consider using application-layer firewalls to inspect traffic to critical backup services
3. Regularly update Computer Associates BrightStor ARCserve Backup software to the latest patched version

2003380.description:
A Trojan-Downloader is a type of malware that is responsible for loading and facilitating the continued proliferation of further payloads upon the victim machine. Typically, Trojan-Downloaders will ensure further infection is successful but reporting a successful install, modifying system settings to ensure future malware can be installed/executed without issue, and enable persistency mechanisms for long term infection. Windows is the most commonly observed platform for this type of infection, however, it is not limited-- Macintosh OS X and Linux are also potential targets for compromise.
Valid Trojan-Downloader activity can include network connectivity to a command and control server to report successful infection on a victim machine. Typically, machines impacted with a Trojan-Downloader will have several system settings modified, such as modifications to the Registry where malicious entries may be made. Additionally, the download of a second-stage payload may occur once the original malware has ran. Trojan-Downloaders have been observed with the ability to exfiltrate sensitive data. Confirmation of hostile IP addresses or domains observed with Trojan-Downloader activity may take place in the ET Intelligence portal.
From a network perspective, malware that falls under the Trojan-Downloader has been observed performing activity that would trigger several Emerging Threats INFO, POLICY, and TROJAN style alerts, such as checking an external IP address, the presence of a downloaded executable, or a suspicious HTTP POST to a server. This combination of Trojan-Downloader alerts, as well as complimentary INFO, POLICY, or TROJAN alerts, would warrant an immediate follow up for a compromised workstation.

2003400.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: ET EXPLOIT US-ASCII Obfuscated Script

This rule detects attempts to exploit a browser interpretation vulnerability using US-ASCII obfuscated scripts. The alert triggers when external hosts send HTTP responses to internal network hosts containing specific obfuscated JavaScript patterns.

The rule identifies content with "US-ASCII" string followed by a specific byte sequence pattern that matches obfuscated script code. This technique attempts to bypass security controls by leveraging character encoding inconsistencies between different web browsers.

## Technical Details

- **Protocol**: HTTP
- **Direction**: External to internal network (to_client)
- **Detection Method**: Content match for "US-ASCII" and PCRE pattern matching for specific byte sequences
- **Classification**: Web application attack
- **SID**: 2003400

## Associated Vulnerability

CVE-2006-3227 describes an interpretation conflict between Internet Explorer and other browsers (Mozilla, Opera, Firefox) where ASCII characters with the 8th bit set are processed differently. Internet Explorer may strip these bits, rendering obfuscated text legible, while other browsers process them differently. This inconsistency allows attackers to bypass content filters and modify the visual presentation of web pages.

The exploit technique leverages encoding ambiguities in web standards to deliver malicious JavaScript that might evade detection by security controls. The specific byte pattern in the rule identifies scripts obfuscated using this technique.

This vulnerability highlights the security risks that arise from inconsistent implementation of standards across different browsers, particularly regarding character encoding interpretation.

2003401.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: ET EXPLOIT US-ASCII Obfuscated VBScript Download File

This rule detects attempts to exploit browser vulnerabilities using obfuscated VBScript content. The alert triggers when external servers send HTTP responses containing specially crafted US-ASCII encoded content to internal network clients.

The rule specifically looks for:
- HTTP traffic from external servers to internal clients
- Content containing "US-ASCII" (case insensitive)
- A specific byte pattern matching obfuscated VBScript using PCRE regex

The PCRE pattern (/\xae[\xef\xcf][\xf0\xd0][\xe5\xc5][\xee\xce]\xa0\xa2[\xe7\xc7][\xe5\xc5][\xf4\xd4]\xa2/) targets a specific obfuscation technique where ASCII characters with the high bit set (8th bit) are used to encode "CreateScript" function calls. When the high bit is stripped during processing by Internet Explorer, these characters become standard ASCII that executes as VBScript.

This obfuscation technique directly exploits CVE-2006-3227, which describes how Internet Explorer processes characters with the high bit set differently than other browsers. When IE encounters these characters, it strips the high bit, converting characters like 0xE5 to 0x65 ('e'), allowing attackers to hide malicious code that becomes visible only during browser rendering. This specific encoding manipulation enables attackers to bypass content filters and security controls.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Examine the full HTTP session data to identify the complete obfuscated script
2. Check if the client browser accessed additional resources after this detection
3. Inspect the client system for signs of code execution or persistence mechanisms
4. Review proxy logs for similar patterns from the same source IP address

The attack technique has been documented by Internet Defence Network in 2007 and remains relevant as legacy encoding vulnerabilities continue to be exploited. Successful exploitation could lead to arbitrary code execution within the context of the browser, potentially enabling system compromise through drive-by downloads.

# Suricata Rule Analysis: ET EXPLOIT US-ASCII Obfuscated VBScript Execute Command

This rule detects attempts to exploit web browsers using obfuscated VBScript code that has been encoded in US-ASCII with specific bit manipulation techniques. The rule targets HTTP traffic from external servers to internal clients, focusing on responses that contain specially crafted content.

The detection mechanism identifies US-ASCII encoded content that contains a specific pattern of bytes matching obfuscated VBScript commands. The PCRE pattern in the rule looks for a sequence of byte pairs where each pair represents alternative encodings of characters that could be used to spell "shellexecute" when certain bits are stripped or interpreted differently by vulnerable browsers.

This detection relates to CVE-2006-3227, which describes an interpretation conflict between Internet Explorer and other web browsers. The vulnerability stems from how different browsers handle ASCII characters with the 8th bit set. Internet Explorer may strip these bits, rendering potentially malicious code as legible and executable text, while other browsers might interpret the content differently. This discrepancy allows attackers to bypass content filters and security mechanisms.

The attack technique leverages character encoding manipulation to disguise malicious VBScript code that executes commands on the victim's system. When successful, this exploit could lead to remote code execution, allowing attackers to gain control over the affected system.

The rule references documentation from internetdefence[.]net and securityfocus[.]com that provide additional technical details about this exploitation technique.

This type of obfuscation technique represents a significant security concern as it exploits fundamental differences in how web browsers process and interpret encoded content, potentially bypassing security controls that rely on pattern matching or signature-based detection.

The rule triggers when HTTP traffic from external servers ($EXTERNAL_NET) on standard HTTP ports flows to internal systems ($HOME_NET), containing "US-ASCII" in the HTTP response body along with a specific pattern of bytes that match obfuscated VBScript.

The detection relies on:
- Flow direction established from server to client
- Presence of "US-ASCII" string (case insensitive)
- A specific byte pattern identified by the PCRE regex that matches obfuscated VBScript characters

This technique exploits CVE-2006-3227, which involves an interpretation conflict between Internet Explorer and other browsers regarding ASCII characters with the 8th bit set. Internet Explorer may strip these bits to render legible text, while other browsers handle them differently. This discrepancy allows attackers to bypass content filters and protection mechanisms by modifying the visual presentation of web pages.

The obfuscation technique attempts to hide malicious VBScript code from security tools while ensuring it remains executable by the target browser. This represents a web application attack that could lead to arbitrary code execution on client systems if successfully exploited.

The rule references documentation from internetdefence[.]net and securityfocus[.]com that provide additional context about this JavaScript/VBScript payload delivery technique.

2003404.msg: ET ADWARE_PUP WhenUClick.com WhenUSave Data Retrieval (DataChunksGZ)
2003404.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with adware/potentially unwanted program (PUP) from WhenUClick[.]com and WhenUSave services.

The rule monitors HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations, specifically targeting requests to a path containing "/DataChunksGZ?update=" with parameters "ver=" and "svr=" in the URI. These patterns indicate the adware is sending data back to its command servers, likely user information or tracking data.

The detection focuses on the data retrieval mechanism used by this adware, specifically through the "DataChunksGZ" endpoint, which suggests compressed data transmission. The "GZ" suffix likely refers to gzip compression. The rule uses the "fast_pattern" modifier to optimize performance by prioritizing the "/DataChunksGZ?update=" pattern for initial packet inspection. The "nocase" modifiers ensure case-insensitive matching for all content patterns, improving detection regardless of capitalization variations.

WhenUClick/WhenUSave is classified as adware or potentially unwanted program that typically gets installed alongside other software. Once installed, it monitors user browsing habits and displays targeted advertisements. The data retrieval functionality detected by this rule represents the adware's communication with its backend servers, potentially exfiltrating user browsing data.

When this rule triggers, security teams should:
1. Identify and isolate affected systems
2. Remove the adware using standard removal tools or manual removal procedures
3. Scan for additional PUPs that may have been installed concurrently
4. Review network logs to determine the scope and duration of data exfiltration
5. Consider implementing additional HTTP filtering rules to block communication with these domains

This detection has medium severity as it indicates privacy concerns rather than critical system compromise. The rule references documentation about this adware at www[.]whenusearch[.]com and www[.]kephyr[.]com, which provide additional context about its behavior and identification methods.

2003408.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Zhelatin malware variant (also known as Storm Worm), specifically its check-in communication pattern. The rule monitors HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations, focusing on specific URL patterns that indicate command and control communication.

The rule identifies established HTTP connections from internal hosts to external servers containing the URI pattern "/adload.php?a1=" followed by multiple parameters ("a3=", "&a4=", "&a5=") in the URL. Additionally, the rule looks for requests that lack a User-Agent header but do contain a Host header, which is an unusual HTTP request configuration often indicative of malware communication rather than legitimate browser traffic.

Zhelatin is a trojan that creates botnets for malicious activities such as spam distribution and distributed denial-of-service attacks. This particular rule targets the check-in process where infected systems communicate with command and control servers to receive instructions.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further command and control communication
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the suspicious traffic for forensic analysis
3. Examine the host for additional indicators of compromise, focusing on persistence mechanisms
4. Check for lateral movement attempts from the compromised system
5. Block the destination IP at network boundaries to prevent further communication

The rule's "established,to_server" flow requirement ensures it only matches outbound HTTP requests from internal clients, reducing false positives. The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" confirms its focus on malware command and control traffic. With SID 2003408 and revision 7, this rule has been updated multiple times to maintain detection efficacy against this threat.

The detection of this traffic indicates an active Zhelatin infection within the monitored network, requiring immediate containment and eradication to prevent data exfiltration, system compromise, and potential botnet participation.

2003411.msg: ET EXPLOIT Solaris telnet USER environment vuln Attack inbound
2003411.et_name: Solaris telnet USER environment vuln Attack inbound
2003411.description:
This rule detects exploitation attempts targeting a vulnerability in the Solaris telnet daemon. The alert triggers when external hosts send specific byte sequences to port 23 (telnet) on internal networks.

The rule identifies a particular pattern in the telnet protocol where an attacker sends a specially crafted USER environment variable containing the bytes "|ff fa 27 00 00 55 53 45 52 01 2d 66|". This sequence corresponds to a telnet negotiation that includes the USER variable followed by the "-f" argument, which is the key component of the exploit.

CVE-2007-0882 describes an argument injection vulnerability in the Solaris telnet daemon (in.telnetd) in Solaris 10 and 11. The vulnerability allows remote attackers to bypass authentication by sending specially crafted "-f" sequences that the daemon misinterprets as valid requests for the login program to skip authentication. This can allow unauthorized access to certain accounts, particularly the bin account.

The rule uses the "established,to_server" flow directive to ensure it only triggers on established connections where data is flowing to the server. The "rawbytes" modifier ensures the pattern is matched against the raw packet data before any normalization.

This vulnerability is classified as "attempted-user" indicating it represents an attempt to gain user privileges on the target system. The references point to technical analyses of the vulnerability on riosec[.]com and the Internet Storm Center.

2003412.msg: ET EXPLOIT Solaris telnet USER environment vuln Attack outbound
2003412.et_name: Solaris telnet USER environment vuln Attack outbound
2003412.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: Solaris Telnet USER Environment Vulnerability

This rule detects outbound connection attempts from internal systems targeting external servers on port 23 (Telnet) that contain exploitation patterns for the Solaris telnet USER environment vulnerability (CVE-2007-0882). The alert triggers when a system on the internal network sends specific exploit content to an external Telnet server.

The rule identifies a particular byte sequence `|ff fa 27 00 00 55 53 45 52 01 2d 66|` which corresponds to a malicious Telnet negotiation sequence containing "USER" followed by the "-f" parameter. This specific pattern indicates an internal host is attempting to exploit the argument injection vulnerability in Solaris in.telnetd on external systems.

CVE-2007-0882 describes a vulnerability in the telnet daemon (in.telnetd) in Solaris 10 and 11 where the daemon incorrectly processes certain "-f" sequences as legitimate requests to bypass authentication. This allows attackers to gain unauthorized access to certain accounts (such as the bin account) without providing credentials.

The rule monitors established TCP connections flowing from internal to external networks (HOME_NET to EXTERNAL_NET), specifically targeting port 23. This directional flow indicates the rule is designed to detect when an internal system is attempting to exploit vulnerable Solaris systems located externally. 2003464.msg: ET ATTACK_RESPONSE Unusual FTP Server Banner (warFTPd)
2003464.description:
This Suricata rule (SID 2003464) detects unusual FTP server banners specifically identifying the presence of warFTPd software in FTP responses.

The rule triggers when an FTP server (port 21) sends a response to a client on the home network containing "220 " followed by "--warFTPd " within the first 40 bytes of the banner. The "220" code is the standard FTP response code for service ready. The "nocase" modifier ensures case-insensitive matching, capturing variations in capitalization of the banner text. The "depth:40" parameter optimizes performance by limiting content inspection to only the first 40 bytes where FTP banners typically appear.

WarFTPd is an older FTP server software with numerous critical vulnerabilities, including buffer overflows and authentication bypasses. The software has been discontinued since approximately 2007, making its presence on modern networks highly suspicious. While the rule classifies this as "trojan-activity," it's important to note this detection could represent either:
- A legitimate but severely outdated and vulnerable FTP server
- A deliberately deployed vulnerable server as part of an attacker's infrastructure
- A system compromised with backdoored FTP services

When this rule triggers, analysts should:
1. Verify if the warFTPd server is an authorized service in your environment
2. If unauthorized, isolate the host and investigate for additional indicators of compromise
3. If authorized, document the business justification and implement compensating controls such as network segmentation and strict access controls
4. Consider packet capture analysis to examine the full FTP session for exploitation attempts
5. Cross-reference the source IP with threat intelligence platforms to identify known malicious actors

The rule references www[.]warftp[.]org for additional context about the software.

This detection focuses on the network response phase of an attack, as indicated by the "ATTACK_RESPONSE" designation in the rule message and the flow direction (established, to_client).

- Malware that deploys freeFTPd as part of its infection chain

2003474.et_name: Asterisk Register with no URI or Version DOS Attempt
2003474.description:
This Suricata rule detects potential Denial of Service (DoS) attempts targeting Asterisk Voice over IP (VoIP) systems through malformed SIP REGISTER requests.

The rule monitors UDP traffic from external networks to port 5060 on the internal network, which is the standard port for Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) communications. It specifically looks for REGISTER requests that lack SIP version information, which violates RFC 3261 (SIP protocol specification).

The detection logic works by:
1. Identifying "REGISTER" followed by carriage return and line feed (0d 0a in hex) in the first 10 bytes, with case-insensitive matching ("nocase" parameter) to catch variations like "Register" or "REGISTER"
2. Confirming the absence of "SIP/" string that would normally indicate protocol version, using "distance:0" to ensure the search begins immediately after the first match position

This type of malformed request can trigger a DoS condition in vulnerable Asterisk PBX systems by causing the server to improperly process the request. Specifically, when the SIP version information is missing, the Asterisk server may allocate excessive resources attempting to parse the malformed header, enter an infinite loop, or crash while trying to process the request. This resource exhaustion leads to service unavailability for legitimate users.

The vulnerability exploits improper input validation in the SIP protocol implementation, where the server fails to properly validate mandatory header fields before processing. According to RFC 3261, all SIP messages must contain a valid version identifier, and the absence of this field should trigger immediate rejection of the request.

The rule references a security advisory from musecurity[.]com (MU-200703-01) that documents this vulnerability, indicating this is a known issue affecting Asterisk VoIP systems.

Organizations running Asterisk or other SIP-based VoIP infrastructure should monitor for these alerts as they indicate potential targeted attacks against their communication systems. Proper patching and SIP protocol validation are essential mitigations for this vulnerability.

5. Consider implementing application allowlisting to prevent similar unwanted software installations

- Classified as "bad-unknown" indicating suspicious but not definitively categorized traffic

This detection is significant because outdated or simplified User-Agent strings are frequently used by malware authors to avoid implementing full browser emulation while still attempting to appear as legitimate web traffic. The rule helps identify potential command and control communications, data exfiltration attempts, or reconnaissance activities using simplified HTTP clients.

As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2003505.msg: ET ADWARE_PUP Toplist.cz Related Spyware Checkin
2003505.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with Toplist.cz spyware activity. The alert triggers when an HTTP request is sent from an internal network to an external destination with a specific user agent pattern.

The rule specifically looks for HTTP requests with user agent strings that begin with "BWL" followed by either " Toplist" or a digit and "_UPDATE". This pattern matching is accomplished through the combination of content and pcre (Perl Compatible Regular Expression) matching. The "startswith" modifier ensures the detection only matches when "BWL" appears at the beginning of the user agent string, reducing false positives.

The detection focuses on established TCP connections flowing from internal clients to external servers, which is typical of the communication behavior of adware/potentially unwanted programs (PUP) related to Toplist.cz. This appears to be a traffic ranking or analytics service that may have spyware capabilities. The "checkin" reference in the rule message suggests this is detecting periodic communication from infected systems to command and control servers.

The rule's classification as "pup-activity" indicates this is considered potentially unwanted program behavior rather than a critical security threat. However, such spyware can collect user information, browsing habits, and potentially other sensitive data without proper user consent.

When this alert triggers, security analysts should:
1. Identify and isolate affected systems for further investigation
2. Examine HTTP traffic logs to determine what data may have been transmitted
3. Scan the affected systems for additional adware/PUP components
4. Consider implementing HTTP user agent filtering at the network perimeter to block these specific patterns
5. Document affected assets and add them to a remediation queue for adware removal

This detection is particularly important for environments with compliance requirements regarding user privacy and data protection.

rule_metadata.affected_product: Wordpress, affected_product Wordpress_Plugins, attack_target Web_Server, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Datacenter, signature_severity Major, tag Wordpress, updated_at 2019_08_22

2003508.et_name: Wordpress wp-login.php redirect_to credentials stealing attempt
2003508.description:
WordPress is a free and open-source content management system (CMS) based on PHP and MySQL. Features include a plugin architecture and a template system. WordPress was used by more than 26.4% of the top 10 million websites as of April 2016. WordPress is the most popular blogging system in use on the Web, at more than 60 million websites.

Wordpress vulnerabilities can be with the platform itself, or more commonly, with the plugins and themes. Vulnerabilities in Wordpress itself have been automatically patched since version 3.7 and since that time have become much less common, and vulnerable installations are quickly patched. Plugins are frequently vulnerable and in June 2013, it was found that some of the 50 most downloaded WordPress plugins were vulnerable to common Web attacks such as SQL injection and XSS. A separate inspection of the top-10 e-commerce plugins showed that 7 of them were vulnerable.

After a successful compromise of a site running a vulnerable plugin or theme, attackers often install a backdoor and then use the web server for:

hosting malware downloads
hosting CnC and malware control panels
hosting phish kits
black hat SEO and affiliate redirects
hactivism/defacement

A common step of investigating a WordPress event is to examine the “last modified” date of files and directories within the root of the WordPress installation. Any modified dates near the date of the attack are clear indicators of compromise and warrant further investigation. Also examining your server logs would typically reveal if a non-file modifying attack was successful.

This rule classification is disabled by default, and can be enabled by people wanting to detect attacks against a web application.

2003513.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic with a suspicious User-Agent string containing a specific typo in "Mozilla" where the second letter is capitalized incorrectly as "MOzilla/4.0".

The rule targets outbound HTTP connections from internal networks to external destinations, specifically looking for the pattern "MOzilla/" at the beginning of the User-Agent header. The unusual capitalization pattern (with an uppercase 'O') is not consistent with legitimate Mozilla User-Agent strings, which typically follow standard capitalization formats.

This type of User-Agent manipulation is a common technique used by malware to appear legitimate while containing subtle differences that can help evade detection. Malware authors often introduce minor variations in User-Agent strings to bypass signature-based detection while still attempting to blend in with normal traffic.

The rule classifies this activity as "trojan-activity," indicating that this User-Agent anomaly is associated with trojan malware communications. The specific pattern may be used by malware command and control communications or data exfiltration attempts that try to disguise themselves as regular web browsing.

The detection is significant because User-Agent anomalies are valuable indicators of compromise, especially when they contain subtle modifications to common strings that might otherwise go unnoticed in large volumes of network traffic.

rule_metadata.affected_product: Web_Server_Applications, attack_target Web_Server, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Datacenter, signature_severity Major, tag SQL_Injection, updated_at 2019_08_22, mitre_tactic_id TA0001, mitre_tactic_name Initial_Access, mitre_technique_id T1190, mitre_technique_name Exploit_Public_Facing_Application

2003516.et_name: Xoops Articles modules print.php SQL injection attempt
2003516.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2003517.msg: ET WEB_SPECIFIC_APPS iPhotoAlbum header.php remote file include

rule_metadata.affected_product: Any, attack_target Server, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Datacenter, signature_severity Major, tag Remote_File_Include, updated_at 2019_08_22, mitre_tactic_id TA0001, mitre_tactic_name Initial_Access, mitre_technique_id T1190, mitre_technique_name Exploit_Public_Facing_Application

2003517.description:
Remote File Include (RFI) is a technique used to exploit vulnerable "dynamic file include" mechanisms in web applications. When web applications take user input (URL, parameter value, etc.) and pass them into file include commands, the web application might be tricked into including remote files with malicious code. File inclusion is typically used for packaging common code into separate files that are later referenced by main application modules. When a web application references an include file, the code in this file may be executed implicitly or explicitly by calling specific procedures. If the choice of module to load is based on elements from the HTTP request, the web application might be vulnerable to RFI.

PHP is particularly vulnerable to file include attacks due to the extensive use of "file includes" in PHP and due to default server configurations that increase susceptibility to a file include attack. Although most examples point to vulnerable PHP scripts, we should keep in mind that it is also common in other technologies such as JSP, ASP and others.

It is common for attackers to scan for LFI vulnerabilities against hundreds or thousands of servers and launch further, more sophisticated attacks should a server respond in a way that reveals it is vulnerable. You may see hundreds of these alerts in a short period of time indicating you are the target of a scanning campaign, all of which may be FPs. If you see a HTTP 200 response in the web server log files for the request generating the alert, you’ll want to investigate to determine if the attack was successful. Typically, after a successful attack, attackers will wget a trojan from a third party site and execute it, so that the attacker maintains control even if the vulnerable software is patched..

This rule classification is disabled by default, and can be enabled by people wanting to detect attacks against web applications.

2003518.et_name: Computer Associates Brightstor ARCServe Backup Mediasvr.exe Remote Exploit
2003518.description:
This rule detects exploitation attempts targeting Computer Associates Brightstor ARCServe Backup software, specifically the Mediasvr.exe component. The rule monitors TCP traffic from external networks to internal networks on high ports (1024-65535).

The detection focuses on specific byte sequences in established connections to server ports. The rule looks for the hex pattern "|00 06 09 7e|" at offset 16, followed by another specific hex pattern "|00 00 00 bf 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00|" within a certain distance. These patterns likely represent malicious payload components used to exploit a vulnerability in the ARCServe Backup software.

This rule identifies attempts to gain administrative access to systems running the vulnerable Brightstor ARCServe Backup software. The "classtype:attempted-admin" indicates attackers are trying to obtain administrative privileges through this exploit. The reference to milw0rm exploit ID 3604 suggests this is a documented vulnerability with a published exploit.

The significance of this threat is high as successful exploitation would grant attackers administrative access to backup systems, potentially compromising sensitive data or using the backup server as a pivot point for further network intrusion.

2003525.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic from internal networks to external servers associated with adware/potentially unwanted program (PUP) activity from Supergames on aavalue[.]com domains.

The rule specifically monitors for HTTP requests to the path "/toolbars/msg/msg_serverside.xml" where the host contains "aavalue[.]com". This combination indicates communication with a known adware/spyware service.

The detection focuses on the EZ-Tracks Toolbar, which is classified as potentially unwanted program (PUP) activity. This toolbar is known to monitor user browsing habits and may collect personal information without adequate user consent. The rule references Sunbelt Software research documenting this threat.

The rule's classification as "pup-activity" confirms this is tracking software that may have been bundled with other applications. Such toolbars often modify browser settings, display unwanted advertisements, and transmit user data to third parties.

The significance of this detection is that it identifies software that, while not necessarily malicious like traditional malware, operates in ways that compromise user privacy and system performance. These applications typically enter systems through software bundles where users may not realize additional components are being installed alongside desired software.

Technical indicators in this rule include the specific HTTP path being requested and the domain pattern, which together form a reliable signature for identifying this particular adware variant's communication.

2003530.msg: ET HUNTING Suspicious Mozilla User-Agent Separator - likely Fake (Mozilla/4.0+(compatible +MSIE+)

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, confidence Medium, signature_severity Unknown, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2020_10_16

2003530.et_name: Suspicious Mozilla User-Agent Separator - likely Fake (Mozilla/4.0+(compatible +MSIE+)
2003530.description:
This rule detects suspicious HTTP traffic with an abnormal User-Agent string that attempts to mimic legitimate Microsoft Internet Explorer traffic but contains formatting anomalies.

The rule specifically targets outbound connections from internal networks to external destinations where the HTTP User-Agent header begins with "Mozilla/4.0+(compatible|3b|+MSIE+/" - a malformed version of the standard MSIE User-Agent string. Legitimate IE User-Agent strings follow a specific format with proper spacing and semicolon placement, while this variant contains unusual plus signs between components and uses a hex-encoded semicolon (|3b|) rather than a standard semicolon character.

This type of User-Agent manipulation is a common technique employed by malware, particularly trojans, to disguise malicious HTTP traffic as legitimate browser requests. The unusual formatting likely represents an attempt by malware authors to evade simple signature-based detection while maintaining enough similarity to legitimate traffic to avoid immediate suspicion.

The rule employs the "startswith" modifier to match only User-Agent headers that begin with the specified pattern, and uses "fast_pattern" optimization to improve performance by prioritizing the most distinctive part of the pattern during initial packet inspection. The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this traffic pattern is associated with trojan malware communication. The high revision number (18) suggests this signature has been refined multiple times to improve detection accuracy while reducing false positives.

Network defenders should investigate any triggers of this rule as they likely indicate compromised hosts attempting command and control communication or data exfiltration using deliberately malformed headers to evade detection.

2003534.msg: ET DELETED Weatherbug Vista Gadget Activity
2003534.description:
This Suricata rule detects network traffic associated with the Weatherbug Vista Gadget application. The rule monitors HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations, specifically looking for established connections where the client is sending requests containing "/Command/VistaGadget_v" in the URI, followed by parameters "UserId=" and "&AppVersion=".

The rule is classified as "trojan-activity," suggesting this legitimate application's communication pattern has been observed in malicious contexts. While the Weatherbug Vista Gadget was a legitimate desktop widget for Windows Vista that provided weather information, threat actors have historically repurposed or mimicked legitimate application traffic for malicious purposes, particularly for data exfiltration or command and control communications.

The specific pattern being detected - the transmission of user identification and version information to external servers - could indicate potential user tracking, unauthorized data collection, or compromised installations of the application. The "established,to_server" flow specification ensures the rule only triggers on active connections initiated from internal clients, reducing false positives from response traffic.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Verify if the Weatherbug Vista Gadget is an approved application in your environment
2. Examine the full HTTP request to identify the specific external domains being contacted
3. Investigate the affected internal host for signs of compromise or unauthorized software
4. Consider that since Windows Vista and its gadget platform are deprecated technologies, any such traffic in modern environments warrants additional scrutiny

The "DELETED" notation in the message indicates this rule has been deprecated from active use in more recent ruleset versions, likely due to the discontinuation of the Vista Gadget platform by Microsoft. However, detection remains valuable in environments where legacy systems may still be in use or where threat actors might leverage outdated application protocols to evade detection.

2003535.msg: ET ATTACK_RESPONSE r57 phpshell footer detected
2003535.description:
This rule detects the presence of r57 PHP shell in HTTP responses from web servers. The r57 shell is a malicious web backdoor that provides attackers with remote command execution capabilities on compromised web servers.

The rule specifically looks for the distinctive footer text "r57shell - http-shell by RST/GHC" in HTTP responses from servers to external clients. This string is a signature component of the r57 PHP shell that appears in its interface.

When triggered, this rule indicates that a compromised web server is hosting the r57 backdoor and is actively serving its interface to remote users. The backdoor allows attackers to:

- Execute system commands
- Browse the file system
- Upload additional malicious files
- Access database credentials
- Establish persistence on the compromised server

The rule is classified as "web-application-activity" which indicates suspicious behavior related to web applications. The flow direction "established,to_client" confirms this is detecting the backdoor being served to clients rather than an attempted upload.

The presence of r57 on a server typically indicates a successful compromise, as these shells are not part of legitimate web applications and are specifically designed for unauthorized access and control.

2003536.msg: ET ATTACK_RESPONSE r57 phpshell source being uploaded
2003536.description:
This rule detects attempts to upload the r57 PHP shell to web servers. The r57 shell is a widely known web backdoor that provides attackers with remote access and control capabilities over compromised web servers.

The rule specifically looks for HTTP traffic from external networks to HTTP servers where the HTTP request body contains two distinctive signatures associated with r57: "/*  (c)oded by 1dt.w0lf" and "/*  RST/GHC http". These strings are part of the source code comments in the r57 shell and serve as reliable indicators of the malicious code. The "fast_pattern" modifier optimizes detection performance by prioritizing the first content match, while the "distance:0" parameter ensures the second signature immediately follows the first one in the HTTP payload.

When deployed, the r57 PHP shell enables attackers to execute arbitrary commands, browse the file system, modify files, and potentially escalate privileges on the compromised server. This backdoor provides comprehensive server management capabilities to unauthorized users, making it a severe security threat.

Upon detection, security teams should immediately:
1. Block the source IP address at the network perimeter
2. Isolate the targeted web server for forensic analysis
3. Examine web server logs to identify successful uploads and potential execution
4. Scan the web directories for r57 shell variants (common filenames include r57.php, shell.php, or randomly generated names)
5. Review authentication logs for compromised credentials that may have facilitated the upload

The rule is classified as "web-application-activity" which indicates it's monitoring for suspicious web application behavior. The reference URL points to documentation about this threat at PestPatrol's spyware center.

Detection of r57 shell uploads indicates an active attempt to compromise web server security, typically following successful exploitation of vulnerabilities in web applications, content management systems, or through compromised credentials.

2003537.msg: ET MALWARE Trojan.Duntek establishing remote connection
2003537.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Trojan.Duntek malware establishing remote connections to command and control servers.

The rule monitors HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations, specifically looking for HTTP requests containing the URI pattern "rfe.php?" followed by parameters including "cmp=dun_tekfirst" and "guid=". These patterns are characteristic of the Trojan.Duntek malware's communication protocol.

The detection focuses on the initial connection phase when the malware attempts to communicate with its remote controller. The "fast_pattern" modifier indicates that "cmp=dun_tekfirst" is an efficient pattern to prioritize during packet inspection.

Trojan.Duntek is a malicious program that enables unauthorized remote access to infected systems. Once established, this connection allows attackers to:
- Extract sensitive information from compromised systems
- Download additional malicious payloads
- Execute commands remotely
- Maintain persistent access to the victim's network

The rule references Symantec's security documentation about this threat, indicating it has been formally analyzed and documented by security researchers. The classification as "trojan-activity" confirms its malicious nature.

This detection is significant as remote access trojans represent a serious security risk that can lead to data exfiltration, system compromise, and potential lateral movement within networks.

2003538.msg: ET MALWARE Klom.A Connecting to Controller

This detection is significant because it identifies active command and control communications from an infected system, indicating a successful compromise. The "trojan-activity" classification highlights that this is malicious software designed to provide unauthorized access to the affected system.

2003541.msg: ET ADWARE_PUP Bravesentry.com Fake Antispyware Updating
2003541.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: ET ADWARE_PUP Bravesentry.com Fake Antispyware

This rule detects network traffic associated with Bravesentry.com, a known fake antispyware application attempting to communicate with its command and control servers.

The rule specifically monitors HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations, focusing on update requests with a distinctive pattern. It triggers when traffic matches update.php requests containing specific parameters ("v=", "&d=", and "&vs=") to domains ending with ".bravesentry[.]com".

The detection logic includes:
- Established HTTP connections from internal to external networks
- URI path containing "/update.php?v=" followed by parameters "&d=" and "&vs="
- Host header containing ".bravesentry[.]com"
- Absence of a User-Agent header in the request

Bravesentry is classified as Potentially Unwanted Program (PUP) that masquerades as legitimate security software. This fake antispyware typically:
- Displays false security alerts to deceive users
- Attempts to convince users to purchase "full versions" to remove non-existent threats
- Periodically connects to its servers for updates or to report installation status

The rule's classification as "pup-activity" confirms its categorization as potentially unwanted software rather than a more severe threat like malware. The references to Sunbelt Software research provide additional context about this specific threat.

This detection is important as fake security applications like Bravesentry can lead to financial fraud through unnecessary purchases and may introduce additional security risks to affected systems.

2003542.msg: ET DELETED Bravesentry.com/Protectwin.com Fake Antispyware Reporting

These applications typically masquerade as legitimate security tools but actually perform malicious activities. The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this is malware designed to appear legitimate while performing unauthorized actions. The references to Sunbelt Software research confirms this is a known threat that has been documented by security researchers.

The detection is significant as fake security applications represent a common social engineering tactic that preys on users' security concerns to distribute malware or perpetrate financial fraud through scare tactics and deception.

2003544.msg: ET ADWARE_PUP Winfixmaster.com Fake Anti-Spyware User-Agent (WinFixMaster)

rule_metadata.attack_target: Client_Endpoint, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Perimeter, confidence High, signature_severity Minor, tag Spyware_User_Agent, updated_at 2020_10_19

2003544.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2003549.msg: ET MALWARE Bandook v1.2 Initial Connection and Report
2003549.et_name: Bandook v1.2 Initial Connection and Report
2003549.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: Bandook v1.2 Trojan Detection

This rule detects network traffic associated with the Bandook v1.2 remote access trojan (RAT) during its initial connection and reporting phase. The rule specifically monitors established TCP connections from internal networks to external destinations on high ports (1024-65535).

The detection focuses on identifying a specific communication pattern where the malware sends a message containing the string "&first& # " followed by a pattern matching "# [numbers]d [numbers]dh [numbers]m # " - likely representing a formatted timestamp or system information being exfiltrated during the initial check-in process.

The rule implements flowbit tracking to prevent repeated alerts for the same Bandook session by setting and checking the "BE.Bandook1.2" flowbit. This helps reduce alert fatigue while maintaining detection capabilities.

Bandook is a remote access trojan that provides attackers with comprehensive control over infected systems. This particular rule targets the initial command and control (C2) communication when the malware first reports to its controller. The detection of this traffic indicates an active Bandook infection within the network, which could lead to data theft, surveillance, or further system compromise.

The rule references documentation from www[.]nuclearwintercrew[.]com and research[.]sunbelt-software[.]com, which provide additional context about this threat. The classification as "trojan-activity" correctly identifies this as malicious software designed to provide unauthorized access to infected systems.

Network defenders should prioritize investigation of any alerts triggered by this rule, as they indicate active malware communication from compromised internal systems.

2003550.msg: ET MALWARE Bandook v1.2 Get Processes

2003550.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with Bandook v1.2 remote access trojan (RAT) when it attempts to enumerate running processes on an infected system.

The rule specifically identifies TCP traffic from any port on the internal network to high ports (1024-65535) on external networks. It triggers when a previously identified Bandook 1.2 session (tracked via the flowbit "BE.Bandook1.2") sends an 8-byte command with the specific hex pattern "|99 9b 86 8a 85 80 9a 9d|", which corresponds to the "Get Processes" command in the Bandook RAT protocol.

Bandook is a full-featured RAT that provides attackers with remote control capabilities over infected systems. This particular alert identifies when the malware is actively querying the victim's running processes, likely for reconnaissance purposes. Process enumeration is a common technique used by attackers to understand what software is running on a compromised system, identify security tools, and determine next steps in their attack chain.

The rule references documentation from nuclearwintercrew[.]com and research.sunbelt-software[.]com, which contain additional information about this threat. The rule classifies this activity as "trojan-activity" with SID 2003550.

2003551.msg: ET MALWARE Bandook v1.2 Kill Process Command
2003551.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Bandook v1.2 remote access trojan (RAT) when it sends kill process commands to a remote server.

The rule specifically monitors outbound TCP traffic from internal networks to external destinations on high ports (1024-65535). It triggers when a previously identified Bandook 1.2 session (tracked via flowbits:isset,BE.Bandook1.2) sends a packet containing the string "kill3d" at the beginning of the payload (offset:0; depth:6) with a size greater than 8 bytes. The flow:established,to_server parameter ensures the alert only triggers on established TCP connections originating from the infected host to the command and control server.

Bandook is a RAT that provides attackers with remote control capabilities over infected systems. This particular rule identifies when the malware is sending commands to terminate processes on the victim machine, which is a common technique used by malware to:
- Disable security software
- Terminate competing malware
- Stop processes that might interfere with its operation
- Hide its activities from the user

The rule references documentation from nuclearwintercrew[.]com and sunbelt-software[.]com/threatdisplay.aspx, which contain additional information about this threat. The classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this is malicious software designed to provide unauthorized access to the infected system.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Immediately isolate the affected system to prevent further command execution
2. Capture and preserve memory dumps and full packet captures for forensic analysis
3. Identify which processes were terminated by examining process logs and system event logs
4. Investigate lateral movement by checking for similar traffic patterns from other internal hosts
5. Perform endpoint scanning to identify the full extent of the Bandook RAT infection
6. Check for data exfiltration evidence, as process termination often precedes information theft

The detection of process termination commands is significant as it represents active malicious control over the compromised system rather than just the presence of the malware.

2003552.msg: ET MALWARE Bandook v1.2 Reporting Socks Proxy Active
