The rule triggers when traffic from an external network (ports 1024-65535) sends a message to any port on the home network containing the exact string "sockson" at the beginning of a 7-byte packet. Additionally, the rule requires that a previous detection has already set the "BE.Bandook1.2" flowbit, indicating this is part of an established Bandook malware communication sequence.

Bandook is a remote access trojan (RAT) that provides attackers with unauthorized control over infected systems. This specific alert identifies the moment when the malware notifies its command and control server that it has successfully established a SOCKS proxy on the victim's machine. SOCKS proxies can be used to route malicious traffic through the compromised host, potentially bypassing network security controls and hiding the true origin of subsequent attacks.

The rule references documentation from www[.]nuclearwintercrew[.]com and research[.]sunbelt-software[.]com, which contain additional information about this threat. The classification as "trojan-activity" confirms this is malicious software designed to provide unauthorized access to systems.

This detection is significant as it indicates an active Bandook infection where the attacker has progressed to establishing proxy capabilities, potentially preparing for further malicious activities through the compromised system.

When this alert triggers, security analysts should:
1. Immediately isolate the affected system from the network to prevent lateral movement
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Identify the source IP address communicating with the infected host and block it at the firewall/IPS
4. Scan the affected system for additional Bandook artifacts, focusing on persistence mechanisms
5. Check for evidence of data exfiltration or additional malware deployment
6. Review network logs to identify any suspicious outbound connections that may have been routed through the SOCKS proxy

The rule triggers when an HTTP request from any internal network host to an external destination contains the string "DIALER" at the beginning of the user agent field. The rule employs the "startswith" modifier to specifically match only when "DIALER" appears at the beginning of the user agent string, and uses the "nocase" modifier to make the detection case-insensitive, capturing variations like "Dialer", "DIALER", or "dialer".

The rule implements a threshold mechanism that limits alerts to 3 occurrences within a 300-second (5-minute) window per source IP address, preventing alert flooding while still capturing the behavior.

Dialer-type applications historically have been associated with premium-rate phone number connections, often without clear user consent. In modern contexts, applications using this user agent may be attempting to establish connections to advertising networks, tracking services, or command and control infrastructure.

The classification as "pup-activity" indicates this is considered lower severity than malware but still represents potentially unwanted software operating on the network. Detection of this traffic pattern may indicate compromised or unauthorized software running on internal systems.

2003569.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2003578.description:

The rule uses http.header_names with to_lowercase modifier to convert all header field names to lowercase before checking for the absence of a referer field ("|0d 0a|referer|0d 0a|"), which is characteristic of this particular data collection behavior.

This type of adware/PUP activity represents a privacy concern as it may lead to unauthorized data collection and potential information leakage. The rule is classified as "pup-activity" which confirms its categorization as potentially unwanted program behavior rather than a critical security threat.

When this rule triggers, analysts should:

2. Check browser extensions and installed programs for unauthorized Baidu components
3. Examine HTTP traffic patterns to determine what user data may have been transmitted
4. Consider implementing content filtering to block communication with these specific URI patterns
5. Remove the unwanted software using standard remediation procedures for PUPs

2003669.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: TopTree Remote File Inclusion Detection

This rule detects attempts to exploit a remote file inclusion vulnerability in the TopTree BBS application. The rule specifically monitors HTTP traffic from external networks to HTTP servers, focusing on requests targeting the tpl_message.php file with a malicious right_file parameter.

The rule identifies requests containing "/templates/default/tpl_message.php?" in the URI followed by "right_file=" parameter that includes a protocol handler (http://, https://, ftp://, ftps://, or php://). This pattern indicates an attempt to include remote files through the vulnerable parameter.

CVE-2007-2544 describes a PHP remote file inclusion vulnerability in templates/default/tpl_message.php in PHP TopTree BBS 2.0.1a and earlier. This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary PHP code by supplying a malicious URL in the right_file parameter.

Remote file inclusion vulnerabilities are particularly dangerous as they can lead to complete server compromise. An attacker can use this vulnerability to execute arbitrary code on the affected server with the privileges of the web server process. This could result in unauthorized access to sensitive data, installation of backdoors, or use of the compromised server as a pivot point for further attacks.

The rule references exploit details available at milw0rm[.]com/exploits/3854, indicating this is a well-documented vulnerability with publicly available exploit code.

2003670.msg: ET WEB_SPECIFIC_APPS Workbench Survival Guide Remote Inclusion Attempt -- headerfile.php path
2003670.et_name: Workbench Survival Guide Remote Inclusion Attempt -- headerfile.php path
2003670.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: Workbench Survival Guide Remote File Inclusion Detection

This rule detects attempts to exploit a remote file inclusion vulnerability in the Workbench Survival Guide application, specifically targeting the headerfile.php component.

The rule triggers when external network traffic attempts to access HTTP servers with specific malicious patterns in the URI. It looks for requests containing "/header.php?" followed by "path=" parameter that includes a protocol specification (http://, https://, ftp://, ftps://, or php://). This pattern is characteristic of remote file inclusion (RFI) attacks.

The vulnerability (CVE-2007-2542) affects Workbench Survival Guide version 0.11, where the header.php script fails to properly validate the "path" parameter. Attackers can exploit this by supplying a URL pointing to malicious PHP code, which the vulnerable application will then include and execute on the server.

When successful, this attack allows threat actors to execute arbitrary PHP code on the target server, potentially leading to complete server compromise. The attacker could gain unauthorized access to sensitive data, install backdoors, or use the compromised server as a launching point for further attacks.

The rule uses fast pattern matching for efficiency and case-insensitive matching to catch evasion attempts. The PCRE regex specifically identifies the protocol handlers that could be used in the attack.

## Response Actions:
1. Immediately block the source IP address at the network perimeter
2. Examine web server logs to identify if the attack was successful
3. Check for unauthorized file creation or modification in web directories
4. Scan the server for potential backdoors or webshells
5. Apply input validation patches to the Workbench Survival Guide application

## Mitigation Strategies:
1. Update Workbench Survival Guide to the latest version
2. Implement proper input validation for all user-supplied parameters
3. Configure web application firewalls to block requests containing protocol handlers in parameters
4. Apply the principle of least privilege to web server processes
5. Consider implementing virtual patching if updates cannot be applied immediately

Note: There is a discrepancy in the rule where the message references "headerfile.php" while the detection pattern looks for "header.php?" in the URI. When investigating alerts from this rule, examine traffic for both filename variations.

2003685.description:
WordPress is a free and open-source content management system (CMS) based on PHP and MySQL. Features include a plugin architecture and a template system. WordPress was used by more than 26.4% of the top 10 million websites as of April 2016. WordPress is the most popular blogging system in use on the Web, at more than 60 million websites.

Wordpress vulnerabilities can be with the platform itself, or more commonly, with the plugins and themes. Vulnerabilities in Wordpress itself have been automatically patched since version 3.7 and since that time have become much less common, and vulnerable installations are quickly patched. Plugins are frequently vulnerable and in June 2013, it was found that some of the 50 most downloaded WordPress plugins were vulnerable to common Web attacks such as SQL injection and XSS. A separate inspection of the top-10 e-commerce plugins showed that 7 of them were vulnerable.

After a successful compromise of a site running a vulnerable plugin or theme, attackers often install a backdoor and then use the web server for:

hosting malware downloads
hosting CnC and malware control panels
hosting phish kits
black hat SEO and affiliate redirects
hactivism/defacement

A common step of investigating a WordPress event is to examine the “last modified” date of files and directories within the root of the WordPress installation. Any modified dates near the date of the attack are clear indicators of compromise and warrant further investigation. Also examining your server logs would typically reveal if a non-file modifying attack was successful.

This rule classification is disabled by default, and can be enabled by people wanting to detect attacks against a web application.

2003749.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2003752.et_name: CreaScripts CreaDirectory SQL Injection Attempt -- error.asp id SELECT
2003752.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

2003823.et_name: Flashgames SQL Injection Attempt -- game.php lid SELECT
2003823.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2003864.description:
This rule detects outbound SMTP (email) traffic on port 587 originating from non-SMTP servers within the network and destined for external systems.

The rule triggers when a system that is not designated as an authorized mail server attempts to send email via port 587 (submission port) to an external destination. Specifically, it looks for the "mail from:" command in the SMTP conversation, indicating an email transmission attempt. The "nocase" modifier ensures detection regardless of letter case variations in the "mail from:" string, improving coverage against evasion techniques.

The rule only applies to established TCP connections ("flow:established"), meaning it focuses on active communication sessions rather than connection attempts, reducing false positives from scanning activity and ensuring the alert triggers only when actual SMTP commands are exchanged.

The detection focuses on potential unauthorized mail relay activity, which could indicate:
- Data exfiltration via email channels
- Compromised internal systems being used to send spam
- Malware with email propagation capabilities
- Unauthorized mail services running on non-mail systems

The rule implements a threshold limiting alerts to once per source IP address every 60 seconds to prevent alert flooding. It's classified as "misc-activity" which indicates suspicious but not necessarily malicious behavior requiring investigation.

This type of activity warrants attention as unauthorized mail relay attempts often indicate policy violations or security incidents. Legitimate email traffic should only originate from designated mail servers, making this pattern a potential indicator of compromise.

2003872.msg: ET WEB_SPECIFIC_APPS Redoable XSS Attempt -- searchloop.php s
2003872.description:
This rule detects attempts to exploit a cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the Redoable WordPress theme. The alert triggers when external traffic targets HTTP servers with a specific malicious request to the searchloop.php file.

The rule identifies traffic containing:
- Requests to "/wp-content/themes/redoable/searchloop.php?" 
- A parameter "s=" in the URL
- The string "script" in the request
- Content matching a regular expression that looks for JavaScript or VBScript tags with pattern "/<?(java|vb)?script>?.*<.+\/script>?/i", which detects various script tag formations including those with optional opening/closing brackets and different script types

The "flow:established,to_server" option ensures the rule only matches established connections from clients to servers, filtering out potential false positives from server responses or connection attempts.

This detection focuses on CVE-2007-2757, which documents XSS vulnerabilities in Redoable 1.2 WordPress theme. The vulnerability allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via the "s" parameter to searchloop.php or header.php files. By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers can execute malicious scripts in victims' browsers, potentially stealing session cookies, credentials, or performing actions on behalf of the victim.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Immediately investigate the HTTP request details, particularly the full content of the "s" parameter
2. Check if the targeted WordPress installation is using the vulnerable Redoable theme version
3. Block the source IP address if malicious intent is confirmed
4. Examine server logs for additional exploitation attempts from the same source
5. Verify if the attack was successful by checking for unexpected JavaScript execution or content modification

Mitigation steps include:
- Update the Redoable theme to a patched version or replace it with a secure alternative
- Implement input validation and output encoding on the affected PHP files
- Consider implementing a Web Application Firewall (WAF) to filter malicious script injection attempts
- Apply Content Security Policy (CSP) headers to restrict script execution sources

The rule is classified as a web-application-attack and includes references to the CVE and a SecurityFocus archive for additional context. The "fast_pattern" option optimizes detection performance by prioritizing the search for the URI path pattern.

2003885.description:
WordPress is a free and open-source content management system (CMS) based on PHP and MySQL. Features include a plugin architecture and a template system. WordPress was used by more than 26.4% of the top 10 million websites as of April 2016. WordPress is the most popular blogging system in use on the Web, at more than 60 million websites.

Wordpress vulnerabilities can be with the platform itself, or more commonly, with the plugins and themes. Vulnerabilities in Wordpress itself have been automatically patched since version 3.7 and since that time have become much less common, and vulnerable installations are quickly patched. Plugins are frequently vulnerable and in June 2013, it was found that some of the 50 most downloaded WordPress plugins were vulnerable to common Web attacks such as SQL injection and XSS. A separate inspection of the top-10 e-commerce plugins showed that 7 of them were vulnerable.

After a successful compromise of a site running a vulnerable plugin or theme, attackers often install a backdoor and then use the web server for:

hosting malware downloads
hosting CnC and malware control panels
hosting phish kits
black hat SEO and affiliate redirects
hactivism/defacement

A common step of investigating a WordPress event is to examine the “last modified” date of files and directories within the root of the WordPress installation. Any modified dates near the date of the attack are clear indicators of compromise and warrant further investigation. Also examining your server logs would typically reveal if a non-file modifying attack was successful.

This rule classification is disabled by default, and can be enabled by people wanting to detect attacks against a web application.

2003888.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: TutorialCMS XSS Detection

This rule detects cross-site scripting (XSS) attempts targeting the TutorialCMS application, specifically exploiting a vulnerability in the browseCat.php script through the catFile parameter.

The rule triggers when external network traffic attempts to inject JavaScript code into the catFile parameter of the browseCat.php script. It identifies HTTP requests containing "/browseCat.php?" followed by "catFile=" and "script" content, with additional pattern matching to detect various script injection techniques.

## Technical Details:

- **Target**: TutorialCMS (Photoshop Tutorials) web application
- **Vulnerability**: Cross-site scripting in browseCat.php via catFile parameter
- **Attack Vector**: HTTP requests with script injection in the catFile parameter
- **Detection Method**: Pattern matching for script tags and variants
- **PCRE Pattern**: `/<?(java|vb)?script>?.*<.+\/script>?/i` - Detects various script tag formats
- **CVE**: CVE-2007-2600
- **Classification**: web-application-attack

## CVE-2007-2600 Information:

This vulnerability affects TutorialCMS 1.00 and earlier versions. The application contains multiple XSS vulnerabilities allowing attackers to inject malicious web script or HTML through various parameters:
1. catFile parameter in browseCat.php and browseSubCat.php
2. id parameter in openTutorial.php, topFrame.php, and admin/editListing.php
3. search parameter in search.php

This rule specifically focuses on the catFile parameter exploitation vector in browseCat.php.

## Security Impact:

Successful exploitation could allow attackers to execute arbitrary JavaScript in victims' browsers, potentially leading to session hijacking, credential theft, or other client-side attacks against users of the vulnerable TutorialCMS installation.

# Suricata Rule Analysis: DVDdb XSS Vulnerability Detection

This rule detects attempts to exploit a cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the DVDdb application, specifically targeting the loan.php script through the movieid parameter.

The rule monitors HTTP traffic from external networks to HTTP servers, looking for specific patterns that indicate an XSS attack attempt against the DVDdb application. It triggers when an HTTP request contains "/loan.php?" followed by "movieid=" parameter and includes script tags that could be used to inject malicious JavaScript.

The detection logic employs multiple content matches and a regular expression (pcre) to identify script tag patterns characteristic of XSS attacks. The fast_pattern option optimizes performance by prioritizing the "/loan.php?" string during initial packet inspection.

This rule addresses CVE-2007-2499, which documents multiple XSS vulnerabilities in DVDdb 0.6 and earlier. These vulnerabilities allow remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via the movieid parameter to loan.php or the s parameter to listmovies.php. When successfully exploited, attackers can execute malicious scripts in victims' browsers, potentially leading to session hijacking, credential theft, or other client-side attacks.

The classification as "web-application-attack" indicates this is targeting a specific web application vulnerability rather than a general network-level threat.

2003921.msg: ET WEB_SPECIFIC_APPS DVDdb XSS Attempt -- listmovies.php s
2003921.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: DVDdb XSS Vulnerability Detection

This rule detects attempts to exploit a cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the DVDdb application's listmovies.php script. The rule specifically monitors HTTP traffic from external networks to HTTP servers, focusing on requests to the listmovies.php endpoint with a potentially malicious "s" parameter containing script tags.

The rule identifies exploitation attempts of CVE-2007-2499, which affects DVDdb version 0.6 and earlier. This vulnerability allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via the "s" parameter to listmovies.php (as well as via the movieid parameter to loan.php, though this specific rule only addresses the listmovies.php vector).

## Technical Details:

- The rule triggers on HTTP requests to "/listmovies.php?" containing both "s=" and "script" parameters
- Uses pattern matching to detect script tag injection patterns via PCRE regex: "/script>?.*<.+\/script>?/i"
- The "fast_pattern" option optimizes performance by prioritizing the "/listmovies.php?" content match
- The "nocase" modifier ensures case-insensitive matching for evasion attempts

XSS vulnerabilities in web applications like DVDdb can lead to session hijacking, credential theft, and client-side malware delivery. Successful exploitation could allow attackers to execute arbitrary JavaScript in victims' browsers, potentially leading to unauthorized access to the application and sensitive user data.

The rule is classified as a "web-application-attack" which appropriately categorizes this type of threat.

References:

2003922.msg: ET WEB_SPECIFIC_APPS Sendcard XSS Attempt -- sendcard.php form

# Suricata Rule Analysis: Sendcard XSS Detection

This rule detects attempts to exploit a cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the Sendcard application's sendcard.php script. The rule monitors HTTP traffic from external networks to HTTP servers, specifically targeting requests to the sendcard.php endpoint that contain potentially malicious script content in the "form" parameter.

The detection mechanism identifies requests containing "/sendcard.php?" in the URI, followed by a "form=" parameter that includes script tags. The rule uses pattern matching to identify various script tag formats (JavaScript or VBScript) through the PCRE regex: "/<?(java|vb)?script>?.*<.+\/script>?/i".

This rule addresses CVE-2007-2472, a documented XSS vulnerability in Sendcard 3.4.1 and earlier versions. Organizations running Sendcard applications should ensure they've updated to versions that patch this vulnerability, as XSS attacks can lead to significant security breaches including account compromise and data theft.

2003924.msg: ET SCAN WebHack Control Center User-Agent Inbound (WHCC/)

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, confidence High, signature_severity Major, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2024_03_12

2003924.description:
This rule detects inbound HTTP traffic containing the user-agent string "WHCC", which is associated with the WebHack Control Center tool. The rule triggers when an external host sends HTTP requests to internal networks with this specific user-agent signature, regardless of source or destination ports.

The WebHack Control Center is a remote access tool that can be used for unauthorized system access and control. When deployed maliciously, it allows attackers to manage compromised systems remotely through HTTP-based communications.

The detection focuses specifically on the HTTP user-agent field containing "WHCC" (case insensitive), which serves as a fingerprint for this tool's communication. The rule employs fast pattern matching on the "WHCC" string to optimize performance by quickly filtering relevant traffic before more intensive inspection occurs.

The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this is considered malicious software that provides unauthorized remote access capabilities. The flow directive ensures the rule only triggers on established connections flowing toward internal servers, which helps reduce false positives.

When this alert triggers, security analysts should:
1. Immediately isolate the affected internal host and investigate for compromise
2. Capture and analyze full packet captures of the communication
3. Examine the source IP address for additional malicious activity
4. Review HTTP logs for other suspicious requests from the same source
5. Check the affected internal system for signs of unauthorized access or persistence mechanisms
6. Block the source IP at network boundaries and implement additional monitoring

This detection is significant because it identifies potential unauthorized remote access attempts using a specific hacking tool. The presence of this user-agent in inbound traffic strongly suggests reconnaissance or active intrusion attempts against internal systems.

2003925.msg: ET USER_AGENTS WebHack Control Center User-Agent Outbound (WHCC/)

rule_metadata.attack_target: Client_Endpoint, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Perimeter, confidence High, signature_severity Minor, tag Spyware_User_Agent, updated_at 2020_10_19

2003926.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2003936.msg: ET MALWARE Bandok phoning home (xor by 0xe9 to decode)

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, confidence Medium, signature_severity Major, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2019_07_26

2003936.et_name: Bandok phoning home (xor by 0xe9 to decode)
2003936.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Bandok malware when it attempts to communicate with its command and control (C2) server.

The rule specifically monitors outbound TCP connections from internal networks to external destinations on high ports (1024-65535). It looks for a distinctive 8-byte hex pattern ("|CF 8F 80 9B 9A 9D CF 95|") at the beginning of packets with a relatively small payload size (less than 80 bytes).

The rule documentation indicates that the detected traffic is encoded using XOR with the key 0xE9, which is a common obfuscation technique used by malware to evade detection. This specific pattern represents the Bandok malware's "phone home" behavior, where infected systems attempt to establish communication with their control infrastructure.

Bandok is a trojan that has been associated with phishing campaigns, particularly those targeting financial institutions. The rule references include documentation from DShield and SecureWorks research about related phishing activities.

The small packet size combined with the specific binary pattern suggests this is detecting a beacon or initial check-in communication from the malware rather than large data exfiltration. This type of detection is critical as it can identify compromised systems in the early stages of an infection before significant damage occurs.

2003937.msg: ET MALWARE Bandook iwebho/BBB-phish trojan leaking user data
2003937.et_name: Bandook iwebho/BBB-phish trojan leaking user data
2003937.description:
This Suricata rule detects network traffic associated with the Bandook trojan, specifically a variant known as "iwebho/BBB-phish" that exfiltrates user data.

The rule monitors HTTP POST requests from internal networks to external destinations, focusing on data exfiltration patterns characteristic of this malware. It triggers when specific HTTP components match the Bandook communication pattern:

- HTTP POST requests with "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" content type of exactly 33 bytes, which is a distinctive characteristic of this malware variant
- Specific HTTP header structure with Content-Type, Host, and Content-Length headers in a particular order
- Request body containing the string "_VISITED_URL=" within the first 100 bytes (optimized as a fast_pattern for efficient matching)

This detection identifies the Bandook trojan's data leakage mechanism, where the malware collects browsing history and other user information before transmitting it to command and control servers. The trojan uses a specific HTTP POST format to transmit stolen data, making this pattern recognizable.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further data exfiltration
2. Capture full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Examine the HTTP POST data to identify what specific information has been compromised
4. Check browser history and system logs to determine the initial infection vector
5. Scan the system with updated anti-malware tools focusing on Bandook indicators
6. Review network logs to identify any additional systems communicating with the same external endpoints

The rule references research from SecureWorks documenting this threat, which is classified as trojan activity. The Bandook malware family has been used in targeted attacks and espionage campaigns, with this particular variant focusing on phishing operations to harvest user data.

The presence of "_VISITED_URL=" in the request body indicates the malware is specifically exfiltrating browsing history data from compromised systems, which represents a significant privacy and security breach for affected users.

2003939.msg: ET WEB_SPECIFIC_APPS Jetbox CMS SQL Injection Attempt -- main_page.php SELECT

rule_metadata.affected_product: Web_Server_Applications, attack_target Web_Server, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Datacenter, confidence Medium, signature_severity Major, tag SQL_Injection, updated_at 2024_03_11, mitre_tactic_id TA0001, mitre_tactic_name Initial_Access, mitre_technique_id T1190, mitre_technique_name Exploit_Public_Facing_Application

2003939.et_name: Jetbox CMS SQL Injection Attempt -- main_page.php SELECT
2003939.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2004011.et_name: WordPress SQL Injection Attempt -- admin-ajax.php cookie SELECT
2004011.description:
WordPress is a free and open-source content management system (CMS) based on PHP and MySQL. Features include a plugin architecture and a template system. WordPress was used by more than 26.4% of the top 10 million websites as of April 2016. WordPress is the most popular blogging system in use on the Web, at more than 60 million websites.

Wordpress vulnerabilities can be with the platform itself, or more commonly, with the plugins and themes. Vulnerabilities in Wordpress itself have been automatically patched since version 3.7 and since that time have become much less common, and vulnerable installations are quickly patched. Plugins are frequently vulnerable and in June 2013, it was found that some of the 50 most downloaded WordPress plugins were vulnerable to common Web attacks such as SQL injection and XSS. A separate inspection of the top-10 e-commerce plugins showed that 7 of them were vulnerable.

After a successful compromise of a site running a vulnerable plugin or theme, attackers often install a backdoor and then use the web server for:

hosting malware downloads
hosting CnC and malware control panels
hosting phish kits
black hat SEO and affiliate redirects
hactivism/defacement

A common step of investigating a WordPress event is to examine the “last modified” date of files and directories within the root of the WordPress installation. Any modified dates near the date of the attack are clear indicators of compromise and warrant further investigation. Also examining your server logs would typically reveal if a non-file modifying attack was successful.

This rule classification is disabled by default, and can be enabled by people wanting to detect attacks against a web application.

2004014.et_name: WordPress SQL Injection Attempt -- admin-ajax.php cookie DELETE
2004014.description:
WordPress is a free and open-source content management system (CMS) based on PHP and MySQL. Features include a plugin architecture and a template system. WordPress was used by more than 26.4% of the top 10 million websites as of April 2016. WordPress is the most popular blogging system in use on the Web, at more than 60 million websites.

Wordpress vulnerabilities can be with the platform itself, or more commonly, with the plugins and themes. Vulnerabilities in Wordpress itself have been automatically patched since version 3.7 and since that time have become much less common, and vulnerable installations are quickly patched. Plugins are frequently vulnerable and in June 2013, it was found that some of the 50 most downloaded WordPress plugins were vulnerable to common Web attacks such as SQL injection and XSS. A separate inspection of the top-10 e-commerce plugins showed that 7 of them were vulnerable.

After a successful compromise of a site running a vulnerable plugin or theme, attackers often install a backdoor and then use the web server for:

hosting malware downloads
hosting CnC and malware control panels
hosting phish kits
black hat SEO and affiliate redirects
hactivism/defacement

A common step of investigating a WordPress event is to examine the “last modified” date of files and directories within the root of the WordPress installation. Any modified dates near the date of the attack are clear indicators of compromise and warrant further investigation. Also examining your server logs would typically reveal if a non-file modifying attack was successful.

This rule classification is disabled by default, and can be enabled by people wanting to detect attacks against a web application.

2004022.et_name: AlstraSoft E-Friends SQL Injection Attempt -- index.php pack UPDATE
2004022.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2004114.msg: ET MALWARE Bancos User-Agent Detected vb wininet

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, malware_family Bancos, confidence High, signature_severity Major, tag Banking_Trojan, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2019_07_26

2004114.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with a banking Trojan (Bancos) based on its distinctive HTTP User-Agent string.

The rule triggers when any internal network host communicates with an external server using HTTP with the specific User-Agent string "vb wininet". This User-Agent is characteristic of the Bancos malware family, which primarily targets banking credentials.

The rule parameters indicate:
- Direction: Outbound traffic from internal networks to external destinations
- Protocol: HTTP
- Specific detection: User-Agent header containing "vb wininet" (case insensitive)
- Classification: Trojan activity
- Flow requirement: Established connection, traffic flowing to server

Bancos is a banking Trojan that typically steals financial credentials through techniques like form grabbing, keylogging, and screen capturing. The "vb wininet" User-Agent suggests the malware was likely developed using Visual Basic and utilizes the WinINet API for HTTP communications.

This detection is significant as banking Trojans directly target financial assets. When this rule triggers, it indicates a likely compromise where the infected system is attempting to communicate with command and control infrastructure using this distinctive User-Agent string.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

2004199.et_name: phpx SQL Injection Attempt -- news.php news_cat_id UPDATE
2004199.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2004237.et_name: Web Wiz Forums SQL Injection Attempt -- page.asp NewsID INSERT
2004237.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

2004300.et_name: Koan Software Mega Mall SQL Injection Attempt -- product_review.php so UPDATE
2004300.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.
