2005159.et_name: xNews SQL Injection Attempt -- xNews.php id UNION SELECT
2005159.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

rule_metadata.attack_target: Client_Endpoint, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Perimeter, confidence High, signature_severity Minor, tag Spyware_User_Agent, updated_at 2020_10_19

2005318.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

The rule specifically identifies POST requests to a specific URI pattern "/zuzu.php?&r=" which indicates a check-in or communication attempt from an infected system to a command and control server.

The rule targets outbound HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations, focusing on established connections where the traffic direction is from the client to the server. The flow:established,to_server condition ensures only complete, established TCP sessions are evaluated, reducing false positives and focusing on actual client-initiated communications. The detection leverages pattern matching against both the HTTP method (POST) and the specific URI path containing "zuzu.php?&r=", with the fast_pattern modifier applied to the URI pattern for optimized performance during rule processing.

This type of communication typically represents a data exfiltration channel or command retrieval mechanism used by adware or PUP software installed on the victim's system. The bizconcept[.]info domain appears to be associated with spyware that monitors user activity and potentially transmits collected information back to its operators.

The classification as "pup-activity" indicates this is considered a potentially unwanted program rather than a critical security threat, but such software often compromises user privacy by collecting browsing habits, search queries, or other personal information without proper consent. These programs may also degrade system performance, display unwanted advertisements, or facilitate further malicious activity.

1. Identify the affected system(s) and isolate them if multiple alerts are observed
2. Examine HTTP logs to determine what data may have been transmitted to bizconcept[.]info

4. Review browser extensions, recently installed applications, and system startup items

2005320.description:
Trojan User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Trojan User-Agent strings that are leveraged by compromised machines.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Trojan often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Trojan User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

2005324.et_name: bbPress SQL Injection Attempt -- formatting-functions.php SELECT
2005324.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2005334.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

2005627.et_name: Portix-PHP SQL Injection Attempt -- archive.php pid SELECT
2005627.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2005657.et_name: WordPress SQL Injection Attempt -- wp-trackback.php SELECT
2005657.description:
WordPress is a free and open-source content management system (CMS) based on PHP and MySQL. Features include a plugin architecture and a template system. WordPress was used by more than 26.4% of the top 10 million websites as of April 2016. WordPress is the most popular blogging system in use on the Web, at more than 60 million websites.

Wordpress vulnerabilities can be with the platform itself, or more commonly, with the plugins and themes. Vulnerabilities in Wordpress itself have been automatically patched since version 3.7 and since that time have become much less common, and vulnerable installations are quickly patched. Plugins are frequently vulnerable and in June 2013, it was found that some of the 50 most downloaded WordPress plugins were vulnerable to common Web attacks such as SQL injection and XSS. A separate inspection of the top-10 e-commerce plugins showed that 7 of them were vulnerable.

After a successful compromise of a site running a vulnerable plugin or theme, attackers often install a backdoor and then use the web server for:

hosting malware downloads
hosting CnC and malware control panels
hosting phish kits
black hat SEO and affiliate redirects
hactivism/defacement

A common step of investigating a WordPress event is to examine the “last modified” date of files and directories within the root of the WordPress installation. Any modified dates near the date of the attack are clear indicators of compromise and warrant further investigation. Also examining your server logs would typically reveal if a non-file modifying attack was successful.

This rule classification is disabled by default, and can be enabled by people wanting to detect attacks against a web application.

2005678.et_name: Nicola Asuni All In One Control Panel (AIOCP) SQL Injection Attempt -- cp_functions_downloads.php download_category DELETE
2005678.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

2005865.et_name: WordPress SQL Injection Attempt -- wp-trackback.php SELECT
2005865.description:
WordPress is a free and open-source content management system (CMS) based on PHP and MySQL. Features include a plugin architecture and a template system. WordPress was used by more than 26.4% of the top 10 million websites as of April 2016. WordPress is the most popular blogging system in use on the Web, at more than 60 million websites.

Wordpress vulnerabilities can be with the platform itself, or more commonly, with the plugins and themes. Vulnerabilities in Wordpress itself have been automatically patched since version 3.7 and since that time have become much less common, and vulnerable installations are quickly patched. Plugins are frequently vulnerable and in June 2013, it was found that some of the 50 most downloaded WordPress plugins were vulnerable to common Web attacks such as SQL injection and XSS. A separate inspection of the top-10 e-commerce plugins showed that 7 of them were vulnerable.

After a successful compromise of a site running a vulnerable plugin or theme, attackers often install a backdoor and then use the web server for:

hosting malware downloads
hosting CnC and malware control panels
hosting phish kits
black hat SEO and affiliate redirects
hactivism/defacement

A common step of investigating a WordPress event is to examine the “last modified” date of files and directories within the root of the WordPress installation. Any modified dates near the date of the attack are clear indicators of compromise and warrant further investigation. Also examining your server logs would typically reveal if a non-file modifying attack was successful.

This rule classification is disabled by default, and can be enabled by people wanting to detect attacks against a web application.

2005868.et_name: WordPress SQL Injection Attempt -- wp-trackback.php DELETE
2005868.description:
WordPress is a free and open-source content management system (CMS) based on PHP and MySQL. Features include a plugin architecture and a template system. WordPress was used by more than 26.4% of the top 10 million websites as of April 2016. WordPress is the most popular blogging system in use on the Web, at more than 60 million websites.

Wordpress vulnerabilities can be with the platform itself, or more commonly, with the plugins and themes. Vulnerabilities in Wordpress itself have been automatically patched since version 3.7 and since that time have become much less common, and vulnerable installations are quickly patched. Plugins are frequently vulnerable and in June 2013, it was found that some of the 50 most downloaded WordPress plugins were vulnerable to common Web attacks such as SQL injection and XSS. A separate inspection of the top-10 e-commerce plugins showed that 7 of them were vulnerable.

After a successful compromise of a site running a vulnerable plugin or theme, attackers often install a backdoor and then use the web server for:

hosting malware downloads
hosting CnC and malware control panels
hosting phish kits
black hat SEO and affiliate redirects
hactivism/defacement

A common step of investigating a WordPress event is to examine the “last modified” date of files and directories within the root of the WordPress installation. Any modified dates near the date of the attack are clear indicators of compromise and warrant further investigation. Also examining your server logs would typically reveal if a non-file modifying attack was successful.

This rule classification is disabled by default, and can be enabled by people wanting to detect attacks against a web application.

2005871.et_name: Simple Web Content Management System SQL Injection Attempt -- page.php id SELECT
2005871.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2006132.et_name: Softwebs Nepal Ananda Real Estate SQL Injection Attempt -- list.asp agent DELETE
2006132.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

2006357.msg: ET ADWARE_PUP User Agent (TEST) - Likely Webhancer Related Spyware

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, confidence Medium, signature_severity Minor, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2020_11_02

2006357.et_name: User Agent (TEST) - Likely Webhancer Related Spyware
2006357.description:
This rule detects potential adware/potentially unwanted program (PUP) activity related to Webhancer spyware. The rule triggers when an HTTP request is made from an internal network to an external destination with a user agent string that is exactly 4 bytes long and contains the string "TEST".

The rule specifically looks for:
- HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations
- Established connections flowing to the server
- A user agent string that is exactly 4 bytes in length containing "TEST"
- The destination host must not be "messagecenter.comodo[.]com" or "symantec[.]com" (legitimate security vendors)

Webhancer is known spyware that monitors user browsing habits and internet usage patterns. This particular rule appears to identify a specific variant or communication pattern used by Webhancer-related software. The unusual user agent string length (4 bytes) combined with the specific content "TEST" represents an atypical browser identification that legitimate applications would not typically use.

The rule's classification as "pup-activity" indicates this is considered potentially unwanted program behavior rather than a critical security threat, but still warrants monitoring as it could lead to privacy violations, data collection without proper consent, or system performance degradation.

rule_metadata.affected_product: Any, attack_target Client_Endpoint, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Perimeter, confidence High, signature_severity Minor, tag User_Agent, updated_at 2020_10_19

2006361.description:
Trojan User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Trojan User-Agent strings that are leveraged by compromised machines.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Trojan often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Trojan User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.
