The rule employs both "startswith" and "endswith" modifiers to ensure the user-agent string contains only "ld" with no additional characters, making it highly specific to this particular malicious behavior.

The rule is classified as "trojan-activity," indicating this traffic pattern is associated with trojan malware communication. This type of minimal user-agent is commonly employed by malware downloaders to fetch additional payloads or communicate with command and control servers while attempting to maintain a low profile.

Detection of this traffic pattern may indicate an infected system on the internal network attempting to communicate with external malicious infrastructure for command and control purposes or to download additional malicious components.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should immediately isolate the affected system and perform a full malware scan. Capture and analyze the complete network traffic from the affected host to identify additional indicators of compromise and potential command and control infrastructure. Examine the destination IP addresses and domains for reputation data and block them at the network perimeter. Collect and analyze system logs, running processes, and scheduled tasks on the affected system to identify persistence mechanisms. Consider implementing additional monitoring for similar minimal user-agent patterns across the network to detect potential variants.

2006395.msg: ET MALWARE Socks666 Connection Initial Packet
2006395.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Socks666 malware's initial connection attempt from an internal host to an external web server.

The rule triggers when a TCP packet with a specific 24-byte size is sent from any port on the internal network to HTTP ports on external networks. It specifically looks for the hexadecimal pattern "|9a 02 06 00|" at the beginning of the packet payload. The "established" flow option ensures that only traffic within established TCP sessions is evaluated, filtering out connection attempts and reducing false positives.

The rule employs flowbits to track the connection state, setting a "BS.BPcheckin" flag that can be used by other rules to identify related traffic patterns. The "flowbits:noalert" option prevents the flowbits mechanism from generating additional alerts when the flag is set, but the rule itself will still generate an alert when matched.

Classified as "trojan-activity," this rule identifies the initial communication attempt of the Socks666 malware, which likely operates as a SOCKS proxy for command and control purposes. The malware appears to use a distinctive binary signature in its initial handshake packet, allowing for detection of infected hosts attempting to establish connections with command and control infrastructure.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected host and investigate for additional indicators of compromise
2. Examine the full session data to identify potential command and control servers
3. Review network logs for other connections from the same host to identify potential lateral movement
4. Collect and analyze memory dumps or disk images from the affected system to identify the malware variant
5. Block the destination IP at network boundaries to prevent further communication

This detection is significant as SOCKS-based trojans can facilitate unauthorized access, data exfiltration, and proxy connections through compromised systems, potentially enabling threat actors to maintain persistent access while evading detection.

2006396.msg: ET MALWARE Socks666 Connect Command Packet
2006396.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Socks666 malware's command and control communications.

The rule specifically identifies TCP traffic from external servers on HTTP ports to internal network hosts, focusing on the "Connect Command Packet" from the Socks666 malware. The detection occurs when a 10-byte packet containing the specific hex pattern "|9a 02 07 00|" at the beginning of the packet is observed.

The rule employs flowbit tracking to ensure detection accuracy, requiring that the "BS.BPcheckin" flowbit has been previously set (likely by another related rule) before triggering this alert. When triggered, it sets another flowbit "BS.BPset" which may be used by subsequent rules in the detection chain.

The classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this traffic is associated with malicious software that maintains unauthorized access to compromised systems. The specific byte pattern likely represents a command protocol used by the Socks666 malware to communicate with infected hosts.

This detection is significant as it identifies active command and control traffic, indicating a system on the network has been compromised and is receiving instructions from an external controller. Socks666 appears to be a SOCKS proxy trojan that allows attackers to route traffic through infected hosts, potentially enabling anonymized attacks, data exfiltration, or further network penetration.

2006397.msg: ET MALWARE Socks666 Successful Connect Packet Packet
2006397.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Socks666 malware when it successfully establishes a connection to a command and control server.

The rule specifically monitors outbound TCP traffic from internal networks to external web servers, looking for a successful connection packet from the Socks666 trojan. It triggers when a packet of exactly 16 bytes containing the specific hex pattern "|9a 02 08 00|" at the beginning of the payload is detected.

The rule employs flowbit logic that requires a previous condition to be met (flowbits:isset,BS.BPset) before this rule can trigger, and then sets another flowbit (BS.BPcheckin) upon detection. This indicates the rule is part of a chain designed to detect a specific sequence of communications.

When triggered, the rule applies session tagging for 300 seconds, meaning all traffic in the session will be logged for 5 minutes after detection, providing analysts with complete session context.

The classtype "trojan-activity" indicates this is malicious traffic associated with trojan malware, specifically the Socks666 variant which likely uses SOCKS protocol for proxy communications. The exact 16-byte packet with the specific hex pattern represents a protocol handshake or command sequence used by this malware family when establishing command and control communications.

This detection is significant as it identifies active command and control traffic, indicating a successful malware infection and ongoing communication with external malicious infrastructure.

2006398.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Socks666 malware command and control (C2) communications. The rule specifically identifies check-in packets sent from infected hosts to external C2 servers over HTTP ports.

The rule targets TCP traffic originating from internal networks ($HOME_NET) to external destinations ($EXTERNAL_NET) on HTTP ports. It looks for established connections with a specific pattern: packets must be exactly 30 bytes in size and contain the hex pattern "|9a 02 01 00|" at the beginning of the payload (offset:0; depth:4).

When this pattern is detected, the rule sets a flowbit called "BS.BPcheckin1" which likely works in conjunction with other rules to identify the complete Socks666 C2 communication sequence. The "noalert" flowbit directive prevents this specific rule from generating alerts on its own, suggesting it's part of a chain of detection rules.

The classification as "command-and-control" indicates this traffic represents malware communicating with its control infrastructure. This type of traffic is particularly concerning as it indicates an active infection where the malware is attempting to receive instructions or exfiltrate data.

The Socks666 malware likely operates as a SOCKS proxy, allowing attackers to route malicious traffic through infected systems, potentially for anonymization purposes or to access internal network resources.

When this rule triggers as part of a detection chain, analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further C2 communication
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures for forensic analysis
3. Examine the affected host for additional indicators of compromise
4. Investigate other systems communicating with the same external destinations
5. Block the destination IP at network boundaries
6. Correlate with other security logs to identify the initial infection vector

2006399.msg: ET MALWARE Socks666 Checkin Success Packet
2006399.description:
This rule detects successful check-in communications from the Socks666 malware to its command and control (C2) server.

The rule triggers when a TCP packet is sent from an external server using HTTP ports to any host on the internal network. It specifically looks for a 4-byte response packet containing the hexadecimal sequence "|9a 02 05 00|" that confirms a successful connection between the infected host and the C2 server.

The rule uses flowbits to ensure this alert only fires after a previous communication has been detected (flowbits:isset,BS.BPcheckin1), indicating this is part of an established malware communication sequence. The "flow:established,to_client" parameter confirms this is traffic flowing from the server back to the client.

Socks666 is malware that typically establishes a SOCKS proxy on infected systems, allowing attackers to route malicious traffic through the compromised host. This specific rule identifies the confirmation packet sent by the C2 server acknowledging a successful check-in from the infected system.

This detection is significant as it indicates an active malware infection with established command and control communications. Once this connection is established, attackers can issue commands, exfiltrate data, or use the infected system as a proxy for further attacks.

2006400.msg: ET MALWARE Downloader.26001 Url Pattern Detected
2006400.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Downloader.26001 malware variant. It monitors HTTP connections from internal networks to external destinations, specifically targeting HTTP requests containing specific URL patterns indicative of command and control communications.

The rule identifies HTTP requests with the following characteristics:
- Contains "install.php?" in the URI
- Contains the parameter "wall_id="
- Contains the parameter "&maddr=0"
- Contains the parameter "&action="

2006401.msg: ET MALWARE Downloader.26001 Url Pattern Detected (lunch_id)
2006401.description:

The rule monitors for HTTP requests containing multiple specific parameters in the URL query string: ".php?" (indicating a PHP script target), "aff_id=" (likely an affiliate identifier), "lunch_id=" (a unique parameter used by this malware), and "&maddr=0" (possibly a memory address parameter). The "lunch_id=" parameter is designated as a fast pattern for efficient matching.

This detection focuses on the HTTP communication pattern used during the malware's operation, specifically when it attempts to contact its command and control infrastructure. The malware likely uses these specific URL parameters to transmit system information, receive instructions, or download additional malicious components.

The rule classifies this activity as "trojan-activity," indicating it's associated with malware that appears legitimate but performs unauthorized actions. 2006403.msg: ET MALWARE General Trojan Checkin by MAC chkmac.php
2006403.et_name: General Trojan Checkin by MAC chkmac.php
2006403.description:
This Suricata rule detects potential Trojan malware command and control (C2) communication based on specific HTTP traffic patterns.

The rule triggers when an internal network host sends an HTTP POST request to an external server containing the URI path "/ctrl/chkmac.php?mac=" which is a known indicator of a Trojan infection. This pattern suggests the malware is reporting back to its controller by sending the infected machine's MAC address as an identifier.

The detection focuses on the initial "check-in" behavior commonly observed when Trojans establish communication with their C2 infrastructure. The malware uses the MAC address as a unique identifier for the compromised system, allowing the threat actor to track and manage infected hosts.

This type of communication represents a significant security concern as it indicates an active malware infection that has already established a foothold in the network and is attempting to communicate with external control servers. The "command-and-control" classification highlights that this traffic is associated with remote control of compromised systems.

The rule uses the fast_pattern modifier to optimize detection performance by prioritizing the distinctive URI pattern during packet inspection.

2006404.description:
This Suricata rule detects network traffic associated with the DownLoader.30525 malware's command and control communication.

The rule triggers when an HTTP POST request is sent from any internal network host to an external destination with the specific URI path "/ctrl/ctrv.php". This pattern matches the check-in behavior of the DownLoader.30525 malware variant.

The rule specifically identifies:
- HTTP POST requests (content:"POST") with case-insensitive matching (nocase)
- Targeting a specific control path "/ctrl/ctrv.php" with case-insensitive matching (nocase)
- Outbound connections from internal networks to external servers
- Established TCP sessions (flow:established,to_server)

This detection is significant as it identifies malware command and control (C2) communication, which indicates an active infection within the protected network. The "fast_pattern" modifier optimizes detection performance by prioritizing the URI path pattern during packet inspection.

The classification as "command-and-control" indicates this traffic represents malware communicating with its control infrastructure, typically to receive instructions, exfiltrate data, or download additional payloads. Detecting this communication provides an opportunity to identify and remediate infected systems before further damage occurs.

When this alert triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent lateral movement
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the communication if possible
3. Examine the affected host for additional indicators of compromise, focusing on persistence mechanisms
4. Check for data exfiltration by reviewing network logs for unusual outbound traffic patterns
5. Scan other systems in the network that communicated with the affected host
6. Document the incident details including SID:2006404 (revision 6) in reports for tracking

2006408.et_name: HTTP Request on Unusual Port Possibly Hostile
2006408.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic originating from internal networks ($HOME_NET) to external destinations ($EXTERNAL_NET) on non-standard HTTP ports. 

The rule triggers when HTTP requests are sent to ports other than those defined in the $HTTP_PORTS variable. This behavior is flagged as "Possibly Hostile" as it may indicate attempts to bypass security controls or policy violations.

The rule uses flowbits to track HTTP protocol usage and avoid false positives by ensuring the alert only triggers once per destination within a 30-second window. The classtype "policy-violation" indicates this activity contravenes expected network usage policies.

This detection is significant because:
- Attackers often use non-standard ports for command and control communications
- Malware frequently attempts to exfiltrate data over HTTP using unusual ports
- Employees may use non-standard ports to bypass content filtering or access restrictions
- Compromised systems might communicate with external servers on unexpected ports

The rule helps identify potential data exfiltration channels, policy violations, or malicious communications that attempt to evade detection by operating outside normal HTTP port ranges.

2006409.msg: ET INFO HTTP POST on unusual Port Possibly Hostile

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, confidence High, signature_severity Informational, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2019_07_26

2006409.et_name: HTTP POST on unusual Port Possibly Hostile
2006409.description:
This rule detects HTTP POST requests originating from internal networks ($HOME_NET) to external destinations ($EXTERNAL_NET) on non-standard HTTP ports.

The rule triggers when an HTTP POST method is used on ports that are not defined in the $HTTP_PORTS variable, and only on established connections where traffic is flowing from internal clients to external servers. Standard HTTP traffic typically occurs on ports 80 and 443, with some legitimate applications using other defined ports. When POST requests occur on unusual ports, this may indicate:

1. Data exfiltration attempts where attackers send information to external servers using non-standard ports to evade detection
2. Command and control (C2) communications where compromised systems communicate with attacker infrastructure
3. Malware beaconing or checking in with control servers
4. Unauthorized applications tunneling HTTP traffic through non-standard ports

The significance of this alert lies in its ability to detect potential policy violations and covert communications. Attackers often use standard protocols like HTTP on non-standard ports to blend in with normal traffic while avoiding security controls that focus on standard service ports.

When investigating this alert, analysts should:
- Verify the destination IP address and port using threat intelligence sources
- Examine the HTTP POST payload content if available
- Check if the source host has a legitimate business need to communicate on non-standard ports
- Correlate with other alerts from the same source IP to identify potential infection patterns
- Review proxy/firewall logs to determine if this traffic should be permitted by policy

The rule is classified as "policy-violation" which indicates it may detect behavior that contravenes organizational security policies rather than a specific exploit. False positives may occur with legitimate applications using custom ports, so context is essential for proper alert triage.

2006411.msg: ET MALWARE Storm Worm HTTP Request
2006411.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic associated with the Storm Worm malware. The rule identifies outbound HTTP GET requests from internal networks to external IP addresses that match specific patterns characteristic of Storm Worm command and control communications.

The rule specifically looks for:
- HTTP GET requests from internal hosts to external destinations
- URI paths that start with "/?" followed by exactly 16 hexadecimal characters
- Destination hosts that are raw IP addresses (not domain names)

The Storm Worm is a significant malware variant that emerged as one of the early major botnets. This detection is important because:
- It identifies infected hosts attempting to communicate with command and control servers
- The specific URI pattern with 16 hexadecimal characters is a known communication fingerprint
- The use of raw IP addresses rather than domain names is a common evasion technique

This rule helps security teams identify compromised systems within their network that are part of the Storm Worm botnet. Immediate investigation and remediation are recommended when this alert triggers, as it indicates active malware communication.

rule_metadata.attack_target: Client_Endpoint, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Perimeter, confidence High, signature_severity Minor, tag Spyware_User_Agent, updated_at 2020_10_19

2006413.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2006417.et_name: Weak Netbios Lanman Auth Challenge Detected
2006417.description:
This rule detects weak NetBIOS LAN Manager authentication challenges being sent from internal servers to external clients.

The rule specifically monitors TCP traffic from port 139 (NetBIOS Session Service) on internal networks to any port on external networks. It identifies Server Message Block (SMB) protocol communications (indicated by the "|ff 53 4d 42|" hex content) that contain a predictable authentication challenge value ("|00 11 22 33 44 55 66 77 88|").

The detection focuses on a significant security weakness in older Windows authentication mechanisms. When a server issues a predictable challenge sequence instead of a properly randomized one, it creates a vulnerability that can be exploited through various authentication attacks. This predictable challenge pattern (sequential bytes 00 through 88) indicates the server is using weak cryptographic practices.

This type of weak challenge is particularly concerning because it undermines the security of the authentication process, potentially allowing attackers to more easily perform offline password cracking or man-in-the-middle attacks against the authentication exchange. The classification as a "policy-violation" indicates this behavior contradicts security best practices and likely organizational security policies.

Organizations should ensure their systems are configured to use more secure authentication protocols like NTLMv2 or Kerberos rather than the older, vulnerable LAN Manager authentication.

2006443.et_name: Possible SQL Injection Attempt DELETE FROM in HTTP URI
2006443.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

rule_metadata.attack_target: Client_Endpoint, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Perimeter, confidence High, signature_severity Minor, tag Spyware_User_Agent, updated_at 2020_10_19

2006553.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

rule_metadata.affected_product: Web_Server_Applications, attack_target Web_Server, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Datacenter, confidence Medium, signature_severity Major, tag SQL_Injection, updated_at 2020_09_04, mitre_tactic_id TA0001, mitre_tactic_name Initial_Access, mitre_technique_id T1190, mitre_technique_name Exploit_Public_Facing_Application

2006591.et_name: Novell ZENworks Patch Management (ZPM) SQL Injection Attempt -- downloadreport.asp agentid SELECT
2006591.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2006603.et_name: Vt-Forum Lite SQL Injection Attempt -- vf_memberdetail.asp user SELECT
2006603.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2006730.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. 2006767.et_name: KLF-DESIGN (aka Kim L. Fraser) KLF-REALTY SQL Injection Attempt -- search_listing.asp agent UNION SELECT
2006767.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

rule_metadata.attack_target: Client_Endpoint, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Perimeter, confidence High, signature_severity Minor, tag Spyware_User_Agent, updated_at 2020_10_19

2006778.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

rule_metadata.affected_product: Web_Server_Applications, attack_target Web_Server, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Datacenter, confidence Medium, signature_severity Major, tag SQL_Injection, updated_at 2020_09_10, mitre_tactic_id TA0001, mitre_tactic_name Initial_Access, mitre_technique_id T1190, mitre_technique_name Exploit_Public_Facing_Application

2006783.et_name: Aspee and Dogantepe Ziyaretci Defteri SQL Injection Attempt -- giris.asp kullanici SELECT
2006783.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2007007.et_name: MidiCart ASP Shopping Cart and ASP Plus Shopping Cart SQL Injection Attempt -- item_show.asp id2006quant UNION SELECT
2007007.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

2007066.msg: ET DELETED Yahoo Chat Signin Inside Webmail
2007066.description:
This rule detects Yahoo Chat sign-in attempts from within Yahoo Webmail services. The rule monitors established TCP connections from internal networks to external networks on port 5050, which is associated with Yahoo Messenger services.

The detection mechanism identifies traffic flowing from client to server (to_server) and requires two sequential content matches: first, it looks for "content-length:" (case insensitive) within the first 15 bytes of the payload. After finding this initial match, the rule then searches for the Yahoo Messenger protocol signature "<Ymsg Command="550"" which indicates a sign-in attempt. The second content match is implicitly relative to the position where the first match ended.

The rule is classified as a "policy-violation," indicating it's primarily intended to identify users attempting to bypass organizational policies by accessing chat services through webmail interfaces. This could represent a security concern as chat protocols may bypass standard monitoring systems or data loss prevention controls.

The significance of this detection relates to potential data exfiltration risks, as chat services embedded within webmail could provide users with an alternative communication channel that might evade standard security monitoring. Organizations often implement policies restricting the use of instant messaging applications due to their potential for unauthorized data sharing.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should investigate the affected user's activity patterns, verify if the chat usage violates organizational policy, and determine whether sensitive information was potentially shared through this channel. Consider implementing additional monitoring for the identified endpoints and reviewing proxy logs to establish the full context of the webmail session.

The rule references yahoo[.]com as a source for additional information about this traffic pattern.

The detection mechanism identifies established connections flowing to the server that contain two specific patterns: "content-length:" (case insensitive) within the first 15 bytes of the payload, followed by "<Ymsg Command="85"" (also case insensitive) anywhere in the payload. The command value "85" appears to be associated with successful Yahoo Chat authentication events.

This rule is classified as a "policy-violation," indicating it's primarily designed to detect activity that may violate organizational security policies rather than an actual attack. Many organizations restrict the use of chat applications within corporate environments due to data leakage concerns and productivity considerations.

The rule appears to be deprecated (indicated by "DELETED" in the message), suggesting Yahoo may have changed their protocol or the service may no longer be widely used. The reference URL points to yahoo[.]com, providing general context about the service being monitored.

Organizations concerned about unauthorized use of chat applications or data exfiltration through messaging platforms would benefit from this type of detection capability as part of their security monitoring strategy.

2007068.msg: ET DELETED Yahoo Chat Activity Inside Webmail
2007068.description:

The detection mechanism identifies established connections to servers containing two specific patterns: "content-length:" (case insensitive) with a depth restriction of 15 bytes for this pattern, followed by the string "<Ymsg Command=" (also case insensitive) anywhere in the payload. The depth:15 parameter applies only to the first content match, not both patterns.

This rule appears to be targeting the Yahoo Messenger protocol being tunneled through webmail sessions. Port 5050 is traditionally associated with Yahoo Messenger services. The rule is classified as a "policy-violation," suggesting it's primarily intended for organizations that restrict chat applications within their network environment.

The detection of Yahoo Chat within webmail could be significant for several reasons:
- It may represent an attempt to bypass network restrictions on chat applications
- Chat protocols can be used for data exfiltration
- Unmonitored communication channels pose security risks in regulated environments

The rule references yahoo[.]com as a source for additional information about the protocol or service being detected.

This is an older rule (as indicated by the "DELETED" tag in the message) that likely targeted legacy Yahoo services that may no longer be widely used in their original form. Security analysts should evaluate whether this rule remains relevant in their current environment, as Yahoo Messenger was officially discontinued in July 2018. Consider disabling this rule if Yahoo services are no longer used in your organization or if it generates excessive false positives.

2007069.msg: ET DELETED Yahoo Chat Activity Inside Webmail (2)

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces.
