SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2007284.msg: ET MALWARE Downloader.Win32.Agent.cav Url Pattern Detected (ping)
2007284.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Downloader.Win32.Agent.cav malware variant. The alert triggers when an HTTP request is made from an internal network to an external destination containing a specific URL pattern in the "/ping/" directory.

The rule specifically looks for HTTP requests with a distinctive pattern where "/ping/" is followed by a 64-character hexadecimal string, another hexadecimal string of variable length, and then another hexadecimal character. This pattern is characteristic of command and control (C2) communication used by the Downloader.Win32.Agent malware family.

The detection focuses on established TCP connections flowing from internal clients to external servers (flow:established,to_server) and examines HTTP URI content. The rule uses case-insensitive matching (nocase) and optimizes performance with fast_pattern on the "/ping/" string, which serves as an efficient initial filter before applying the more complex regular expression.

The "ping" functionality of this malware is commonly used for beaconing or heartbeat communications between infected systems and C2 servers. This type of communication allows the malware to verify connectivity with its control infrastructure and potentially receive further instructions.

This threat is significant because downloader malware serves as the initial stage in multi-phase attacks, retrieving additional malicious payloads after establishing a foothold on the victim system. The structured URL pattern with hexadecimal identifiers suggests the malware may be transmitting system identification information or receiving encoded commands.

When this alert triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system and capture full packet captures of the communication
2. Examine the HTTP requests to identify potential data exfiltration or command reception
3. Investigate the affected host for additional indicators of compromise, focusing on persistence mechanisms and downloaded payloads
4. Check for similar traffic patterns from other internal hosts that may indicate lateral movement
5. Consider potential false positives from legitimate applications using similar URL structures, particularly development or monitoring tools

The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this is malicious software designed to appear legitimate while performing unauthorized actions on the infected system.

2007296.et_name: Doug Luxem Liberum Help Desk SQL Injection Attempt -- status.asp id INSERT
2007296.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

2007321.et_name: Doug Luxem Liberum Help Desk SQL Injection Attempt -- update.asp uid DELETE
2007321.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

2007399.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. 2007499.et_name: ActiveNews Manager SQL Injection Attempt -- activenews_search.asp query SELECT
2007499.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

It looks for URLs containing "hash?http" and ".com/demo.php?" strings, with particular focus on domains like "ucleaner[.]com", "udefender[.]com", or "ufixer[.]com" followed by "/demo.php?" in the request path.

This detection identifies malicious software masquerading as legitimate security applications. These fake security products typically trick users into believing their systems are infected, then prompt them to install the purported solution, which is actually malware. The specific pattern suggests a command and control or installation mechanism where the malware communicates with its distribution servers.

The rule is classified as "trojan-activity" indicating the traffic is associated with trojan malware behavior. The "fast_pattern" modifier on the "hash?http" content match optimizes detection performance by using this distinctive string pattern for initial packet filtering.

This type of threat represents a significant social engineering risk, as users may believe they are installing legitimate security software while actually compromising their systems with malware that could lead to data theft, system compromise, or further malware installation.

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2007584.et_name: TrendMicro ServerProtect Exploit possible worma(little-endian DCERPC Request)
2007584.description:
This Suricata rule detects exploitation attempts targeting TrendMicro ServerProtect software through TCP port 5168. The rule identifies a potential worm that uses DCERPC (Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Call) requests with little-endian encoding to exploit a buffer overflow vulnerability in the application.

The rule triggers when external traffic meets specific criteria:
- Targets port 5168 on the internal network
- Contains an established TCP connection flowing to the server
- Has a payload size greater than 1000 bytes
- Contains specific byte patterns that match the exploit signature:
  * Initial byte "|05|" indicating a DCERPC bind request
  * "|10 00 00 00|" representing the fragment length field in the DCERPC header
  * "|00 00 88 88 28 25 5b bd d1 11 9d 53 00 80 c8 3a 5c 2c 04 00 03 00|" which contains the UUID of the vulnerable RPC interface
  * "|1c 13 74 65|" appearing later in the payload, part of the malicious buffer overflow attempt

When this rule triggers, security teams should:
1. Immediately isolate affected ServerProtect systems from the network
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the traffic for forensic analysis
3. Check ServerProtect logs for successful exploitation indicators
4. Scan the system for unauthorized processes, files, or network connections
5. Apply TrendMicro's security patches for ServerProtect if available
6. Block the source IP at network boundaries to prevent further exploitation attempts

For investigation, examine the full DCERPC request to identify the specific exploit variant and potential payload. The large payload size (>1000 bytes) typically indicates shellcode or other malicious instructions embedded within the overflow attempt.

The rule references documentation from the SANS Internet Storm Center (isc.sans.org/diary.html?storyid=3310) which contains additional technical details about this threat, including IOCs and exploitation patterns.

This vulnerability is particularly concerning for organizations using TrendMicro ServerProtect, as successful exploitation could lead to unauthorized system access, malware installation, or lateral movement within a network. Organizations should prioritize patching vulnerable ServerProtect installations and implement network segmentation to limit potential lateral movement if exploitation occurs.

2007605.description:
This rule (SID 2007605) identifies outbound MSN Messenger traffic containing a specific social engineering message used by the Singworm trojan. The rule triggers when an established TCP connection from any internal network host to an external destination on port 1863 (the standard MSN Messenger port) contains the text "Here are the new smiles for MSN, they are incredible!"

The detection focuses on the flow:established parameter, ensuring it only matches active, established TCP sessions rather than connection attempts. This helps reduce false positives by targeting actual communication rather than scanning activity. The rule specifically looks for the exact message content that serves as a reliable indicator of the Singworm trojan's propagation technique.

The Singworm trojan attempts to spread by sending deceptive messages to contacts through MSN Messenger. The message entices recipients to download what appears to be new emoticons but is actually malicious software. This technique leverages social engineering to trick users into executing malicious code.

If this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further propagation
2. Examine the host for additional indicators of compromise, focusing on recently downloaded files and executed programs
3. Review network logs to identify any successful connections to external domains following the alert
4. Scan the system with updated antivirus/anti-malware tools specifically targeting the Singworm trojan
5. Check other systems that may have communicated with the infected host

The "DELETED" prefix in the rule name indicates this detection has been deprecated, likely because MSN Messenger is no longer widely used as a communication platform. However, if triggered in a modern environment, it could indicate either legacy systems still running MSN Messenger or newer malware repurposing similar techniques on current platforms. The rule is classified as "trojan-activity" which correctly identifies the threat category.

2007611.description:
This rule detects potential malware infection reports being sent via SMTP (port 25) from internal networks to external mail servers. The rule specifically identifies emails with two distinctive characteristics: they have "X-Priority: 1" and "X-Library: Indy" headers, followed by a nearly empty message body containing only a period.

The Indy library is a legitimate networking component used in Delphi and C++ Builder applications, but in this context, it appears to be leveraged by malware. The high priority setting (X-Priority: 1) combined with the Indy library header and minimal message body (just a period) creates a distinctive pattern associated with automated infection reports sent by malware.

This pattern is significant because many malware variants send "call home" messages or infection status reports to command and control servers. The rule monitors established TCP connections from internal networks ($HOME_NET) to external mail servers ($EXTERNAL_NET) on port 25, focusing specifically on outbound traffic (flow:established,to_server). The minimal message body containing only a period character (represented as "|0d 0a 0d 0a 2e 0d 0a|" in hex) is particularly suspicious as legitimate emails rarely have such content. The rule's "within:30" parameter ensures that this empty message body pattern must appear within 30 bytes after the header pattern, further refining detection accuracy.

The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this traffic pattern is associated with trojan malware that has compromised internal systems and is attempting to communicate with external controllers. This detection is important for identifying compromised hosts within the protected network that may be part of a larger malware campaign.

This type of anomalous User-Agent string is significant because legitimate applications follow standard formatting conventions for User-Agent headers. The specific "0:0:" pattern followed by a fixed-length string likely represents an obfuscation technique used by malware to hide its communications or potentially to transmit encoded data to its controllers.

2007621.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: ET DELETED Kaiten IRCbotnet Login Detection

This rule detects network traffic associated with Kaiten IRC botnet command and control (C2) communications, specifically the login sequence to an IRC server.

The rule monitors outbound TCP connections from internal networks to external destinations, focusing on the characteristic IRC login patterns used by the Kaiten malware. The detection mechanism identifies a specific sequence where:

1. The malware sends "NICK" followed by a space within the first 5 bytes
2. "USER" appears within 32 bytes after the NICK command
3. The string "localhost localhost:" is present within 32 bytes after USER
4. A regular expression validates the complete pattern: NICK [username] followed by USER [username] localhost localhost:

Kaiten is a well-documented IRC-based botnet malware primarily targeting Linux systems, especially IoT devices with weak security configurations. Once infected, compromised devices connect to IRC servers where attackers can issue commands to perform distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, execute arbitrary commands, or propagate to other vulnerable systems.

The "DELETED" designation in the rule name suggests this specific detection signature has been deprecated or replaced by newer detection methods, though the threat itself remains relevant in the threat landscape.

The rule is classified as "trojan-activity" indicating its focus on malicious software that provides unauthorized remote access to compromised systems.

This rule detects network traffic associated with the Kaiten IRC botnet, specifically targeting response messages from infected systems. The rule has been marked as deleted but remains significant for historical and reference purposes.

The rule monitors established TCP connections from internal networks to any destination where IRC communication has been initiated (indicated by the flowbits:isset,irc.start). It searches for specific command and control patterns in the traffic, including "NOTICE" messages containing distinctive Kaiten botnet response strings.

- File transfer notifications ("Receiving file" and "Saved as")

The reference to Wikipedia's IRC bot page provides additional context about the general functionality of IRC bots, which Kaiten leverages for command and control infrastructure.

The classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this is malicious software that provides unauthorized remote access to infected systems, enabling attackers to control compromised hosts for malicious purposes.

2007623.description:
This rule detects command and control (C2) traffic associated with the Kaiten IRC botnet. The rule specifically monitors for IRC server responses containing commands sent to infected hosts.

The rule targets TCP traffic from any source to internal networks, focusing on established connections from IRC servers. The "TSUNAMI" command referenced in the rule is particularly significant as it's a common instruction to initiate flooding attacks. Other commands like "UDP" likely instruct bots to perform UDP-based DDoS attacks, while "GETSPOOFS" and "SPOOFS" commands are typically used to manage IP spoofing capabilities within the botnet.

This detection is important because Kaiten botnets can harness significant computing resources from compromised devices to conduct large-scale DDoS attacks against targets, potentially causing service disruptions and financial damage.

These commands enable various malicious capabilities including network reconnaissance (portscan, nmap), denial of service attacks (udpflood, tcpflood, httpflood), system manipulation (system, linuxhelp), exploitation (milw0rm, rfi), anti-forensics (logcleaner), and botnet management (join, part, help, sendmail).

The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" indicates it's detecting malware that provides unauthorized remote access to infected systems. When this rule triggers, security analysts should:

2007633.msg: ET MALWARE Suspicious User-Agent - Matcash related Trojan Downloader (Ismazo Advanced Loader)

rule_metadata.affected_product: Any, attack_target Client_Endpoint, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Perimeter, confidence High, signature_severity Major, tag User_Agent, tag Trojan_Downloader, updated_at 2020_10_16

2007633.et_name: Suspicious User-Agent - Matcash related Trojan Downloader (Ismazo Advanced Loader)
2007633.description:
A Trojan-Downloader is a type of malware that is responsible for loading and facilitating the continued proliferation of further payloads upon the victim machine. Typically, Trojan-Downloaders will ensure further infection is successful but reporting a successful install, modifying system settings to ensure future malware can be installed/executed without issue, and enable persistency mechanisms for long term infection. Windows is the most commonly observed platform for this type of infection, however, it is not limited-- Macintosh OS X and Linux are also potential targets for compromise.
Valid Trojan-Downloader activity can include network connectivity to a command and control server to report successful infection on a victim machine. Typically, machines impacted with a Trojan-Downloader will have several system settings modified, such as modifications to the Registry where malicious entries may be made. Additionally, the download of a second-stage payload may occur once the original malware has ran. Trojan-Downloaders have been observed with the ability to exfiltrate sensitive data. Confirmation of hostile IP addresses or domains observed with Trojan-Downloader activity may take place in the ET Intelligence portal.
From a network perspective, malware that falls under the Trojan-Downloader has been observed performing activity that would trigger several Emerging Threats INFO, POLICY, and TROJAN style alerts, such as checking an external IP address, the presence of a downloaded executable, or a suspicious HTTP POST to a server. This combination of Trojan-Downloader alerts, as well as complimentary INFO, POLICY, or TROJAN alerts, would warrant an immediate follow up for a compromised workstation.

2007634.msg: ET DELETED Storm Worm Encrypted Traffic Outbound - Likely Search by md5
2007634.et_name: Storm Worm Encrypted Traffic Outbound - Likely Search by md5
2007634.description:
This rule detects network traffic patterns historically associated with Storm Worm botnet activity by monitoring specific UDP communication characteristics.

The rule triggers on UDP traffic from any internal network host using high ports (1024-65535) to external destinations also using high ports. It specifically looks for UDP packets with a payload size of exactly 25 bytes, which was characteristic of Storm Worm's encrypted command and control communications, particularly when conducting MD5-based searches.

A key feature of this detection is the threshold condition, which only generates an alert when a single source IP sends at least 40 matching packets within a 60-second window. This threshold helps reduce false positives by focusing on the high-volume, automated nature of botnet communications.

The Storm Worm (also known as Peacomm) was a significant botnet threat primarily active between 2007-2008 that used peer-to-peer communication protocols. While this specific threat is largely historical, the traffic pattern may still be relevant as similar communication techniques could be employed by current malware variants.

If this rule triggers, investigation steps should include:
1. Capture and analyze packet contents to verify if this is malicious traffic or a false positive
2. Check the affected system for unusual processes, network connections, and system modifications
3. Review logs for additional indicators of compromise such as unexpected DNS queries or connection attempts
4. Compare findings against current threat intelligence to determine if this represents a modern threat variant

This rule serves both as a historical detection mechanism and as a potential indicator of similar communication techniques used by newer threats.

2007635.msg: ET DELETED Storm Worm Encrypted Traffic Inbound - Likely Connect Ack
2007635.et_name: Storm Worm Encrypted Traffic Inbound - Likely Connect Ack
2007635.description:
This rule detects potential Storm Worm botnet traffic entering a protected network. It specifically targets UDP packets with a payload size of exactly 2 bytes sent from external sources to internal network destinations, both using high ports (1024-65535).

The rule implements a threshold mechanism that triggers only when 10 or more matching packets are observed within a 60-second window, tracking by destination address. This pattern recognition helps identify the encrypted command and control acknowledgment traffic characteristic of Storm Worm infections.

Storm Worm was a significant botnet threat that utilized peer-to-peer communication and encryption to maintain resilience. The small packet size (2 bytes) combined with the specific port ranges is indicative of the botnet's encrypted acknowledgment messages.

The rule classifies this activity as "trojan-activity," reflecting its association with malware that maintains unauthorized access to compromised systems. The inbound nature of these packets suggests potential command and control communication with already infected internal hosts.

Network defenders should investigate any systems triggering this alert as they may be compromised endpoints participating in the Storm botnet infrastructure.

2007636.msg: ET DELETED Storm Worm Encrypted Traffic Inbound - Likely Search by md5
2007636.et_name: Storm Worm Encrypted Traffic Inbound - Likely Search by md5
2007636.description:
This rule detects inbound encrypted traffic associated with the Storm Worm botnet, specifically targeting traffic that appears to be searching by MD5 hash.

The rule monitors UDP traffic from external networks to internal networks on high ports (1024-65535), looking for packets with a specific size of 25 bytes. The threshold configuration triggers an alert only when 40 or more matching packets are detected within a 60-second window, tracking by destination IP.

Storm Worm is a known botnet that emerged in 2007, using encrypted communications to evade detection. This particular rule focuses on a specific pattern of encrypted traffic that likely represents search queries using MD5 hashes, which could indicate command and control communications or data exfiltration attempts.

The rule is classified as "trojan-activity," indicating malicious software behavior. The specific packet size (25 bytes) and threshold settings suggest this rule was created after analyzing the botnet's communication patterns to reduce false positives while effectively identifying the threat.

This detection is significant as Storm Worm infections can lead to data theft, system compromise, and incorporation of infected systems into larger botnet operations for distributed attacks.

2007637.msg: ET DELETED Storm Worm Encrypted Traffic Outbound - Likely Connect Ack
2007637.et_name: Storm Worm Encrypted Traffic Outbound - Likely Connect Ack
2007637.description:
This rule detects potential Storm Worm botnet command and control traffic. It monitors UDP communications from internal network hosts to external destinations where both source and destination ports are in the high range (1024-65535).

The rule specifically targets UDP packets with a payload size of exactly 2 bytes, which is characteristic of encrypted acknowledgment messages sent by Storm Worm infected systems. The threshold condition requires 10 such packets within 60 seconds from the same source before triggering an alert, which helps reduce false positives by identifying sustained suspicious communication patterns rather than isolated packets.

Storm Worm was a significant botnet threat that used peer-to-peer communication methods and encryption to evade detection. This rule focuses on the outbound encrypted acknowledgment messages that infected systems would send after establishing a connection to the botnet infrastructure.

The rule is classified as "trojan-activity" indicating it detects malware communication rather than exploitation attempts. The specific message "Likely Connect Ack" suggests these are acknowledgment packets sent after initial connection establishment.

This detection is important as Storm Worm infections could lead to data theft, system compromise, participation in distributed denial-of-service attacks, and further malware distribution.

2007640.msg: ET DELETED Storm Making initial outbound connection
2007640.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Storm worm botnet making its initial outbound connection. The rule specifically targets established TCP connections from internal networks to external destinations using high ports (1024-65535) with a specific payload size of 4 bytes.

The rule utilizes flowbits to track the state of Storm botnet communications, setting a flag (BE.stormtcp.init) once the initial connection is detected while preventing multiple alerts for the same session. The "noalert" flowbit option suppresses immediate alerting, as this rule is likely part of a chain that requires additional conditions to be met before generating an actual alert.

Storm was a significant botnet that emerged in 2007, spreading primarily through email attachments and using peer-to-peer communication for command and control. This detection focuses on identifying the initial callback traffic from an infected system to external command and control infrastructure.

The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" indicates it's detecting malicious software that has already compromised a system and is attempting to establish communication with its operators. This detection is particularly important as it can identify infected systems before they fully participate in botnet activities such as spam distribution, DDoS attacks, or data theft.

2007641.msg: ET DELETED Storm Controller Response to Drone via tcp
2007641.et_name: Storm Controller Response to Drone via tcp
2007641.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Storm botnet's command and control (C2) communications. Specifically, it identifies responses from a Storm controller server to an infected client (drone) over TCP.

The rule triggers when:
- Traffic originates from external networks on high ports (1024-65535)
- Destined for any port on the internal network
- The session has been previously identified as Storm TCP traffic (flowbits:isset,BE.stormtcp.init)
- The communication is part of an established TCP connection from the server
- The data payload is exactly 4 bytes in size

The Storm botnet (also known as Peacomm) was a significant botnet that emerged in 2007, using peer-to-peer communication for resilience. This rule specifically identifies the controller's response to an infected machine, which typically contains command instructions or acknowledgments.

The rule is classified as "trojan-activity" indicating malicious software communication. The small payload size (4 bytes) is characteristic of the Storm botnet's efficient command protocol, allowing it to send instructions with minimal network footprint.

Detection of this traffic pattern indicates an active Storm botnet infection within the network, with machines communicating with external command and control infrastructure.

rule_metadata.attack_target: Client_Endpoint, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Perimeter, confidence High, signature_severity Minor, tag Spyware_User_Agent, updated_at 2020_10_19

2007643.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2007644.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Win32.Agent.cah malware communicating with its command and control (C2) server.

The rule monitors HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations, specifically looking for HTTP requests with a distinctive pattern of parameters that indicate a malware check-in sequence. The detection focuses on HTTP URI patterns containing multiple parameters including "?v=", "&mid=", "&r1=", "&tm=201", "&av=", "&os=Windows", "&uid=", and "cht=".

These parameters likely represent a structured communication protocol where the malware is reporting system information to its C2 server, including:
- Version information ("?v=")
- Machine identifier ("&mid=")
- Timestamp information ("&tm=201")
- Antivirus details ("&av=")
- Operating system ("&os=Windows")
- Unique identifier ("&uid=")

The rule is classified as "command-and-control" traffic, indicating this is part of the malware's C2 infrastructure. The "fast_pattern" option on the "&os=Windows" content match suggests this is a distinctive identifier for this particular malware family.

This detection is significant as it identifies active malware infections attempting to communicate with external control servers. Such communications typically enable threat actors to maintain persistence, exfiltrate data, or deploy additional payloads to compromised systems.

2007646.msg: ET MALWARE Farfli User Agent Detected

2007647.msg: ET DELETED Casalemedia.com Related User Agent (0 0 ...)
2007647.description:
This rule detects suspicious HTTP traffic with an abnormal User-Agent header format. The alert triggers when internal network hosts send HTTP requests to external servers with a User-Agent header containing the unusual pattern "0:0:" followed by at least 120 characters.

The rule specifically looks for HTTP requests with a malformed User-Agent header that begins with "0:0:" - a pattern not used by legitimate browsers or applications. The PCRE (Perl Compatible Regular Expression) pattern matches User-Agent headers with this specific format followed by at least 120 additional characters, which suggests an attempt to hide malicious data in the header.

This detection targets command and control (C2) communications or data exfiltration attempts. Malware often uses unusual User-Agent strings to transmit encoded data or commands while appearing as normal web traffic. The specific pattern "0:0:" followed by a long string is characteristic of trojan activity attempting to evade detection.

The rule is classified as "trojan-activity" indicating it's associated with malware that maintains persistent access to compromised systems. The connection to casalemedia[.]com in the rule name suggests this pattern may have been observed in relation to traffic involving this domain, potentially as part of a malware campaign that abuses legitimate advertising infrastructure.

The "DELETED" prefix in the rule message indicates this specific detection may have been superseded by newer rules or is no longer actively maintained, though it remains in the ruleset for backward compatibility.

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, deprecation_reason Performance, performance_impact Significant, signature_severity Major, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2024_04_11

2007650.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with a Mac Trojan's command and control (C2) communication pattern.

The rule monitors HTTP GET requests from internal networks to external destinations, specifically looking for unusual Accept-Language header patterns that violate standard formatting. The pattern being detected is a 20-character alphanumeric string immediately following the Accept-Language header, which is not consistent with legitimate language specification formats.

The detection focuses on:
- HTTP GET requests from internal hosts to external servers
- The presence of "HTTP/1.1" followed by an Accept-Language header in the request
- A specific pattern match using regular expression that identifies exactly 20 alphanumeric characters after the Accept-Language header

This type of traffic pattern indicates a compromised Mac system attempting to communicate with a command and control server. The malware authors have implemented this unusual Accept-Language header format as a covert communication channel to avoid detection by standard security controls. The 20-character string likely serves as an identifier or encoded command between the infected host and the C2 server.

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" indicates this is part of the post-exploitation phase where an already infected system is maintaining communication with its controller. This represents an active infection where data exfiltration, additional payload delivery, or remote command execution may be occurring.

2007651.description:
This Suricata rule detects the presence of x2300 phpshell, a PHP-based web shell, in HTTP responses from monitored web servers to external networks.

The rule triggers when the specific string "x2300 Locus7Shell" is found in HTTP response data from a web server. The rule uses the `file.data` modifier to inspect the normalized HTTP response body content, allowing detection regardless of transfer encoding or compression methods. This indicates that a compromised server is delivering a known malicious PHP shell to clients.

PHP web shells like x2300 Locus7Shell provide attackers with remote command execution capabilities on compromised web servers. Once deployed, these tools allow threat actors to:
- Execute arbitrary system commands
- Browse the file system
- Upload/download files
- Establish persistence
- Potentially pivot to other systems within the network

The rule's classification as "web-application-activity" and the flow direction (to_client) indicate this is detecting the actual delivery of the web shell code rather than an exploitation attempt. The flow direction is particularly significant as it confirms the web shell is being served from your infrastructure to external clients, indicating a server compromise has already occurred.

The reference URL points to the RFxn Vulnerability Database which contains additional information about this specific threat. The high revision number (rev:9) suggests this rule has been updated multiple times to improve detection accuracy.

When this alert triggers, security analysts should:
1. Immediately isolate the affected server to prevent further data exfiltration
2. Capture and preserve the full HTTP session data for forensic analysis
3. Examine web server logs to identify the initial compromise vector and timeline
4. Search for additional webshell variants and backdoors on the affected system
5. Investigate lateral movement attempts from the compromised server
6. Implement file integrity monitoring to detect future unauthorized file modifications
7. Consider full system restoration from known clean backups after investigation

Detection of web shells in server responses is critical as they represent a severe security breach that grants attackers ongoing access to the compromised system.

2007652.description:
This Suricata rule detects responses from HTTP servers that contain evidence of c99shell, a PHP-based web shell commonly used by attackers after compromising web servers.

The rule triggers when HTTP servers send traffic containing the string "c99shell" to external networks. The flow directive specifies that the alert applies to established connections flowing from the server to the client, indicating this detects the server's response rather than the initial attack.

C99shell is a powerful PHP web shell that provides attackers with extensive control over compromised web servers. Once deployed, it enables file management, command execution, database access, and other administrative functions. Attackers typically upload this web shell after exploiting vulnerabilities in web applications, particularly those built with PHP.

The detection of c99shell in server responses indicates a likely server compromise. When this rule triggers, it suggests that an attacker has already successfully deployed the web shell and is actively interacting with it. The presence of this web shell represents a severe security breach that grants unauthorized administrative access to the affected web server.

The rule references www[.]rfxn[.]com/vdb.php as a source of additional information about this threat. The classification "web-application-activity" categorizes this as suspicious web application behavior that warrants investigation.

2007653.description:
This Suricata rule detects HTTP responses from web servers that contain the string "RFI Scanner" in the HTTP response body.

The rule targets traffic flowing from HTTP servers ($HTTP_SERVERS) on standard HTTP ports ($HTTP_PORTS) to external networks, specifically examining established connections where data is flowing to the client. The `flow:established,to_client` parameter ensures that only server responses in established TCP sessions are inspected, filtering out connection attempts or client requests. The rule uses the `file.data` keyword to specifically normalize and inspect the HTTP response body content, which allows for more accurate detection by focusing only on the response payload rather than headers or other protocol elements.

When the string "RFI Scanner" appears in the HTTP response content, an alert is generated.

Remote File Inclusion (RFI) scanners are tools used to detect vulnerabilities in web applications that allow attackers to include remote files, typically through URL parameters. These vulnerabilities can lead to code execution, data theft, or complete system compromise. The presence of "RFI Scanner" in server responses may indicate:

1. A security tool or scanner has identified an RFI vulnerability
2. A compromised server is responding with information about RFI scanning capabilities
3. A defensive mechanism has detected and is reporting an RFI scanning attempt

The rule is classified as "web-application-activity" which indicates it's monitoring for potentially suspicious web application behavior rather than definitively malicious activity. The reference to rfxn[.]com suggests this may be related to a known security tool or vulnerability database.

This detection is significant because RFI vulnerabilities represent a serious security risk that can lead to unauthorized code execution on vulnerable web servers. Administrators should investigate any triggers of this rule to determine if their systems have been compromised or if legitimate security testing is occurring.

2007654.msg: ET ATTACK_RESPONSE C99 Modified phpshell detected
2007654.description:
This Suricata rule (SID 2007654) detects responses from HTTP servers containing the string "C99 Modified," which indicates the presence of a C99 PHP shell on the server. 

The rule triggers when an HTTP server sends content containing this specific string to an external client. The "flow:established,to_client" parameter confirms this is examining server responses rather than incoming requests. The "file.data" keyword instructs Suricata to inspect the HTTP response body.

C99 is a well-known PHP web shell that provides attackers with remote access to compromised web servers. The "Modified" variant referenced in this rule is a customized version of the original C99 shell. When present on a server, this web shell allows attackers to:

- Execute arbitrary commands on the server
- Browse the file system
- Upload/download files
- Modify website content
- Access database information
- Establish persistence on the compromised system

The detection of this shell in server responses indicates a likely compromised web server. This is particularly concerning as web shells provide attackers with significant control over the affected system and can serve as a foothold for further network penetration.

Recommended response actions upon detection:
1. Immediately isolate the affected server to prevent lateral movement
2. Capture and preserve forensic evidence including logs and file system artifacts
3. Identify the compromised file(s) containing the C99 shell code
4. Determine the initial infection vector by reviewing access logs
5. Remove the malicious code and restore from clean backups if available
6. Reset all credentials associated with the compromised server
7. Scan for additional backdoors or persistence mechanisms
8. Patch vulnerabilities that may have enabled the initial compromise

The rule references www[.]rfxn[.]com/vdb.php as a source of additional information about this threat. The classification "web-application-activity" indicates this is related to potentially malicious web application behavior.

Technical Note: This rule is revision 8, suggesting it has been refined multiple times to improve detection accuracy.

2007655.description:
This Suricata rule detects responses from web servers containing a PHP shell named "lila.jpg". The rule triggers when an HTTP server sends content to an external client that includes the string "CMD PHP", which is characteristic of PHP command shells disguised as image files.

The rule specifically monitors HTTP traffic from servers to clients (flow:established,to_client) and inspects the file data for the presence of the "CMD PHP" marker. The file.data keyword enables inspection of HTTP response bodies after any transfer encoding is processed, allowing detection of malicious content even when obfuscated through HTTP encoding mechanisms. This indicates the server is likely compromised and is serving a PHP web shell to visitors.

PHP shells are malicious scripts that provide attackers with remote command execution capabilities on compromised web servers. In this case, the threat actor has disguised the shell as a JPG image file (lila.jpg) to evade detection, but the content reveals its true nature as a command execution tool.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should immediately:
1. Isolate the affected web server to prevent further command execution
2. Capture and preserve the full HTTP session data for forensic analysis
3. Examine the server for additional backdoors or modified files
4. Review web server logs to identify the initial compromise vector and any executed commands
5. Scan for persistence mechanisms that may have been established

The rule's classification as "web-application-activity" indicates this is related to potentially malicious web application behavior. The reference to rfxn[.]com/vdb.php suggests this is a known threat documented in the R-fx Networks vulnerability database. This rule (SID:2007655) has undergone 8 revisions (rev:8), indicating ongoing maintenance to improve detection accuracy.

This detection is significant because PHP shells represent a severe security breach, allowing attackers to maintain persistent access to compromised servers, execute arbitrary commands, and potentially pivot to other systems within the network.

2007656.description:
This Suricata rule detects HTTP responses from web servers that contain specific content associated with an Albanian hacking group's web shell or defacement signature.

The rule triggers when HTTP servers respond to clients with content containing the string "UNITED ALBANIANS aka ALBOSS PARADISE". This signature is characteristic of compromised web servers that have been defaced or have had malicious PHP scripts (specifically "id.php") installed.

The rule specifically monitors established HTTP connections flowing from servers to clients (flow:established,to_client), indicating it's looking for responses from compromised servers rather than the initial compromise attempt. The "file.data" keyword instructs Suricata to inspect the HTTP response body.

This detection is significant because it identifies servers that have already been compromised. 2007659.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

The rule specifically looks for established TCP connections going to DNS servers (flow:established,to_server), containing the hexadecimal representation of the suspicious domain query. The use of TCP for DNS communications can sometimes indicate tunneling attempts or evasion techniques, as standard DNS typically uses UDP.

The rule classifies this activity as "trojan-activity," indicating that it's associated with malware behavior. The specific version (3.0) suggests this is a known variant with documented behavior patterns.

This detection is significant because DNS-based command and control is a common technique used by malware to maintain persistence and receive instructions while potentially evading traditional network security controls. The TCP-based DNS communication adds another layer of suspicion to this activity.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system and investigate for additional signs of compromise
2. Examine DNS logs for other suspicious queries to the same domain or similar patterns
3. Capture and analyze full packet captures to identify potential data exfiltration
4. Check for persistent connections to the identified domain
5. Scan the system with updated anti-malware tools focusing on E-Jihad variants

This rule detects inbound HTTP traffic associated with the E-Jihad 3.0 DDoS tool targeting web servers.

The rule identifies HTTP GET requests with a specific user agent string containing "Attacker" and having a precise size of 8 bytes. This pattern matches the signature of the E-Jihad 3.0 tool when used to conduct denial-of-service attacks against web servers.

The rule specifically monitors traffic from external networks ($EXTERNAL_NET) to HTTP servers ($HTTP_SERVERS) with established connections flowing to the server. The classification as "denial-of-service" indicates this traffic is part of a coordinated attempt to overwhelm web services and disrupt their availability.

E-Jihad 3.0 is a known DDoS tool that generates a high volume of HTTP requests to exhaust server resources. The detection of this traffic pattern allows security teams to identify and mitigate incoming DDoS attacks before they significantly impact web service availability.

Organizations should implement appropriate traffic filtering, rate limiting, and DDoS mitigation strategies when this alert triggers, as it indicates an active denial-of-service attempt against their web infrastructure.

2007690.description:
This Suricata rule detects network traffic associated with a potentially unwanted program (PUP) called IEDefender, which is categorized as fake antispyware software.

The rule triggers when an HTTP request is sent from any internal network device to an external destination with a specific User-Agent string containing "IEDefender " at the beginning of the string (case insensitive). Specifically, it's looking for User-Agent strings identifying as "IEDefender 2.1".

IEDefender presents itself as legitimate security software but is actually classified as adware or potentially unwanted software. This type of application typically uses deceptive tactics to convince users they have security issues on their systems, often to encourage purchase of a "full version" to remove non-existent threats.

The rule's classification as "pup-activity" confirms this is monitoring for potentially unwanted program behavior rather than a critical security threat. The traffic pattern indicates an infected or compromised system attempting to communicate with command and control servers or update sources associated with this fake security product.

Organizations should investigate systems generating these alerts as they may have unwanted software installed that could degrade system performance, display unwanted advertisements, or potentially collect user information without proper consent.

2007692.description:
This Suricata rule detects network traffic associated with the Basine Trojan's command and control (C2) communication pattern.

The rule monitors HTTP traffic originating from internal networks ($HOME_NET) to external destinations ($EXTERNAL_NET), specifically looking for HTTP POST requests containing distinctive patterns in the request body. The detection focuses on HTTP request bodies containing the parameters "a=", "&b=reported", and "&d=report" in a specific combination, which represents the Basine Trojan's check-in format to its C2 server.

The Basine Trojan is malware that establishes persistent communication with remote servers to receive commands and exfiltrate data. When infected systems check in with the C2 infrastructure, they use this specific HTTP parameter structure to identify themselves and report status information.

The rule employs the "fast_pattern" modifier on the "&b=reported" content match to optimize detection performance. The "classtype:command-and-control" classification indicates this is specifically targeting C2 communications, which are critical security events as they represent active malware operation and potential data exfiltration.

Network defenders should prioritize alerts triggered by this rule as they indicate active malware infection requiring immediate investigation and remediation. The communication pattern detected represents the initial check-in phase of the infection lifecycle, where the malware announces its successful installation to the operator's infrastructure.

2007693.msg: ET ADWARE_PUP Zredirector.com Related Spyware User-Agent (BndDriveLoader)

rule_metadata.attack_target: Client_Endpoint, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Perimeter, confidence High, signature_severity Minor, tag Spyware_User_Agent, updated_at 2020_10_19

2007693.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2007695.et_name: Windows 98 User-Agent Detected - Possible Malware or Non-Updated System
2007695.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations where the User-Agent string contains "Windows 98" while excluding legitimate traffic containing specific headers.

The alert identifies potential security concerns when Windows 98 User-Agent strings appear in outbound HTTP traffic. Windows 98 is an obsolete operating system that reached end-of-life status in 2006 and no longer receives security updates, making it highly vulnerable to exploitation.

The rule specifically looks for:
- HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations
- Established connections flowing to servers
- User-Agent headers containing "Windows 98"
- Absence of "X-Trend-ActiveUpdate" and "HTTrack" headers (to reduce false positives)

This detection is significant for several reasons:
1. Legitimate Windows 98 systems represent a severe security risk due to numerous unpatched vulnerabilities
2. Malware often spoofs outdated User-Agent strings to appear as legacy systems
3. Attackers may use these outdated User-Agents to evade detection systems expecting modern browser signatures

The rule is classified as a "policy-violation" which indicates it may be detecting activity that contravenes organizational security policies regarding supported operating systems.

2007698.msg: ET MALWARE Vanquish Trojan HTTP Checkin
2007698.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Vanquish Trojan's command and control (C2) communication patterns. The rule specifically monitors HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations, focusing on HTTP requests that contain multiple specific parameters in the URI that are characteristic of the Vanquish Trojan's check-in behavior.

The rule identifies HTTP requests containing multiple parameters including "ip=", "&v=1&s=", "&h=", "&kb=", "&o=", "&c=", "&un=", "&m=", "&w=", and "&ss=". These parameters likely represent system information being exfiltrated to the C2 server, such as IP address, version information, host details, operating system data, username, and other system metrics.

The Vanquish Trojan is a malware variant that establishes persistent communication with its command and control infrastructure. This communication allows the threat actor to maintain control over infected systems, exfiltrate sensitive information, and potentially deploy additional payloads.

The detection of this traffic pattern indicates an active Vanquish Trojan infection within the network. This represents a significant security incident as the malware has already established a foothold and is actively communicating with external control servers. The "command-and-control" classification in the rule highlights the severity of this threat, as it represents an active control channel between the compromised system and the attacker's infrastructure.

Network defenders should immediately isolate affected systems, conduct forensic analysis, and implement remediation procedures when this alert triggers.

2007700.msg: ET MALWARE ExplorerHijack Trojan HTTP Checkin
2007700.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the ExplorerHijack Trojan's command and control (C2) communication pattern. The rule specifically identifies HTTP requests from internal networks to external destinations that match the characteristic checkin pattern of this malware.

The ExplorerHijack Trojan establishes communication with its C2 server through HTTP requests containing multiple specific parameters. The HTTP request contains several identifying parameters including system information and victim identifiers. The rule looks for HTTP traffic with multiple parameter patterns in the URI including "php?i=", "&v=", "&win=Windows", "&un=", "&uv=", "&s=", "&onl=", "&ip=", "&f=".

This communication represents the malware's beaconing or "check-in" behavior, where it reports to its controller and potentially receives instructions. The parameters likely transmit system information such as Windows version, username, IP address, and other system identifiers that allow the attacker to track and manage infected systems.

The rule specifically targets established TCP connections with traffic flowing from the infected client to the C2 server (flow:established,to_server), which helps reduce false positives by focusing only on outbound communication attempts. This directional specification is important as it captures the initial check-in behavior rather than server responses.

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" indicates this is part of the malware's infrastructure communication. This type of traffic is particularly significant as it represents active malware infection and ongoing control of compromised systems. Detecting C2 traffic is critical as it provides an opportunity to identify compromised hosts before additional malicious activities occur.

The rule has undergone seven revisions (rev:7) indicating ongoing maintenance and refinement to improve detection accuracy and reduce false positives as the malware and its communication patterns evolve.

Network defenders should investigate any systems triggering this alert as they likely have an active ExplorerHijack Trojan infection requiring immediate remediation.

2007701.msg: ET DELETED Storm Worm Encrypted Variant 1 Traffic (1)
2007701.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Storm Worm encrypted variant. The rule specifically targets UDP traffic from internal network hosts to external destinations where both source and destination ports are in the range of 1024-65535.

The rule looks for UDP packets with a specific size of 25 bytes containing the hex pattern "|10 a6|" within the first two bytes of the packet. A threshold condition is applied to trigger the alert only when two or more matching packets are observed from the same source within a 60-second window.

Storm Worm was a significant malware family that utilized peer-to-peer communication for command and control operations. This particular rule appears to identify a specific encrypted communication pattern used by a variant of the malware. The encrypted nature of the traffic makes traditional signature-based detection more difficult, but this rule identifies a consistent pattern in the packet structure.

The classification of "trojan-activity" indicates this is malicious software designed to provide unauthorized access to infected systems. The specific packet size and byte pattern combination helps reduce false positives while identifying the malware's network communications.

The threshold condition helps prevent alert fatigue by only triggering when multiple matching packets are observed, which is consistent with the behavior of malware maintaining command and control communications.

2007702.msg: ET DELETED Storm Worm Encrypted Variant 1 Traffic (2)
2007702.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Storm Worm encrypted variant. The rule specifically targets UDP traffic from internal network hosts to external destinations, where both source and destination ports are in the range of 1024-65535.

The detection focuses on UDP packets with a specific size of 25 bytes containing the hex pattern "|10 a0|" within the first two bytes of the packet. The threshold configuration triggers an alert only when two matching packets are observed from the same source within a 60-second window.

2007703.et_name: Apple Quicktime RTSP Content-Type overflow attempt
2007703.description:
WEB_CLIENT signatures are designed to alert on attacks against web client software, primarily attacks against web browsers such as Internet Explorer, Firefox, Chrome, and Safari.  These exploit based attacks target vulnerabilities in the web browser which can be used to compromise an endpoint.  Most of the WEB_CLIENT signatures detect Javascript type attacks against client software.

Often times, these attacks can be seen in in use by Exploit Kits (EKs) to force a client to download malicious code as part of a drive by download attack.

With its liberal rules on use of whitespace, the lack of strict format, commonly leveraged Javascript obfuscation by legitimate websites, Javascript is a hard language to write signatures for.  These signatures have a medium confidence level on their own; however when observed with other Exploit Kit signatures, the confidence should be considered high, especially if the server is known to be malicious in ET Intelligence.
