2007711.msg: ET DELETED Srizbi registering with controller
2007711.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Srizbi botnet communicating with its command and control infrastructure. Note that this rule has been marked as DELETED in the ruleset (SID: 2007711), indicating it may be outdated or replaced by newer detection methods.

The rule monitors UDP traffic originating from any port on the internal network to external destinations using ports 1024 and above. It specifically looks for UDP packets with a size of exactly 20 bytes containing two instances of the hexadecimal pattern "|2d|" (ASCII hyphen character) at specific positions. The first hyphen must be at offset 6, and the second must be exactly 6 bytes after the first one. Additionally, the rule includes a negated content match to ensure the packet does not contain the string "server." preceded by a null byte ("|00|server.").

The detection focuses on the characteristic communication pattern used by Srizbi botnet malware when registering with its controller servers. This represents the initial check-in process where infected systems announce their presence to the command and control infrastructure.

Srizbi was a significant botnet primarily used for sending spam emails. At its peak, it was responsible for distributing large volumes of unwanted email traffic across the internet. The botnet utilized a custom protocol for command and control communications, which this rule helps identify.

If this traffic is detected, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further communication
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures for forensic analysis
3. Examine the source host for indicators of compromise, focusing on persistence mechanisms
4. Scan the affected system with updated anti-malware tools
5. Check for additional systems exhibiting similar communication patterns
6. Consider implementing temporary blocks for the destination IP addresses at the network perimeter

The presence of this traffic indicates an active Srizbi infection requiring immediate remediation to prevent spam distribution, data exfiltration, and potential deployment of additional malware.

2007712.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Srizbi botnet malware. The rule specifically identifies outbound HTTP GET requests from internal networks to external destinations on high ports (1024 and above) that contain distinctive HTTP headers used by Srizbi when requesting command templates from its control servers.

The rule looks for three specific HTTP headers in the request:
- X-Flags header
- X-TM header
- X-BI header

These custom headers serve as a signature for Srizbi botnet communication when requesting templates from command and control servers. The rule references research from SecureWorks related to a Srizbi campaign that used Ron Paul-themed spam.

Srizbi was a significant botnet known for its spam distribution capabilities. When infected, systems would make these specially crafted HTTP requests to receive templates and instructions from command and control servers. The botnet was notable for its ability to send large volumes of spam emails and its resilient command and control infrastructure.

The detection of this traffic indicates an active Srizbi infection on the network that is attempting to communicate with its command and control infrastructure, which requires immediate remediation to prevent further compromise and potential data exfiltration or spam distribution.

2007715.msg: ET ATTACK_RESPONSE Off-Port FTP Without Banners - user
2007715.description:
This rule detects potential trojan activity involving FTP protocol elements used over non-standard ports without proper server banners.

The rule specifically monitors for inbound traffic containing FTP USER command strings being sent TO internal network clients from external sources on high ports (1024 and above). This is suspicious because legitimate FTP servers typically operate on standard ports (21/20) and include proper protocol banners in their communications.

The detection focuses on established TCP connections where data is flowing to the client (flow:established,to_client). It looks for packets larger than 7 bytes (dsize:>7) containing "USER " at the beginning of the payload (content:"USER "; depth:5; offset:0), followed by a carriage return and line feed character sequence (content:" |0d 0a|"; distance:1). When detected, it sets a flowbit called "ET.strippedftpuser" which may be used by other rules for correlation.

This pattern indicates potential command and control (C2) traffic where an attacker's server is mimicking FTP protocol elements to communicate with compromised internal hosts. The presence of a USER command string in server-to-client traffic is particularly suspicious as in legitimate FTP sessions, USER commands are sent from clients to servers, not the reverse direction.

When this alert triggers, security analysts should:
1. Identify the affected internal host and examine its process list for suspicious applications
2. Review full packet captures to understand the complete communication pattern
3. Check for other related alerts using the ET.strippedftpuser flowbit
4. Isolate the affected system if malicious activity is confirmed

The classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this behavior is commonly associated with malware maintaining persistence or communicating with remote controllers while attempting to blend in with normal network traffic.

2007717.msg: ET ATTACK_RESPONSE Off-Port FTP Without Banners - pass
2007717.description:
This rule (SID 2007717) detects suspicious FTP-like traffic that may indicate trojan activity. It specifically identifies FTP PASS commands occurring on non-standard ports without proper FTP banners.

The rule targets established TCP connections from internal networks (ports 1024 and above) to external destinations (also ports 1024 and above), focusing on traffic flowing to the client. It looks for FTP authentication sequences where a stripped FTP username has already been identified (via the flowbit "ET.strippedftpuser") and then sets a flowbit indicating a stripped FTP password was detected.

The detection pattern requires:
- A packet with payload size greater than 7 bytes
- Content starting with "PASS " within the first 5 bytes
- A carriage return and line feed sequence (\r\n) following some content

This rule identifies potentially malicious activity where FTP-like authentication occurs on non-standard ports without proper FTP protocol banners. This technique is commonly used by trojans and backdoors to hide command and control communications by mimicking FTP traffic patterns while avoiding standard FTP ports (21/20) that might be more closely monitored.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Identify the involved hosts and examine their full communication patterns
2. Investigate the source host for signs of compromise or unauthorized software
3. Capture and analyze full packet captures to determine what data is being transferred
4. Check for other indicators of compromise on the affected systems
5. Consider blocking the external IP if confirmed malicious

The classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this pattern is associated with malware that maintains persistent access to compromised systems while evading detection by using stripped-down FTP-like communications on unusual ports.

2007723.msg: ET ATTACK_RESPONSE Off-Port FTP Without Banners - retr
2007723.description:
This rule detects potential trojan activity involving off-port FTP traffic without standard banners.

The alert triggers when a client receives data containing the "RETR" command string over non-standard ports (above 1024) after previously sending stripped FTP authentication credentials. The rule specifically looks for the "RETR" string at the beginning of packets larger than 7 bytes. This is unusual because in normal FTP protocol operations, "RETR" is a client-to-server command requesting file retrieval, not something typically sent from server to client.

This detection focuses on malicious activity where attackers use FTP-like protocols over non-standard ports to evade detection. The flow direction (to_client) combined with FTP command strings indicates potential command and control traffic or malicious data exfiltration channels disguised as FTP traffic. The rule relies on a previously set flowbit "ET.strippedftppass" which indicates prior detection of suspicious FTP authentication traffic in the session.

The "tag:session,300,seconds" directive ensures continued monitoring of the session for 5 minutes after detection, capturing additional related traffic. The classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this behavior is commonly associated with malware communications where attackers may be using inverted protocol behaviors to confuse detection systems.

This detection is significant because it identifies protocol anomalies where server responses contain client command strings, potentially indicating backdoor communications, covert channels, or data exfiltration mechanisms designed to bypass security controls.

2007725.msg: ET ATTACK_RESPONSE Unusual FTP Server Banner on High Port (WinFtpd)
2007725.et_name: Unusual FTP Server Banner on High Port (WinFtpd)
2007725.description:
This rule detects FTP server banner responses from WinFtpd running on high ports (1024 and above) directed toward internal networks.

The alert triggers when a TCP connection from any external source using a high port (1024 or higher) sends a response to any internal network destination containing the string "220 WinFtpd" at the beginning of the packet. The rule specifically looks for small packets (less than 18 bytes) with established connections flowing toward the client. The content match is performed with case-insensitive comparison (nocase) and only examines the first 11 bytes of the packet (depth:11) starting from the beginning (offset:0).

This detection is significant because legitimate FTP servers typically run on standard ports (21/TCP), not high ports. The presence of WinFtpd banners on non-standard high ports often indicates:

1. A compromised system running unauthorized FTP services
2. Malware using WinFtpd components for data exfiltration
3. Command and control infrastructure leveraging FTP for communication

The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this pattern is commonly associated with trojan malware that establishes covert FTP services for data theft or remote access. The small packet size requirement (dsize:<18) helps reduce false positives by focusing on the specific banner format used by malicious implementations.

Network administrators should investigate any systems triggering this alert (SID:2007725, revision 7) to determine if unauthorized FTP services are running or if systems have been compromised.

2007726.msg: ET ATTACK_RESPONSE Unusual FTP Server Banner on High Port (StnyFtpd)
2007726.et_name: Unusual FTP Server Banner on High Port (StnyFtpd)
2007726.description:
This rule detects suspicious FTP server banner responses on non-standard high ports that identify themselves as "StnyFtpd". The alert triggers when a server operating on a high port (1024 or above) responds to a client in the protected network with this specific banner.

The rule identifies potential trojan activity where malicious software may be masquerading as an FTP server. StnyFtpd is not a common legitimate FTP server implementation, and its presence on high ports is particularly suspicious. The small data size requirement (less than 30 bytes) further narrows detection to minimal banner responses characteristic of this specific threat.

The "flow:established,to_client" parameter ensures the rule only matches traffic in an established TCP connection flowing from the server to the client, focusing on server responses rather than client requests. The rule specifically looks for the string "220 StnyFtpd" at the beginning of the response packet (offset:0), examining only the first 12 bytes (depth:12) to efficiently match the 11-character target string while minimizing false positives. The "nocase" option ensures detection regardless of character case variations.

This detection is significant because trojans often use FTP functionality for data exfiltration or to receive commands. The presence of an unusual FTP server implementation on a non-standard port suggests a compromised system where malware has established command and control capabilities or data transfer mechanisms.

When this alert triggers, security analysts should:
1. Identify and isolate the affected system immediately
2. Examine the source IP and port for additional suspicious connections
3. Capture and analyze full packet captures to determine what data may have been transferred
4. Check the affected system for other indicators of compromise, particularly malware that includes FTP functionality
5. Review firewall logs for additional connections to/from the suspicious server

False positives may occur with legitimate custom FTP implementations. Verify whether the detected server is part of authorized infrastructure before escalation. The combination of the unusual server name, high port usage, and minimal banner size makes true positives more likely in most enterprise environments.

2007727.msg: ET P2P Possible Torrent Download via HTTP Request

2007727.et_name: Possible Torrent Download via HTTP Request
2007727.description:
This Suricata rule (SID 2007727) detects HTTP requests from internal networks to external destinations that appear to be BitTorrent file downloads.

The rule triggers when an HTTP request contains a URI ending with ".torrent" (case insensitive), indicating a potential BitTorrent metadata file download. The rule specifically excludes legitimate domains "mapfactor.com" and "verismic.blob.core.windows.net" to reduce false positives.

BitTorrent is a peer-to-peer file sharing protocol commonly used for legitimate purposes but also frequently employed to distribute unauthorized copyrighted content, malware, or other prohibited materials. Organizations often restrict BitTorrent usage due to:

1. Bandwidth consumption concerns
2. Potential copyright infringement liability
3. Security risks from downloading untrusted files
4. Data exfiltration risks

The rule is classified as a "policy-violation," indicating it detects behavior that may contravene organizational acceptable use policies rather than an immediate security threat. Network administrators should investigate triggered alerts to determine if the torrent download represents authorized activity or a policy violation requiring remediation.

The rule has undergone 12 revisions (rev:12), suggesting ongoing refinement to improve detection accuracy and reduce false positives.

2007742.msg: ET MALWARE Storm C&C with typo'd User-Agent (Windoss)

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, confidence High, signature_severity Major, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2020_10_16

2007742.description:
This Suricata rule detects network traffic associated with the Storm botnet command and control (C&C) communications. The rule specifically identifies HTTP requests from internal networks to external destinations that contain a deliberately misspelled User-Agent string with "Windoss" instead of "Windows" in the User-Agent header.

The rule targets HTTP traffic with a specific User-Agent string beginning with "Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windoss NT" - a deliberate misspelling of "Windows" as "Windoss." This technique is commonly employed by malware authors to evade simple signature-based detection while maintaining compatibility with malicious C&C servers that are programmed to recognize these specific markers.

Storm botnet malware uses this distinctive User-Agent string as an identifier when communicating with its command and control infrastructure. The misspelling serves as both a stealth technique and an authentication mechanism for the C&C server to identify legitimate bot communications.

2007820.msg: ET ADWARE_PUP Rabio Spyware/Adware Initial Registration
2007820.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: ET ADWARE_PUP Rabio Spyware/Adware Initial Registration

This rule detects network traffic associated with Rabio spyware/adware making its initial registration communication to command and control servers.

The rule specifically monitors HTTP POST requests from internal networks to external destinations, looking for a distinctive registration pattern in the HTTP request body. The pattern begins with "REGISTER|7c|" (where |7c| represents the pipe character in hexadecimal) followed by a sequence of numbers separated by pipe characters.

The detection uses both a fast pattern match and a more specific PCRE regular expression to validate the format: "/REGISTER\x7c\d+\x7c\d+\x7c\d+\x7c\d/", which matches "REGISTER" followed by a pipe and several number sequences separated by pipes.

Rabio is classified as potentially unwanted program (PUP) that exhibits adware and spyware functionality. This initial registration traffic represents the moment when the software first communicates with its control servers after installation, potentially sending system information and establishing a communication channel for future data exfiltration or command reception.

The rule references documentation about Rabio at www[.]spywareguide[.]com and www[.]rabio[.]com, which provide additional context about this software's capabilities and behaviors.

This detection is important as it identifies the presence of potentially unwanted software that may compromise user privacy by collecting and transmitting data without proper consent.

2007821.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2007827.description:
A Trojan-Downloader is a type of malware that is responsible for loading and facilitating the continued proliferation of further payloads upon the victim machine. Typically, Trojan-Downloaders will ensure further infection is successful but reporting a successful install, modifying system settings to ensure future malware can be installed/executed without issue, and enable persistency mechanisms for long term infection. Windows is the most commonly observed platform for this type of infection, however, it is not limited-- Macintosh OS X and Linux are also potential targets for compromise.
Valid Trojan-Downloader activity can include network connectivity to a command and control server to report successful infection on a victim machine. Typically, machines impacted with a Trojan-Downloader will have several system settings modified, such as modifications to the Registry where malicious entries may be made. Additionally, the download of a second-stage payload may occur once the original malware has ran. Trojan-Downloaders have been observed with the ability to exfiltrate sensitive data. Confirmation of hostile IP addresses or domains observed with Trojan-Downloader activity may take place in the ET Intelligence portal.
From a network perspective, malware that falls under the Trojan-Downloader has been observed performing activity that would trigger several Emerging Threats INFO, POLICY, and TROJAN style alerts, such as checking an external IP address, the presence of a downloaded executable, or a suspicious HTTP POST to a server. This combination of Trojan-Downloader alerts, as well as complimentary INFO, POLICY, or TROJAN alerts, would warrant an immediate follow up for a compromised workstation.

2007829.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with Illusion Bot (also known as Lussilon), a malware variant that communicates with command and control (C2) servers.

The rule specifically identifies HTTP POST requests from internal networks to external destinations that contain distinctive patterns in both the URI and request body characteristic of Illusion Bot infection activity. The detection focuses on the malware's check-in process where infected systems report their status to the C2 infrastructure.

Key indicators in this rule include:
- HTTP POST method
- URI containing "?act=online&" parameter (marked as fast pattern for efficient matching)
- Additional URI parameters "s4=", "&s5=", and "&nickname="
- HTTP request body starting with "msg_out=" parameter

This detection is classified as command-and-control traffic, indicating the rule targets the communication channel between infected hosts and the malware operators' infrastructure. The C2 communication allows attackers to maintain persistence, exfiltrate data, and issue commands to compromised systems.

The Illusion Bot malware represents a significant threat as it establishes persistent control channels that enable threat actors to maintain access to compromised environments and potentially conduct further malicious activities including data theft, lateral movement, or deployment of additional payloads.

2007831.msg: ET MALWARE Downloader General Bot Checking In via HTTP Post (bot_id push)
2007831.et_name: Downloader General Bot Checking In via HTTP Post (bot_id push)
2007831.description:
This rule detects HTTP POST requests from internal networks to external destinations that match patterns consistent with botnet command and control (C2) communication.

The rule specifically identifies malware that functions as a downloader, which is checking in with its C2 server by sending specific data parameters in an HTTP POST request body. The detection requires an established TCP connection flowing from the client to the server and looks for several key parameters being transmitted:

- "bot_id=" - A unique identifier for the infected machine
- "&build_id=" - The malware version or build number
- "&sport=" - Likely the source port used by the malware
- "&hport=" - Possibly a hidden or hosting port used for additional services
- "&ping=" - Likely a connectivity check or heartbeat mechanism
- "&speed=" - Possibly reporting the victim's connection speed

The rule performs case-insensitive matching on the POST method to ensure detection regardless of capitalization variations.

This communication pattern represents a typical check-in sequence where an infected host (bot) reports its status to a command and control server. The bot provides identifying information and system details that allow the threat actor to inventory their compromised systems and potentially issue commands.

The detection is significant because it identifies active malware infections on the network that have already established communication with external control infrastructure. This type of traffic indicates a successful compromise and ongoing control of internal systems by malicious actors, potentially enabling data exfiltration, additional payload delivery, or participation in distributed attacks.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further communication with C2 infrastructure
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the communication if possible
3. Collect memory dumps and disk images from the affected system for forensic analysis
4. Analyze HTTP headers and POST data for additional indicators of compromise
5. Investigate other systems that have communicated with the same external destinations
6. Block the destination IP/domain at network boundaries
7. Scan the affected system with updated anti-malware tools to identify the specific malware variant

These URL patterns represent a check-in mechanism used by the malware to communicate with its command and control server.

The detection focuses on the initial communication (or "beacon") from an infected system to its controller. The parameters in the URL likely transmit system information such as:
- pid: Possibly a process ID or unique identifier for the infected machine
- dt: Likely a timestamp or date-related information
- v: Probably version information of the malware

This type of traffic indicates an active malware infection where the compromised system is attempting to establish communication with its command and control infrastructure. The "command-and-control" classification indicates this is part of a botnet or remote control mechanism for the malware.

The significance of this threat is high as it represents an active malware infection that has already bypassed preventative security controls and is attempting to establish external communications, potentially leading to data exfiltration, additional payload downloads, or remote system control.

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" indicates this is part of the C2 infrastructure used by the malware to maintain persistence and receive instructions. This type of communication is a critical detection point as it represents active malware operation and potential data exfiltration or command reception.

The specific formatting of the HTTP request body with process information suggests the malware is collecting and transmitting system reconnaissance data, which is a common behavior in the initial stages of an infection when the malware is establishing details about the compromised environment.

2007847.et_name: Sony ImageStation (SonyISUpload.cab 1.0.0.38) ActiveX Buffer Overflow Exploit
2007847.description:
ActiveX controls are Microsoft Internet Explorer’s native version of plug-ins and can be leveraged by non browse applications as well..  ActiveX provides web application developers a facility to execute code on a client machine through the web browser.  Unfortunately, ActiveX controls have been a significant source of security problems both due to vulnerabilities in the ActiveX control itself, in the browser which can allow the activeX control to bypass security, as well as the fact that it has extensive capabilities to attacker drive code.
ActiveX controls are very powerful and can be used for legitimate and nefarious purposes including monitoring your personal browsing habits, install malware, generate pop-ups, log your keystrokes and passwords, and do other malicious things. ActiveX controls are actually not Internet Explorer-only. They also work in other Microsoft applications, such as Microsoft Office. Other browsers, such as Firefox, Chrome, Safari, and Opera, all use other types of browser plug-ins. ActiveX controls only function in Internet Explorer. A website that requires an ActiveX control is an Internet Explorer-only website.
If you see these ActiveX controls alerts firing, they are unlikely to succeed in exploiting all but legacy windows systems running older versions of IE. ActiveX controls are Microsoft Internet Explorer’s native version of plug-ins and can be leveraged by non browse applications as well.. 2007859.description:
A Trojan-Downloader is a type of malware that is responsible for loading and facilitating the continued proliferation of further payloads upon the victim machine. Typically, Trojan-Downloaders will ensure further infection is successful but reporting a successful install, modifying system settings to ensure future malware can be installed/executed without issue, and enable persistency mechanisms for long term infection. Windows is the most commonly observed platform for this type of infection, however, it is not limited-- Macintosh OS X and Linux are also potential targets for compromise.
Valid Trojan-Downloader activity can include network connectivity to a command and control server to report successful infection on a victim machine. Typically, machines impacted with a Trojan-Downloader will have several system settings modified, such as modifications to the Registry where malicious entries may be made. Additionally, the download of a second-stage payload may occur once the original malware has ran. Trojan-Downloaders have been observed with the ability to exfiltrate sensitive data. Confirmation of hostile IP addresses or domains observed with Trojan-Downloader activity may take place in the ET Intelligence portal.
From a network perspective, malware that falls under the Trojan-Downloader has been observed performing activity that would trigger several Emerging Threats INFO, POLICY, and TROJAN style alerts, such as checking an external IP address, the presence of a downloaded executable, or a suspicious HTTP POST to a server. This combination of Trojan-Downloader alerts, as well as complimentary INFO, POLICY, or TROJAN alerts, would warrant an immediate follow up for a compromised workstation.

2007863.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Banload banking trojan's HTTP command and control communications.

The rule triggers when an HTTP POST request is sent from an internal network to an external destination with the following specific characteristics:

1. The traffic flow is established and directed to a server
2. The User-Agent string starts with "Mozilla/3.0 (compatible; Indy Library)" where the semicolon is represented in hex (|3b 20|)
3. The HTTP request body contains the string "tipo="

Banload is a malware family primarily targeting banking customers in Brazil and other Latin American countries. It typically arrives through phishing emails or malicious downloads and is designed to steal banking credentials and financial information.

The specific pattern identified in this rule represents the malware's check-in behavior with its command and control server. The use of the Indy Library in the User-Agent is significant as it's a component often used by malware authors for HTTP communications rather than legitimate web browsing.

The "tipo=" parameter in the POST body likely represents part of the command structure used by the malware to communicate with its controllers, possibly indicating the type of information being exfiltrated or the command being requested.

If this alert triggers, security teams should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent data exfiltration
2. Capture full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Examine the host for additional indicators of compromise, particularly focusing on browser extensions and scheduled tasks
4. Review recent email activity and downloads on the affected system to identify the initial infection vector
5. Check for lateral movement attempts from the compromised host

This detection is classified as "command-and-control" traffic, indicating it's monitoring for active malware infections attempting to communicate with their operators.

2007864.msg: ET MALWARE Banload HTTP Checkin Detected
2007864.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Banload banking trojan's HTTP command and control communications. The rule specifically identifies HTTP requests from internal networks to external servers that contain distinctive URL patterns used by Banload malware during check-in procedures.

The rule monitors for HTTP requests containing multiple specific parameters in the URL query string: "php?mac=", "&hdd=", "&ver=", "&ie=", and the distinctive string "++++++++" - all of which are characteristic of Banload's communication protocol. These parameters likely transmit system information such as MAC address, hard drive details, malware version, and Internet Explorer version to the command and control server. The "fast_pattern" modifier on the "php?mac=" content match optimizes detection performance by prioritizing this distinctive pattern during initial packet inspection.

The "flow:established,to_server" directive ensures the rule only triggers on established TCP connections where traffic is flowing from the infected client to the C2 server, reducing false positives by focusing on outbound communication attempts rather than server responses or connection attempts.

Banload is a banking trojan primarily targeting Brazilian financial institutions. The malware typically arrives through phishing emails or compromised websites and is designed to steal banking credentials and financial information from infected systems. When installed, it establishes communication with command and control servers to receive instructions and exfiltrate stolen data.

The "classtype:command-and-control" designation indicates this rule detects malware communicating with its control infrastructure, representing an active infection in the network. This is a high-severity threat as it indicates successful compromise and ongoing control of internal systems by malicious actors.

Detection of this traffic pattern should trigger immediate incident response procedures to isolate affected systems, as financial data theft is likely the primary objective of this malware.

2007865.msg: ET DELETED Winreanimator.com Fake AV Install Attempt
2007865.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations attempting to access a fake antivirus installation page associated with winreanimator[.]com.

The rule specifically monitors for HTTP requests containing the URI pattern "/inst.php?wmid=" followed by multiple parameters including "&p=", "&l=", and "&s=" in the URL. These parameters likely represent tracking or configuration values used during the malicious software installation process. The rule employs case-insensitive matching (nocase) for all URI content patterns to catch evasion attempts using mixed capitalization.

The detection focuses on established connections flowing from internal clients to external servers (established,to_server), identifying attempts by compromised hosts to download or install fraudulent antivirus software. Fake antivirus programs typically employ social engineering tactics to convince users their systems are infected, then prompt them to install malicious software under the guise of security protection.

This type of trojan activity is particularly concerning as it may lead to:
- Installation of actual malware while claiming to remove non-existent threats
- Collection of payment information for "premium" versions of the fake software
- Theft of personal data or credentials
- Establishment of persistence mechanisms on the victim system

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further communication with malicious infrastructure
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures if available for forensic analysis
3. Examine the host for indicators of compromise, focusing on recently installed software
4. Review web proxy/firewall logs to identify previous communications with winreanimator[.]com
5. Scan the system with legitimate antivirus tools to identify any malware already installed
6. Consider reimaging the system if compromise is confirmed

The rule classifies this activity as "trojan-activity" which accurately reflects the deceptive nature of fake antivirus distribution campaigns. The established connection from an internal host to an external server suggests a user has already been directed to the malicious domain and is in the process of installing the fraudulent software.

2007869.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2007874.msg: ET EXPLOIT Now SMS/MMS Gateway HTTP BOF Vulnerability
2007874.et_name: Now SMS/MMS Gateway HTTP BOF Vulnerability
2007874.description:
This rule detects exploitation attempts targeting a buffer overflow vulnerability in the Now SMS/MMS Gateway application.

The rule monitors TCP traffic from external networks to port 8800 on internal networks, specifically looking for HTTP GET requests containing malformed Authorization headers. The vulnerability occurs when an attacker sends an excessively long Base64-encoded string (255 or more characters) in the Basic Authentication header, potentially triggering a buffer overflow condition.

The detection pattern uses multiple content matches and a PCRE regular expression to identify the malicious pattern in the HTTP Authorization header. The rule specifically looks for:
- GET requests
- Authorization headers containing "Basic" authentication
- Base64-encoded credentials exceeding 255 characters in length

This vulnerability affects the Now SMS/MMS Gateway web interface and could allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code by sending specially crafted HTTP requests with oversized authentication headers. According to the Bugtraq reference (ID 27896), this is a serious vulnerability that could lead to complete system compromise.

The rule references additional technical details available at aluigi[dot]altervista[dot]org/adv/nowsmsz-adv.txt, which likely contains proof-of-concept information or technical analysis of the vulnerability.

The classification as "web-application-attack" indicates this is targeting a web-based service, and organizations running Now SMS/MMS Gateway services should ensure they're patched against this vulnerability.

2007875.msg: ET EXPLOIT Now SMS/MMS Gateway SMPP BOF Vulnerability
2007875.et_name: Now SMS/MMS Gateway SMPP BOF Vulnerability
2007875.description:
This rule detects a buffer overflow vulnerability exploitation attempt targeting Now SMS/MMS Gateway's SMPP (Short Message Peer-to-Peer) protocol implementation.

The rule monitors established TCP connections from external networks to port 2775 on internal networks, which is the standard port for SMPP communications. It identifies potential exploitation by looking for specific binary patterns (`|00 00 00 04|` followed by `|00 00 00 01|` at a distance of 1 byte) and then uses a regular expression to detect oversized input of 1000 or more alphanumeric characters, which is characteristic of a buffer overflow attack.

The vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code by sending specially crafted packets to the SMPP service. When exploited, this could lead to complete system compromise, allowing attackers to gain unauthorized access to the SMS/MMS gateway and potentially intercept or manipulate message traffic.

This vulnerability is documented in Bugtraq ID 27896, with technical details available in Luigi Auriemma's security advisory. The buffer overflow exists in the handling of SMPP protocol fields, where input validation is insufficient, allowing attackers to overflow buffers with excessive data.

Upon detection, security analysts should:
1. Immediately isolate affected systems to prevent further exploitation
2. Capture and preserve packet captures for forensic analysis
3. Check for signs of successful exploitation including unexpected processes or connections
4. Apply vendor patches specifically addressing this vulnerability (NowSMS version updates)
5. Implement network segmentation to restrict access to SMPP services

While the rule uses the classtype "web-application-attack" (as defined in the Suricata classification system), note that SMPP is a telecommunications protocol rather than a traditional web application protocol. This classification reflects the severity of the attack rather than the exact nature of the targeted service.

False positives may occur with legitimate large SMPP transactions, so analysts should verify alerts by examining the full packet capture and confirming the presence of exploitation patterns in the SMPP traffic.

2007876.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: ExtremeZ-IP Vulnerability Detection

This rule detects exploitation attempts targeting ExtremeZ-IP File and Print Server through UDP port 427, which hosts the Service Location Protocol (SLP) service. The rule specifically identifies malicious packets containing the string "language" and a specific hexadecimal pattern that represents an attempt to exploit vulnerabilities in the ExtremeZ-IP implementation.

The rule targets CVE-2008-0767, a vulnerability affecting ExtremeZ-IP File and Print Server version 5.1.2x15 and earlier. This vulnerability occurs because the application fails to properly validate the "number of URLs" field against the actual packet length. When attackers send a packet with a large integer in this field to UDP port 427, it triggers an out-of-bounds read operation, resulting in a denial of service condition by crashing the daemon.

The hexadecimal content pattern in the rule ("|65 7a 69 70 3a 2f 2f...|") appears to represent a malformed SLP request targeting the vulnerability. When decoded, this pattern begins with "ezip://" which is likely part of the exploitation technique.

This rule is classified as "successful-dos" indicating its primary concern is detecting denial of service attacks that have a high likelihood of success against vulnerable systems. The external references to Bugtraq ID 27718 and the security advisory from Luigi Auriemma provide additional context about this vulnerability.

Network administrators should ensure ExtremeZ-IP installations are patched to versions newer than 5.1.2x15 to mitigate this vulnerability.

2007878.et_name: Apple QuickTime <= 7.4.1 QTPlugin.ocx Multiple Remote Stack Overflow
2007878.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: Apple QuickTime ActiveX Vulnerability

This rule detects exploitation attempts targeting a stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability in Apple QuickTime's QTPlugin.ocx ActiveX control. The rule specifically monitors HTTP traffic from external servers to internal clients that could contain malicious code targeting this vulnerability.

The rule identifies traffic containing the QuickTime ActiveX control CLSID "02BF25D5-8C17-4B23-BC80-D3488ABDDC6B" followed by specific function calls that are known to be vulnerable, including SetBgColor, SetMovieName, SetTarget, SetMatrix, or SetHREF methods with numeric string parameters.

## Vulnerability Details

The rule detects exploitation of CVE-2008-0778, which affects Apple QuickTime versions 7.4.1 and earlier. This vulnerability involves multiple stack-based buffer overflows in the QTPlugin.ocx ActiveX control that can be triggered when overly long arguments are passed to several methods including SetBgColor, SetHREF, SetMovieName, SetTarget, and SetMatrix.

## Attack Vector and Impact

Attackers can exploit this vulnerability by crafting malicious web pages containing JavaScript that passes excessively long strings to the vulnerable methods. When a victim with a vulnerable QuickTime installation visits such a page, the buffer overflow can cause:

1. Denial of service (application crash)
2. Potential arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the current user

The attack requires no user interaction beyond visiting a malicious website, making it particularly dangerous as a drive-by download attack vector.

## Detection Logic

The rule uses several techniques to identify exploitation attempts:
- Monitors HTTP responses (flow:established,to_client)
- Searches for the QuickTime ActiveX control CLSID
- Looks for calls to the vulnerable methods
- Uses PCRE regex to identify potentially malicious string parameters

This vulnerability was publicly disclosed in 2008 with exploit code available, increasing the likelihood of exploitation attempts in the wild.

2007880.description:

The rule targets outbound HTTP connections from internal networks to external destinations where the User-Agent string contains nothing but a hyphen. Normal User-Agent strings typically identify the client application, operating system, and version information to web servers. A User-Agent consisting of only a dash character is highly anomalous and does not conform to standard browser or legitimate application behavior.

This pattern is associated with trojan activity, as indicated by the rule's classification. Malware often uses minimalist or deliberately obscured User-Agent strings to avoid detection while maintaining HTTP communication with command and control servers. The single dash may represent an attempt to provide the minimum required HTTP header while avoiding distinctive identification patterns.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Immediately isolate the affected system from the network to prevent further command and control communication
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the suspicious traffic for forensic analysis
3. Examine the destination IP address and domain for reputation indicators and cross-reference with threat intelligence feeds
4. Investigate the affected system for additional indicators of compromise, focusing on running processes, network connections, and system modifications
5. Collect and analyze system logs, browser history, and other artifacts to determine the initial infection vector
6. Perform memory analysis to identify potential malware persistence mechanisms
7. Document all findings for potential incident response escalation

The rule's significance lies in its ability to detect covert communication channels established by malware. Legitimate applications virtually never use such simplified User-Agent strings, making this an effective indicator of compromise with minimal false positive risk. The traffic pattern suggests an attempt to maintain network connectivity while evading detection based on known malware User-Agent signatures.

The rule has been revised 12 times (rev:12), indicating ongoing refinement to maintain its effectiveness against this specific technique.

2007884.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations where the User-Agent string exactly matches "Example". The rule is categorized as potentially unwanted program (PUP) activity, which typically refers to adware or other software that may be unwanted but not necessarily malicious.

The alert triggers when an HTTP request is made from any host on the internal network to any external destination with the specific User-Agent string. The flow parameters ensure the connection is established and the traffic is moving from client to server. The "startswith" and "endswith" modifiers indicate that "Example" must be the complete User-Agent string, not part of a larger string.

This type of detection is significant because custom or unusual User-Agent strings are often used by adware, tracking software, or potentially unwanted applications to communicate with command and control servers. Legitimate applications typically use standard User-Agent strings that identify the browser or application making the request.

The rule has been revised 12 times (rev:12), suggesting ongoing maintenance to keep it effective against evolving threats. The rule's classification as "pup-activity" indicates it's considered lower risk than malware but still worthy of monitoring in security-conscious environments.

Network administrators should investigate systems generating this alert to determine if unauthorized software is installed and communicating with external servers.

2007886.msg: ET DELETED Anti-virus-pro.com Fake AV Checkin
2007886.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with a fake anti-virus program communicating with its command and control infrastructure.

The rule monitors HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations, specifically looking for established connections to a server containing a stat.php script with a distinctive machine_id parameter format. The detection focuses on the URI pattern "/stat.php?machine_id={" followed by a specific format validated through PCRE, where the machine_id follows a UUID-like pattern of hexadecimal character groups separated by hyphens (e.g., XXXXXX-XXXXXX-XXXXXX-XXXXXX-XXXXXX).

This traffic pattern is associated with fake anti-virus software that typically:

1. Falsely reports security issues on victims' systems
2. Attempts to convince users to purchase "full versions" to remove non-existent threats
3. May install additional malware or steal sensitive information
4. Generates revenue through social engineering tactics

The rule specifically identifies the "check-in" behavior where infected systems communicate with command and control servers, sending unique machine identifiers that allow the malicious operators to track infected systems.

When investigating alerts from this rule:
1. Examine the full HTTP request to identify the complete destination domain
2. Check the infected host for signs of fake anti-virus software installation
3. Review browser history for visits to suspicious security software websites
4. Isolate affected systems to prevent further communication with C2 infrastructure
5. Scan the system with legitimate security tools to identify and remove the malware

This type of threat represents a significant risk as fake anti-virus software exploits users' security concerns to facilitate financial fraud and potentially deploy additional malicious payloads to compromised systems.

2007889.et_name: Cacti SQL Injection Vulnerability graph_view graph_list UNION SELECT
2007889.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2007898.msg: ET MALWARE Sohanad Checkin via HTTP
2007898.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic associated with the Sohanad malware's command and control (C2) communication pattern.

The rule triggers when an internal host makes an HTTP GET request to an external server with the specific URI path "/cs/bux/check.php". This represents a check-in attempt by the Sohanad malware to its C2 infrastructure. Additionally, the rule looks for the absence of a User-Agent HTTP header, which is atypical for legitimate web traffic but common in certain malware communications.

Sohanad is a family of malware that typically spreads via removable drives and establishes persistent C2 connections. This particular rule identifies the initial or periodic check-in behavior where the infected system attempts to contact its control server to receive instructions or deliver stolen information.

The rule is classified as "command-and-control" which indicates its focus on detecting the communication channel between infected hosts and malicious infrastructure rather than the initial infection vector. This type of detection is critical for identifying compromised systems within a network, even after the initial infection has occurred.

Network defenders should investigate any systems triggering this alert as they likely indicate an active Sohanad infection requiring immediate remediation to prevent data exfiltration or further system compromise.

2007899.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic containing a specific User-Agent string that may indicate adware or potentially unwanted program (PUP) activity.

The rule triggers when an HTTP request is sent from an internal network to an external destination with the User-Agent string "HTTP_CONNECT" that is exactly 12 bytes in length. The rule uses both content matching to identify the specific string and the bsize operator to verify the exact byte length of the User-Agent field. This particular User-Agent is abnormal and does not conform to standard browser User-Agent formats, suggesting it may be associated with adware or PUP communications.

The rule specifically monitors established connections flowing from internal hosts to external servers. The "classtype:pup-activity" classification indicates this is related to potentially unwanted programs that may be installed alongside legitimate software.

This detection is significant because non-standard User-Agent strings are often employed by adware and PUPs to communicate with command and control servers or to deliver advertisements. The specific string "HTTP_CONNECT" appears to be mimicking HTTP protocol terminology, which is unusual for a legitimate User-Agent and suggests an attempt to disguise the true nature of the traffic.

Network administrators should investigate systems generating this traffic as they may be infected with adware or unwanted software that could be collecting user information, displaying unwanted advertisements, or performing other undesirable activities.

The rule has been assigned SID 2007899 and is currently at revision 9, indicating it has been updated multiple times to improve detection accuracy and reduce false positives.

2007900.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2007901.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Banker.OPX banking malware's command and control communications.

The rule specifically identifies HTTP POST requests from internal networks to external destinations containing the distinctive pattern "TIPO=CLIENTE&NOME=" in the HTTP request body. This pattern represents a check-in mechanism used by infected systems to communicate with command and control servers.

The rule targets established connections flowing from internal hosts to external servers, focusing on the specific data format used by this banking malware variant during its communication phase. The "nocase" modifier ensures case-insensitive matching for both the POST method and the request body pattern, increasing detection effectiveness against evasion techniques. The "fast_pattern" directive indicates this string is used by the IDS engine for initial packet matching, optimizing performance by quickly filtering relevant traffic before deeper inspection.

Banking malware like Banker.OPX typically steals financial credentials, intercepts banking sessions, and may facilitate unauthorized transactions. The classification as "command-and-control" indicates this traffic represents infected systems reporting to their control infrastructure rather than the initial infection vector.

The threat significance is high as this detection indicates an active malware infection within the protected network that has already established communication with external control servers, potentially leading to financial data theft or fraudulent transactions.

Upon detection, security analysts should: 1) Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further data exfiltration; 2) Capture and preserve full packet captures for forensic analysis; 3) Identify and remediate the infection source through endpoint investigation; 4) Implement temporary blocking rules for the destination IP; and 5) Scan other systems for similar indicators of compromise, particularly those handling financial transactions.

2007903.et_name: 4XEM VatDecoder VatCtrl Class ActiveX Control Url Property Buffer Overflow Vulnerability
2007903.description:
ActiveX controls are Microsoft Internet Explorer’s native version of plug-ins and can be leveraged by non browse applications as well..  ActiveX provides web application developers a facility to execute code on a client machine through the web browser.  Unfortunately, ActiveX controls have been a significant source of security problems both due to vulnerabilities in the ActiveX control itself, in the browser which can allow the activeX control to bypass security, as well as the fact that it has extensive capabilities to attacker drive code.
ActiveX controls are very powerful and can be used for legitimate and nefarious purposes including monitoring your personal browsing habits, install malware, generate pop-ups, log your keystrokes and passwords, and do other malicious things. ActiveX controls are actually not Internet Explorer-only. They also work in other Microsoft applications, such as Microsoft Office. Other browsers, such as Firefox, Chrome, Safari, and Opera, all use other types of browser plug-ins. ActiveX controls only function in Internet Explorer. A website that requires an ActiveX control is an Internet Explorer-only website.
If you see these ActiveX controls alerts firing, they are unlikely to succeed in exploiting all but legacy windows systems running older versions of IE.  To help validate whether the signature is triggering a valid compromise you should look for other malicious signatures related to the client endpoint which is triggering.  This includes Exploit Kit, Malware, and Command and Control signatures, along with looking to see if the web server is known to be malicious in ET Intelligence.

2007913.msg: ET MALWARE Dialer.MC(vf) HTTP Request - Checkin

2007914.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the SDBot worm making HTTP check-in attempts to command and control servers.

The rule specifically targets HTTP traffic from internal networks to external web servers, focusing on established connections with a specific pattern of communication. The detection mechanism identifies SDBot by its distinctive HTTP request characteristics:

1. A specific User-Agent string: "Mozilla/3.0 (compatible; Indy Library)" with a precise size of 38 bytes
2. A particular HTTP header structure ending with "User-Agent" followed by two carriage return/line feed sequences (represented by hex values |0d 0a|)
3. HTTP request body content starting with "quem=dodoi&tit=" and containing "&txt=" within the first 40 bytes after the initial pattern

SDBot is a malware family that creates backdoors on infected systems, allowing remote attackers to control compromised machines. This particular HTTP check-in represents the infected host communicating with its command and control infrastructure, potentially to receive instructions, deliver stolen data, or confirm its active status.

Upon detection, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further command and control communication
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Examine the HTTP request body content after "&txt=" as it likely contains encoded system information or command responses
4. Investigate other network traffic from the same host for additional malicious connections
5. Collect memory dumps and system artifacts from the infected host for malware analysis

The rule classifies this activity as "trojan-activity," indicating the serious nature of this threat. Detection of this traffic pattern suggests an active SDBot infection in the network that requires immediate remediation to prevent data theft, system compromise, or use of the infected system in further attacks.

2007917.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Dropper-497 (Yumato) malware's initial command and control communication.

The rule monitors outbound TCP connections from internal networks to external destinations on high ports (above 1024, excluding port 9997). It specifically looks for a 5-byte payload containing the hexadecimal pattern "|30 30 30 0d 0a|", which translates to "000" followed by a carriage return and line feed.

This pattern represents the initial check-in beacon that the Dropper-497 (Yumato) malware sends to its command and control server after successfully infecting a system. The small, fixed-size payload (5 bytes) with a distinctive pattern is characteristic of malware beaconing behavior designed to establish communication while maintaining a low network footprint.

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" indicates this traffic represents malware attempting to establish or maintain communication with its control infrastructure. This initial check-in is a critical detection point as it identifies compromised systems before additional malicious activities occur, potentially allowing for early intervention and remediation.

The detection of this traffic pattern indicates an active Dropper-497 infection in the environment, which could lead to further payload delivery, data exfiltration, or other malicious activities if not addressed promptly.

2007918.msg: ET MALWARE Dropper-497 (Yumato) System Stats Report
2007918.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Dropper-497 (Yumato) malware when it sends system statistics reports to command and control servers.

The rule monitors outbound TCP connections from internal networks to external destinations on high ports (1024 and above). It specifically looks for established connections containing a distinctive binary header (|00 00 00 83|) followed by XML-formatted system information including CPU and memory statistics enclosed in specific tags (<CPU></CPU> and <MEM></MEM>).

This detection identifies when the Yumato malware is actively reporting system information back to its operators. The malware collects system resource statistics and transmits them in a structured format, allowing attackers to monitor infected systems and potentially make decisions about further exploitation based on the victim's hardware capabilities.

The rule is classified as "trojan-activity," indicating this is part of a malicious remote access or data exfiltration operation. System statistics reporting is a common feature in backdoors and remote access trojans, as it helps attackers determine which compromised systems are worth targeting for specific payloads or further exploitation.

The structured format of the data with XML tags suggests this is a relatively sophisticated malware with well-defined communication protocols rather than a simple script.

2007919.msg: ET MALWARE Dropper-497 Yumato Reply from server
2007919.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Dropper-497 Yumato malware variant.

The rule monitors TCP traffic from external networks (ports 1024 and above) to any port on the internal network. It specifically identifies server responses containing the string "YUMATO" followed by carriage return and line feed characters (0d 0a in hexadecimal) and then the string "1234" within the first 12 bytes of the payload.

This detection focuses on command and control (C2) communication patterns where an infected host receives specific formatted responses from a malware server. The "flow:established,to_client" parameter ensures the rule only triggers on traffic flowing from the server to the client in an established TCP connection.

The "classtype:trojan-activity" designation indicates this is related to trojan malware activity, which typically involves unauthorized access and control of victim systems. The presence of a specific string pattern ("YUMATO" followed by CR/LF and "1234") suggests a hardcoded protocol identifier or authentication mechanism used by the malware to verify communication with its C2 infrastructure.

This type of traffic represents a significant security concern as it indicates active malware infection and ongoing communication with malicious infrastructure, potentially leading to data exfiltration, additional payload delivery, or remote command execution.

2007920.msg: ET DELETED Dropper-497 (Yumato) Status Reply from server
2007920.description:
This rule (SID:2007920, revision 4) detects network traffic associated with the Dropper-497 (Yumato) malware family. It specifically identifies status reply messages sent from external servers to hosts on the internal network. Note that this rule is marked as DELETED, indicating it is no longer an active detection and may have been superseded by newer rules or determined to be ineffective.

The rule monitors established TCP connections from external networks (ports 1024-7989 and 7991 and above) to any port on the internal network. It looks for a specific 4-byte pattern "|32 31 0d 0a|" which translates to "21\r\n" in ASCII. This pattern represents a status reply from a command and control server to an infected host.

The small payload size (exactly 4 bytes) combined with the specific content pattern indicates a concise communication protocol used by the malware for status updates or command acknowledgments. The rule classifies this activity as "trojan-activity," confirming its association with malware operations.

This detection is significant because it identifies active command and control communications between compromised internal systems and external malicious infrastructure. Such traffic indicates a successful infection where the malware has established a communication channel with its operators, potentially enabling data exfiltration, further payload delivery, or remote control of the infected system.

If this alert triggers, security teams should:
1. Isolate the affected internal host immediately to prevent further command execution or data exfiltration
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Examine the affected system for indicators of compromise, focusing on persistence mechanisms
4. Review historical network logs to identify when the initial infection occurred
5. Scan other systems on the network for similar communication patterns that may indicate additional infections

While this rule is marked as deleted, the detection pattern may still be valuable for historical analysis or as a reference for custom rule development targeting similar malware communication patterns.

2007921.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic with a suspicious User-Agent string that consists solely of the word "Explorer" originating from internal networks to external destinations.

The rule targets adware or potentially unwanted programs (PUP) that use an abnormally simplified User-Agent header. Legitimate web browsers typically include version information, operating system details, and other identifying characteristics in their User-Agent strings. A User-Agent containing only "Explorer" is highly unusual and likely indicates automated or malicious software attempting to masquerade as Internet Explorer while avoiding detection.

The detection focuses on outbound HTTP requests where the entire User-Agent string matches exactly "Explorer" (enforced by the startswith and endswith modifiers). This pattern is commonly associated with adware, browser hijackers, or data collection tools that attempt minimal disguise while communicating with command and control servers. The rule specifically monitors established connections flowing to external servers, which helps eliminate false positives from incomplete or fragmented traffic.

When this rule triggers (SID: 2007921), security analysts should:
1. Identify the source host and examine its process list for suspicious applications
2. Review full packet captures to analyze the complete HTTP session and destination
3. Check for additional suspicious network connections from the same host
4. Consider isolating the affected system if malicious activity is confirmed
5. Document findings and add any discovered command and control servers to blocklists

The rule's classification as "pup-activity" indicates this behavior is associated with potentially unwanted programs rather than more severe threats like malware or exploits. However, such traffic should still be investigated as it may indicate compromised systems or unauthorized software operating within the network.

The high revision number (rev:13) suggests this signature has been refined multiple times to reduce false positives while maintaining detection effectiveness.

2007922.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Backdoor.Win32.VB.brg malware's command and control (C&C) communication.

The rule monitors outbound TCP connections from internal networks to external destinations on high ports (1024 and above). It specifically looks for the string "Status*(Idle...)*" in the TCP payload, where the special characters are hex-encoded as |2a 28| for "*(" and |2e 2e 2e 29 2a| for "...)*". The rule enforces strict positioning requirements, checking only the first 17 bytes of the payload (depth:17) starting from the beginning of the data (offset:0).

The backdoor appears to be a Visual Basic-based Windows malware that communicates with its C&C server using this specific format to indicate the infected system's status. The "Idle" status message likely represents the malware reporting back to its controller that it's awaiting further instructions.

This detection is significant because it identifies active command and control communication from an infected system, indicating a successful compromise. The classtype "command-and-control" correctly categorizes this as malicious traffic associated with remote control of the compromised system.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further C&C communication
2. Capture full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Examine the destination IP address and port for additional intelligence
4. Scan the system for other indicators of compromise, particularly Visual Basic-based malware artifacts
5. Check for persistent mechanisms that may allow the malware to survive reboots
6. Review network logs to identify when the initial infection occurred and potential lateral movement

The rule's SID (2007922) and revision number (5) suggest this threat has been tracked and the detection logic refined over time to improve accuracy.

2007923.msg: ET MALWARE Suspicious User-Agent - Possible Trojan Downloader (Digital)

rule_metadata.affected_product: Any, attack_target Client_Endpoint, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Perimeter, confidence Medium, signature_severity Major, tag User_Agent, tag Trojan_Downloader, updated_at 2020_10_16

2007923.description:
A Trojan-Downloader is a type of malware that is responsible for loading and facilitating the continued proliferation of further payloads upon the victim machine. Typically, Trojan-Downloaders will ensure further infection is successful but reporting a successful install, modifying system settings to ensure future malware can be installed/executed without issue, and enable persistency mechanisms for long term infection. Windows is the most commonly observed platform for this type of infection, however, it is not limited-- Macintosh OS X and Linux are also potential targets for compromise.
Valid Trojan-Downloader activity can include network connectivity to a command and control server to report successful infection on a victim machine. Typically, machines impacted with a Trojan-Downloader will have several system settings modified, such as modifications to the Registry where malicious entries may be made. Additionally, the download of a second-stage payload may occur once the original malware has ran. Trojan-Downloaders have been observed with the ability to exfiltrate sensitive data. Confirmation of hostile IP addresses or domains observed with Trojan-Downloader activity may take place in the ET Intelligence portal.
From a network perspective, malware that falls under the Trojan-Downloader has been observed performing activity that would trigger several Emerging Threats INFO, POLICY, and TROJAN style alerts, such as checking an external IP address, the presence of a downloaded executable, or a suspicious HTTP POST to a server. This combination of Trojan-Downloader alerts, as well as complimentary INFO, POLICY, or TROJAN alerts, would warrant an immediate follow up for a compromised workstation.

Windows is the most commonly observed platform for this type of infection, however, it is not limited-- Macintosh OS X and Linux are also potential targets for compromise.
Valid Trojan-Downloader activity can include network connectivity to a command and control server to report successful infection on a victim machine. Typically, machines impacted with a Trojan-Downloader will have several system settings modified, such as modifications to the Registry where malicious entries may be made. Additionally, the download of a second-stage payload may occur once the original malware has ran. Trojan-Downloaders have been observed with the ability to exfiltrate sensitive data. Confirmation of hostile IP addresses or domains observed with Trojan-Downloader activity may take place in the ET Intelligence portal.
From a network perspective, malware that falls under the Trojan-Downloader has been observed performing activity that would trigger several Emerging Threats INFO, POLICY, and TROJAN style alerts, such as checking an external IP address, the presence of a downloaded executable, or a suspicious HTTP POST to a server. This combination of Trojan-Downloader alerts, as well as complimentary INFO, POLICY, or TROJAN alerts, would warrant an immediate follow up for a compromised workstation.
