2007927.description:
Spyware User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Spyware User-Agent strings that are leveraged by machines installed with potentially unwanted applications.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

2007931.description:
ActiveX controls are Microsoft Internet Explorer’s native version of plug-ins and can be leveraged by non browse applications as well..  ActiveX provides web application developers a facility to execute code on a client machine through the web browser.  Unfortunately, ActiveX controls have been a significant source of security problems both due to vulnerabilities in the ActiveX control itself, in the browser which can allow the activeX control to bypass security, as well as the fact that it has extensive capabilities to attacker drive code.
ActiveX controls are very powerful and can be used for legitimate and nefarious purposes including monitoring your personal browsing habits, install malware, generate pop-ups, log your keystrokes and passwords, and do other malicious things. ActiveX controls are actually not Internet Explorer-only. They also work in other Microsoft applications, such as Microsoft Office. Other browsers, such as Firefox, Chrome, Safari, and Opera, all use other types of browser plug-ins. ActiveX controls only function in Internet Explorer. A website that requires an ActiveX control is an Internet Explorer-only website.
If you see these ActiveX controls alerts firing, they are unlikely to succeed in exploiting all but legacy windows systems running older versions of IE.  To help validate whether the signature is triggering a valid compromise you should look for other malicious signatures related to the client endpoint which is triggering.  This includes Exploit Kit, Malware, and Command and Control signatures, along with looking to see if the web server is known to be malicious in ET Intelligence.

2007932.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: Symantec BackupExec Calendar Control Vulnerability

This rule detects exploitation attempts targeting a buffer overflow vulnerability in Symantec BackupExec's PVCalendar ActiveX control. The rule monitors HTTP traffic from external servers to internal clients, specifically looking for malicious content that could exploit CVE-2007-6017.

The detection focuses on the PVCalendar.ocx ActiveX control (identified by CLSID "22ACD16F-99EB-11D2-9BB3-00400561D975") when combined with specific parameters that indicate exploitation attempts. The rule looks for the control's GUID, "0x40000" parameter, either "_DOWText" or "_MonthText" properties, and the "Save" method.

CVE-2007-6017 affects the PVATLCalendar.PVCalendar.1 ActiveX control in Symantec Backup Exec for Windows Server versions 11d (11.0.6235, 11.0.7170) and 12.0 (12.0.1364). The vulnerability exposes an unsafe Save method that allows remote attackers to cause denial of service conditions or create/overwrite arbitrary files by manipulating the _DOWText and _MonthText properties.

The attack vector is particularly concerning as it requires no authentication - simply visiting a malicious webpage with a vulnerable browser can trigger the exploit. When successful, attackers can write files to victims' systems, potentially leading to remote code execution.

This vulnerability represents a significant risk to organizations using affected Symantec Backup Exec versions, as it could allow attackers to compromise client systems through drive-by download attacks.

2007937.description:
This rule detects a heap overflow vulnerability in Borland VisiBroker Smart Agent service.

The rule monitors UDP traffic from external networks to port 14000 on internal networks, which is the default port for the VisiBroker Smart Agent. It specifically looks for packets containing the byte sequence "|44 53 52 65 71 75 65 73 74|" (which translates to "DSRequest" in ASCII) followed by a string of 50 or more alphanumeric characters, which could indicate an attempt to exploit the heap overflow vulnerability.

The heap overflow vulnerability (Bugtraq ID 28084) affects the Smart Agent component of Borland VisiBroker. When exploited, attackers can send specially crafted packets containing oversized data to trigger a heap-based buffer overflow, potentially leading to denial of service conditions or remote code execution. The vulnerability exists in the way the Smart Agent processes DSRequest messages with excessive data.

The PCRE pattern "/[0-9a-zA-Z]{50}/R" in the rule detects attempts to send 50 or more consecutive alphanumeric characters after the DSRequest identifier, which is a signature of this exploit. The reference URL points to Luigi Auriemma's security advisory that provides technical details about this vulnerability.

Organizations running Borland VisiBroker services should implement network filtering to restrict access to port 14000/UDP, apply vendor patches if available, or consider implementing application-level filtering to validate input length. Additionally, monitoring for alerts triggered by this rule can help identify potential exploitation attempts targeting this service.

The rule targets established TCP connections originating from any port above 1024 on the internal network to any port above 1024 on external networks. It specifically looks for a 2-byte payload containing the exact string "OK" being sent to the C&C server.

The "trojan-activity" classification indicates this traffic is associated with malware that maintains persistent communication with attacker-controlled infrastructure. The rule has been marked as "DELETED" in the ruleset, suggesting it may have been replaced by newer detection methods or is no longer considered effective.

Vipdataend is a trojan that establishes communication channels with remote servers for data exfiltration and command reception. The "OK" message likely represents a status update or acknowledgment sent from the infected host to the C&C server, confirming successful execution of commands or the operational status of the malware.

This type of simple, short confirmation message is a common technique used by malware authors to minimize detection by avoiding complex or large data transfers that might trigger network monitoring systems.

2007964.msg: ET DELETED Vipdataend C&C Traffic - Server Status OK
2007964.et_name: Vipdataend C&C Traffic - Server Status OK
2007964.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Vipdataend command and control (C&C) infrastructure, specifically server status acknowledgments from external C&C servers to compromised internal hosts.

The rule targets TCP traffic from external networks to internal networks on high ports (1024 and above) containing the exact content "OK" with a payload size of exactly 2 bytes. This pattern represents a server status acknowledgment message sent from the Vipdataend C&C server to infected internal systems.

The rule is designed to identify communication between command and control servers and compromised internal hosts. The "OK" response is a simple status confirmation mechanism used by the C&C infrastructure to maintain connection with infected systems. This type of minimal, predictable response pattern is common in malware C&C protocols to avoid detection while confirming command execution or system availability.

The classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this traffic is associated with malicious software that has compromised internal systems. The rule specifically looks for established connections with traffic flowing from external C&C servers to internal compromised hosts, suggesting this is part of an ongoing communication channel rather than initial infection activity.

Detection of such traffic indicates active malware infection within the network requiring immediate response. Recommended actions include:
1. Isolate the affected internal system(s) receiving these communications
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures for forensic analysis
3. Examine the compromised host for persistence mechanisms and additional malware components
4. Review network logs to identify initial infection vectors and potential lateral movement
5. Block the external IP addresses at network boundaries to prevent further C&C communication

2007967.msg: ET MALWARE Universal1337 FTP Upload of Compromised Data
2007967.et_name: Universal1337 FTP Upload of Compromised Data
2007967.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Universal1337 trojan, specifically when it attempts to exfiltrate compromised data via FTP.

The rule monitors outbound TCP connections from internal networks to external destinations on high ports (1024 and above). It identifies the Universal1337 malware by looking for specific patterns in the traffic: a line of hash symbols followed by a carriage return and line feed, another line of hash symbols at distance 0 from the previous match, and the string " Universal1337 " at distance 0 from the second content match. The flow:established,to_server directive ensures that only established connections from the client to the server are evaluated, filtering out connection attempts and server responses.

When triggered, this indicates that a system on the internal network is likely infected with the Universal1337 trojan and is actively transmitting stolen data to an external FTP server. The malware uses a distinctive signature in its communications that includes the Universal1337 identifier.

Upon detection, security teams should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further data exfiltration
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Examine the source IP to identify the compromised host and check for additional infections
4. Review firewall and proxy logs to determine what data may have been exfiltrated
5. Analyze the destination IP/domain for additional threat intelligence and block it at network boundaries
6. Scan the affected system with updated anti-malware tools focusing on Universal1337 indicators

The rule is classified as "trojan-activity" which appropriately categorizes the threat as malicious software designed to steal information. According to the reference URL included in the rule, Universal1337 is a known trojan with documented capabilities for compromising systems and exfiltrating data.

This detection is significant as it indicates active data exfiltration from the network, representing a security breach that requires immediate investigation and remediation to prevent data loss.

2007968.msg: ET MALWARE Universal1337 Email Upload of Compromised Data
2007968.et_name: Universal1337 Email Upload of Compromised Data

The rule monitors outbound SMTP traffic (TCP port 25) from internal networks to external mail servers, specifically looking for distinctive patterns in the email content that match the Universal1337 trojan's communication signature.

The rule identifies three key content patterns that must appear in sequence: a line of hash symbols followed by a carriage return and line feed, another sequence of hash symbols, and the string " Universal1337 ". These patterns serve as identifiers for data being uploaded by the malware.

Universal1337 is a trojan that collects sensitive information from infected systems and attempts to send this data to attackers via email. When active, the malware packages stolen information and transmits it through SMTP, using a distinctive formatting pattern that this rule detects.

The detection is significant because it identifies active data exfiltration - the actual transmission of compromised information leaving the network. This represents a serious security breach where sensitive data is already being sent to external parties.

The rule references documentation about the Universal1337 trojan at www[.]megasecurity[.]org/trojans/u/universal1337/Universal1337v2[.]html, which provides additional context about this threat.

2007975.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations that matches patterns commonly associated with trojan downloader check-in communications.

The rule identifies HTTP requests containing specific URL parameters that follow a pattern used by malware to report system information back to command and control servers. Specifically, it looks for HTTP requests with a URL path ending in ".php?pid=" followed by parameters including "mac=", "&amd=", and "&win64=". These parameters likely represent system information being exfiltrated, such as processor architecture details (AMD), 64-bit Windows status, and MAC address. The "nocase" modifier ensures detection regardless of letter case, preventing evasion through case manipulation.

The "flow:established,to_server" requirement ensures the rule only triggers on established TCP connections originating from the internal network, reducing false positives by focusing on outbound client requests rather than server responses or connection attempts.

The detection focuses on the initial communication phase when an infected system reports back to its controller. This check-in process typically includes system fingerprinting data that helps the attacker determine what additional payloads to deliver or commands to issue.

This type of communication is significant as it represents an active malware infection attempting to establish command and control communications. Once this channel is established, attackers can download additional malicious components, exfiltrate data, or execute remote commands on the compromised system.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further command and control communication
2. Capture full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Examine the HTTP requests to identify the complete C2 infrastructure
4. Investigate the affected system for persistence mechanisms and additional malware components
5. Check other systems for similar communication patterns using the identified indicators

False positives may occur with legitimate applications using similar parameter structures. Verify by examining the destination domain reputation and the complete HTTP request content.

2007979.msg: ET MALWARE Backdoor.Win32.VB.brg C&C Reporting Version
2007979.description:
This rule detects command and control (C2) communication from the Backdoor.Win32.VB.brg malware variant. The rule specifically identifies when an infected system reports its version information to a remote C2 server.

The rule monitors outbound TCP traffic from internal networks to external destinations on high ports (1024 and above). It looks for established connections containing the specific byte pattern "Version(*" followed by ")*" within 8 bytes, which represents the version reporting format used by this backdoor.

The Backdoor.Win32.VB.brg is a Visual Basic-based backdoor that provides remote attackers with unauthorized access to compromised Windows systems. When infected, the malware communicates with its C2 infrastructure to report system information, including version details of the implant.

This detection is significant because version reporting is typically part of the initial check-in process when malware establishes communication with its command infrastructure. Identifying this traffic allows security teams to detect compromised systems in the early stages of an infection, before extensive data exfiltration or lateral movement occurs.

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" indicates this is part of the malware's operational infrastructure rather than the initial infection vector.

2007980.msg: ET MALWARE Backdoor.Win32.VB.brg C&C Kill Command Send
2007980.description:
This rule detects command and control (C2) communication associated with the Backdoor.Win32.VB.brg malware variant. Specifically, it identifies kill commands being sent from an external server to an infected host within the protected network.

The rule monitors established TCP connections from external networks (using high ports 1024 and above) to any port on internal networks, focusing on traffic flowing from the server to the client. It looks for relatively small packets (less than 35 bytes) containing the string "kill-" at the beginning of the payload. The rule further validates the traffic using a regular expression that matches a specific command format: "kill-" followed by an IP address, a colon, a port number, a percentage sign, and a digit (e.g., "kill-192.168.1.1:4444%1").

This detection is significant because it identifies active control of compromised systems by attackers. The "kill" command likely terminates processes or connections on the infected host, potentially as part of maintaining persistence, evading detection, or preparing for other malicious activities. The command format suggests the malware reports back specific information about the target system, including IP address, port, and possibly a process identifier.

When this rule triggers, immediate investigation is warranted. Security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system to prevent further command execution
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Examine the affected host for signs of compromise, focusing on running processes, network connections, and system modifications
4. Identify and block the external C2 server IP at network boundaries
5. Scan the environment for other systems exhibiting similar communication patterns

The rule is classified as "command-and-control" which indicates it detects communication between compromised hosts and their controlling infrastructure. This type of traffic represents an active intrusion where attackers have already established a foothold in the environment and are issuing commands to compromised systems.

2007981.msg: ET MALWARE Backdoor.Win32.VB.brg C&C Kill Command Acknowledge
2007981.description:

The rule triggers when TCP traffic from any port on the internal network is sent to a high port (1024 or above) on an external network, containing the specific string "Status(*UDP Attack Running!*)" with a packet size of exactly 29 bytes. This indicates the malware is confirming successful execution of a UDP flooding attack command received from its controller.

This detection is significant as it identifies active malware communication during an attack sequence. The backdoor appears to have DDoS capabilities, specifically UDP flooding functionality, which can be used to disrupt services and networks. The acknowledgment message provides confirmation to the attacker that their attack instructions were received and executed.

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" correctly identifies this as malicious traffic associated with botnet operations. The specific message format suggests this is part of a structured communication protocol between the malware and its controller, where the infected system reports back on attack status.

Network defenders should prioritize investigation of any systems triggering this alert as they indicate active malware infections with potential for both data theft and participation in DDoS attacks against other organizations.

Banking Trojans are specialized malware designed to steal financial credentials and banking information from infected systems. This particular rule detects the HTTP-based communication channel used by the malware to transmit stolen data to attacker-controlled servers.

2007986.msg: ET MALWARE Emogen Reporting via HTTP

The rule identifies potential adware or potentially unwanted program (PUP) activity by monitoring for the specific pattern "User-Agent: " (with two spaces following the colon) in HTTP headers. 2007994.description:
Trojan User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Trojan User-Agent strings that are leveraged by compromised machines.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Trojan often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Trojan User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

2007998.et_name: Rediff Bol Downloader ActiveX Control Remote Code Execution
2007998.description:
ActiveX controls are Microsoft Internet Explorer’s native version of plug-ins and can be leveraged by non browse applications as well..  ActiveX provides web application developers a facility to execute code on a client machine through the web browser.  Unfortunately, ActiveX controls have been a significant source of security problems both due to vulnerabilities in the ActiveX control itself, in the browser which can allow the activeX control to bypass security, as well as the fact that it has extensive capabilities to attacker drive code.
ActiveX controls are very powerful and can be used for legitimate and nefarious purposes including monitoring your personal browsing habits, install malware, generate pop-ups, log your keystrokes and passwords, and do other malicious things. ActiveX controls are actually not Internet Explorer-only. They also work in other Microsoft applications, such as Microsoft Office. Other browsers, such as Firefox, Chrome, Safari, and Opera, all use other types of browser plug-ins. ActiveX controls only function in Internet Explorer. A website that requires an ActiveX control is an Internet Explorer-only website.
If you see these ActiveX controls alerts firing, they are unlikely to succeed in exploiting all but legacy windows systems running older versions of IE.  To help validate whether the signature is triggering a valid compromise you should look for other malicious signatures related to the client endpoint which is triggering.  This includes Exploit Kit, Malware, and Command and Control signatures, along with looking to see if the web server is known to be malicious in ET Intelligence.

The detection focuses on the initial or ongoing communication between infected systems and the attacker's infrastructure rather than the initial infection vector.

2008005.description:

The rule triggers when traffic from internal networks to external networks on high ports (1024 and above) contains two specific strings: "*************CD-Key Pack**************" followed by "|0d 0a|Microsoft Windows Product ID CD Key|3a|". These strings indicate the malware is collecting and transmitting Windows product keys and system information. The distance:0 modifier ensures the second content match occurs immediately after the first string, confirming the specific data structure used by this malware variant.

The backdoor uses FTP as its exfiltration channel, as indicated by the rule context and the structured format of the data being sent. The hex values "|0d 0a|" represent carriage return and line feed characters, showing the malware formats its output in a specific way when sending stolen information.

This detection is significant because it identifies credential theft activity - specifically the harvesting of Windows product keys which can be used for software piracy or to create unauthorized installations. The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" confirms this is malicious behavior associated with backdoor functionality.

The established flow direction (to_server) indicates this rule triggers on outbound connections from compromised hosts attempting to send harvested data to attacker-controlled servers.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further data exfiltration
2. Examine FTP logs to identify the destination server and any previously exfiltrated data
3. Conduct memory forensics to identify the full backdoor capabilities and persistence mechanisms
4. Search for additional indicators of compromise across the environment, particularly other systems communicating with the same external destinations
5. Review network traffic for other instances of sensitive data exfiltration that may have occurred

This rule (SID:2008005, revision 4) has been refined over time to accurately detect this specific malware variant with minimal false positives.

2008012.msg: ET MALWARE Winquickupdates.com/Mycashloads.com Related Trojan Install Report
2008012.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations that appears to be a Trojan infection reporting back to command and control servers.

The rule specifically monitors for HTTP requests to "/newuser.php?saff=" followed by either numeric values or strings starting with "x". This pattern matches communication from infected systems to the domains winquickupdates[.]com or mycashloads[.]com, which are associated with Trojan distribution.

The detection focuses on the "phone home" behavior where newly infected systems register themselves with the malware operators. The HTTP URI pattern represents a callback mechanism where the malware reports successful installation to its command infrastructure, likely including an affiliate ID (indicated by the "saff" parameter) for tracking distribution channels.

The PCRE pattern "/^(?:\d+|x.+)/R" specifically examines the content after the "saff=" parameter, using the "R" modifier to match against the raw URI buffer rather than the normalized one, ensuring detection even if URI encoding is used to evade detection.

The "flow:established,to_server" directive ensures the rule only triggers on established TCP connections originating from internal hosts and directed to external servers, focusing specifically on outbound request traffic rather than server responses.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further command and control communication
2. Capture full packet captures of the traffic for forensic analysis
3. Examine the specific "saff" parameter value to identify the infection vector or campaign
4. Scan the system with updated anti-malware tools focusing on Trojan detection
5. Check for additional indicators of compromise including registry modifications, scheduled tasks, and persistence mechanisms

This threat is classified as "trojan-activity" which indicates malicious software that misrepresents itself as legitimate while performing unauthorized actions. The rule targets the initial reporting phase of an infection, which is a critical point for detecting compromises before further malicious activities occur.

2008013.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic with a suspicious User-Agent header that contains only the word "Internet" from internal networks to external destinations.

The rule targets adware or potentially unwanted programs (PUP) that use an abnormally simple and non-standard User-Agent string. Legitimate browsers typically include detailed information in their User-Agent headers (browser name, version, operating system, etc.), while this rule identifies traffic where the entire User-Agent is just "Internet".

This pattern is significant because it deviates from standard browser behavior and is likely associated with adware or PUP communication. The rule uses the "startswith" and "endswith" modifiers to ensure the User-Agent string contains only the word "Internet" with no additional characters before or after it.

The classification "pup-activity" indicates this is related to potentially unwanted programs rather than more severe threats like malware or exploitation attempts. While not necessarily malicious, such traffic may indicate the presence of unwanted software that could impact system performance, collect user data, or display unwanted advertisements.

Network defenders should investigate systems generating this traffic to identify and potentially remove the associated adware or PUP.

2008015.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations where the User-Agent string contains "Win95".

The alert identifies outbound HTTP connections with a User-Agent string containing "Win95", which is significant because Windows 95 is an obsolete operating system that has been unsupported for decades. Modern legitimate software would not typically identify itself as running on this platform.

The presence of such User-Agent strings in contemporary network traffic strongly indicates adware or potentially unwanted program (PUP) activity. Malicious software often uses outdated or unusual User-Agent strings to disguise its communication or as part of its command and control infrastructure.

The rule specifically monitors established connections from internal clients to external servers (flow:established,to_server), ensuring it only captures outbound request traffic rather than responses. The fast_pattern modifier indicates that "Win95" is used as an efficient pattern for initial packet matching, improving performance.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Identify the source system generating the traffic and isolate it for further investigation
2. Capture full packet data of the session for detailed analysis of the HTTP requests and responses
3. Examine the destination IP/domain for reputation and historical context
4. Perform endpoint scanning on the source system for potential adware/PUP infections
5. Review other traffic from the same source for additional suspicious patterns

This detection is important because it may reveal compromised systems within the network that are communicating with external servers using suspicious identifiers. Such traffic could indicate data exfiltration, command and control communication, or other malicious activity disguised as coming from legacy systems.

The rule has undergone multiple revisions (currently at revision 14), suggesting ongoing maintenance to improve detection accuracy and reduce false positives over time.

2008016.msg: ET ADWARE_PUP Servicepack.kr Fake Patch Software Checkin
2008016.description:
This rule detects HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations associated with Servicepack[.]kr, a known fake patch software provider. The rule specifically identifies check-in communications from potentially unwanted programs (PUP) installed on the local network.

The detection focuses on HTTP requests containing multiple specific parameters in the URI, including "kind", "ver", "ver2", "ver3", "pid", "supportid", and "uniq". These parameters are likely used by the adware/PUP to report installation status, version information, and unique identifiers back to command and control servers.

The rule targets established HTTP connections flowing from internal hosts to external servers, suggesting this is post-infection traffic where the adware is communicating with its operators. The "fast_pattern" option indicates that ".php?kind=" is used as the primary pattern for efficient matching.

This type of adware/PUP typically masquerades as legitimate system update software but instead delivers unwanted advertisements, collects user data, or installs additional unwanted software. The check-in behavior detected by this rule likely represents the adware reporting successful installation or requesting further instructions.

When this alert triggers, security analysts should:
1. Identify and isolate the affected host(s) generating the traffic
2. Examine the host for unauthorized software installations, particularly fake system update tools
3. Collect and analyze full HTTP session data to determine what information is being exfiltrated
4. Use endpoint detection tools to locate and remove the PUP/adware components
5. Scan the affected system for additional malware that may have been installed alongside the PUP
6. Block the destination domains/IPs at the network perimeter to prevent further communication
7. Review system logs to determine initial infection vector and timeline

The classification as "pup-activity" confirms this is related to potentially unwanted programs rather than more severe malware categories, though such software still poses privacy and security risks to affected systems.

2008019.description:
A Trojan-Downloader is a type of malware that is responsible for loading and facilitating the continued proliferation of further payloads upon the victim machine. Typically, Trojan-Downloaders will ensure further infection is successful but reporting a successful install, modifying system settings to ensure future malware can be installed/executed without issue, and enable persistency mechanisms for long term infection. Windows is the most commonly observed platform for this type of infection, however, it is not limited-- Macintosh OS X and Linux are also potential targets for compromise.
Valid Trojan-Downloader activity can include network connectivity to a command and control server to report successful infection on a victim machine. Typically, machines impacted with a Trojan-Downloader will have several system settings modified, such as modifications to the Registry where malicious entries may be made. Additionally, the download of a second-stage payload may occur once the original malware has ran. Trojan-Downloaders have been observed with the ability to exfiltrate sensitive data. Confirmation of hostile IP addresses or domains observed with Trojan-Downloader activity may take place in the ET Intelligence portal.
From a network perspective, malware that falls under the Trojan-Downloader has been observed performing activity that would trigger several Emerging Threats INFO, POLICY, and TROJAN style alerts, such as checking an external IP address, the presence of a downloaded executable, or a suspicious HTTP POST to a server. This combination of Trojan-Downloader alerts, as well as complimentary INFO, POLICY, or TROJAN alerts, would warrant an immediate follow up for a compromised workstation.

2008020.msg: ET WORM Win32.Socks.s HTTP Post Checkin
2008020.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Win32.Socks.s worm attempting to communicate with command and control servers.

The rule monitors HTTP POST requests from internal networks to external destinations, specifically targeting POST requests to PHP scripts where the HTTP request body begins with the string "proc=[System Process]" followed by a newline character (0a in hexadecimal).

The detection focuses on the worm's check-in behavior, where infected systems report back to their controllers using a specific HTTP POST format. The presence of "[System Process]" in the request body indicates the malware is likely collecting and exfiltrating system process information as part of its reconnaissance activities.

This type of communication pattern is characteristic of trojan backdoor activity, allowing remote attackers to maintain persistence and control over infected systems. The worm leverages HTTP, a commonly allowed protocol in most network environments, to bypass security controls.

The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this is malicious software designed to provide unauthorized access to the affected system. Network defenders should investigate any triggers of this rule as they likely indicate an active infection requiring immediate remediation.

2008021.msg: ET MALWARE Turkojan C&C Initial Checkin (ams)
2008021.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Turkojan remote access trojan's command and control (C&C) communications.

The rule specifically identifies the initial check-in phase of the Turkojan malware when it attempts to communicate with its C&C server. It triggers when a TCP connection from any internal network host connects to an external destination using a high port (1024 or above) and sends a packet containing exactly 3 bytes with the content "ams".

The key detection components include:
- Direction: Internal to external network communication
- Protocol: TCP
- Destination ports: 1024 and above
- Payload size: Exactly 3 bytes
- Specific content: The string "ams"
- Flow type: Established connection, traffic flowing to server

Turkojan is a remote access trojan (RAT) that provides attackers with unauthorized control over infected systems. This initial check-in communication represents the first step in establishing a command and control channel, allowing the attacker to issue commands to the compromised host. The detection of this traffic pattern indicates a likely system compromise requiring immediate investigation.

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" highlights its significance in identifying malware that maintains persistent communication with external controlling servers, a critical phase in the cyber kill chain that enables attackers to maintain presence and execute additional malicious activities on compromised systems.

2008022.msg: ET MALWARE Turkojan C&C Info Command (MINFO)
2008022.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Turkojan remote access trojan's command and control (C2) communications.

The rule specifically identifies the "MINFO" command sent from a C2 server to an infected host on the internal network. This command is part of the Turkojan C2 protocol and is used to transmit machine information requests to the compromised system.

The rule parameters indicate:
- Direction: External to internal network traffic
- Protocol: TCP
- Source: External network using port 81 or higher
- Destination: Any port on the home network
- Payload size: Exactly 5 bytes
- Content match: The string "MINFO"
- Flow: Established connection, traffic flowing to the client (from C2 server to infected host)

Turkojan is a commercial remote access trojan that provides attackers with capabilities to control compromised systems, steal information, and monitor user activities. The "MINFO" command is sent from the C2 server to the infected client to request machine information from the compromised system.

This detection is significant as it identifies active command and control communications from a known malware family. The presence of this traffic confirms a system on the network is compromised and under remote control by an unauthorized party.

Recommended response actions:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent lateral movement
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures for forensic analysis
3. Examine the compromised host for persistence mechanisms and additional malware
4. Investigate how the initial infection occurred
5. Check for data exfiltration evidence by reviewing network logs for suspicious outbound connections
6. Scan other systems on the network for similar indicators of compromise

2008023.msg: ET MALWARE Turkojan C&C Info Command Response (MINFO)
2008023.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Turkojan remote access trojan's command and control (C&C) communications.

The rule specifically identifies outbound TCP connections from internal networks to external servers on port 81 that contain the string "MINFO|7c|" within the first 6 bytes of the payload. The payload size is also constrained to be less than 100 bytes. This pattern represents a specific command response format used by the Turkojan malware when communicating with its C&C server.

Turkojan is a remote access trojan (RAT) that provides attackers with unauthorized access to compromised systems. The "MINFO" command appears to be related to machine information gathering, where the malware is sending system details back to the attacker's infrastructure. The "|7c|" represents the hexadecimal value for the pipe character (|) which serves as a delimiter in the command structure.

This detection is significant as it identifies active C&C communications from an infected host, indicating a system compromise. The established flow and direction (to_server) parameters ensure the rule only triggers on outbound traffic from an infected host to the C&C server, reducing false positives.

Organizations detecting this traffic should immediately isolate the affected system, as it indicates an active malware infection with potential data exfiltration and remote control capabilities.

2008024.msg: ET MALWARE Turkojan C&C Logs Parse Command (LOGS1)
2008024.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Turkojan remote access trojan's command and control (C&C) communications, specifically when the C&C server sends the "LOGS1" command to an infected host.

The rule triggers on TCP traffic from external networks (using high ports 1024 and above) to any port on internal networks when the payload is exactly 5 bytes and contains the string "LOGS1" within the first 5 bytes of the packet. The flow directive ensures the alert only fires on established connections where traffic is flowing toward the client.

Turkojan is a commercial remote access trojan (RAT) that provides attackers with extensive control over infected systems. The "LOGS1" command appears to be part of the C&C protocol used to request or parse logs from compromised hosts. This communication pattern indicates an active infection where the C&C server is instructing the malware to transmit collected logs back to the attacker.

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" highlights its significance in detecting post-compromise activity where an attacker is actively controlling a compromised system within the network. Detection of such traffic warrants immediate investigation as it indicates an active malware infection with external control.

When this Emerging Threats (ET) rule with SID 2008024 (revision 5) triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further data exfiltration
2. Capture full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Identify and examine all connections from the compromised host to the C&C server IP address
4. Search for additional Turkojan indicators across the environment, including registry modifications and persistence mechanisms
5. Collect and preserve memory dumps and system logs from the affected host for malware analysis
6. Block the C&C server IP at network boundaries to prevent further communication

2008025.msg: ET MALWARE Turkojan C&C Logs Parse Response Response (LOGS1)
2008025.et_name: Turkojan C&C Logs Parse Response Response (LOGS1)
2008025.description:
This Suricata rule detects network traffic associated with the Turkojan remote access trojan's command and control (C2) communications. Specifically, it identifies when an infected system on the internal network sends a specific response pattern to an external C2 server.

The rule triggers when TCP traffic from any internal network host is sent to an external destination using a high port (1024 or above). It looks for the specific byte sequence "|08 00 00 00|LOGS1|5b|" at the beginning of the packet payload (offset:0; depth:10), which appears to be a protocol marker for the "LOGS1" command response in Turkojan's C2 protocol. The flow:established,to_server parameter ensures the rule only matches traffic in an established TCP connection flowing from the client to the server, reducing false positives.

Turkojan is a commercial remote access trojan (RAT) that provides attackers with comprehensive control over infected systems. This particular rule detects when an infected host is responding to a command to exfiltrate logs to the C2 server. The "[" character (hex 5b) following "LOGS1" likely indicates the beginning of a data structure containing the stolen log information.

This detection is significant as it identifies active data exfiltration from a compromised system. When Turkojan exfiltrates logs, it may be sending sensitive information such as keystrokes, screenshots, or system information to the attacker's infrastructure.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further data exfiltration
2. Capture full packet captures of the communication if possible for forensic analysis
3. Examine the affected system for persistence mechanisms and additional malware
4. Check for lateral movement attempts from the compromised host
5. Investigate what data may have been exfiltrated by examining system logs and Turkojan artifacts
6. Block the destination IP at the network perimeter and add it to threat intelligence feeds

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" correctly identifies this as malicious communication between an infected host and its controller.

2008026.description:
This rule detects command and control (C2) traffic associated with the Turkojan remote access trojan. The rule specifically identifies keepalive communications where an infected system sends the string "BAGLANTI?" to a remote server.

The rule targets outbound TCP connections from internal networks to external destinations using high ports (1024 and above). It only triggers on established connections with traffic flowing from the client to the server, and specifically looks for network packets with a data size of exactly 9 bytes containing the Turkish word "BAGLANTI?" (which translates to "CONNECTION?" in English).

Turkojan is a commercial remote access trojan that provides attackers with capabilities including keylogging, screen capture, file access, and remote control of infected systems. This particular rule identifies the periodic keepalive messages that infected systems send to maintain their connection with the command and control infrastructure.

The detection of this traffic pattern indicates an active Turkojan infection in the environment, with the compromised system already communicating with its controller. This represents a significant security incident as the attacker likely has complete control over the infected system and access to sensitive data.

When this rule triggers, immediate response actions should include: 1) Isolate the affected system from the network to prevent further communication with C2 servers, 2) Capture and preserve full packet captures for forensic analysis, 3) Identify the source IP address and investigate all systems that have communicated with the compromised host, and 4) Initiate incident response procedures for malware containment and eradication.

For remediation, conduct a full system scan with updated anti-malware tools, perform memory forensics to identify persistence mechanisms, and consider rebuilding the affected system from trusted media. Additionally, review network logs to identify when the initial infection occurred and what other systems may have been compromised.

This rule is classified as "command-and-control" (classtype), has a Suricata ID of 2008026, and is currently at revision 3.

2008027.msg: ET MALWARE Turkojan C&C Browse Drive Command (BROWSC)
2008027.description:
This rule detects command and control (C2) traffic associated with the Turkojan remote access trojan, specifically identifying when an infected system receives a command to browse drives.

The rule targets established TCP connections from external networks (ports 1024 and above) to any port on the internal network. It looks for relatively small packets (less than 100 bytes) containing the string "BROWS" within the first 5 bytes, followed by a colon character (":") within the next 2 bytes.

Turkojan is a remote access trojan that provides attackers with complete control over infected systems. This particular rule identifies the specific command sequence used when the attacker instructs the malware to enumerate and browse the victim's drives - a reconnaissance activity typically performed early in an attack to locate valuable data.

The "BROWSC" command pattern represents the attacker's instruction to the malware to provide information about the victim's file system. This capability allows attackers to navigate through directories, identify sensitive files, and prepare for data exfiltration.

This detection is significant as drive enumeration often precedes data theft, indicating an active intrusion where the attacker is manually exploring the compromised system to identify valuable information.

2008028.msg: ET MALWARE Turkojan C&C Browse Drive Command Response (metin)
2008028.et_name: Turkojan C&C Browse Drive Command Response (metin)
2008028.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Turkojan remote access trojan's command and control (C2) communications, specifically when it responds to a "Browse Drive" command.

The rule monitors TCP traffic from internal networks to external networks on high ports (1024 and above). It identifies a specific pattern in the traffic where the string "metin" preceded by two null bytes (|00 00|) and followed by the hexadecimal values 0x0D and 0x3A (carriage return and colon characters) appears at a specific position in the packet payload. The offset:2 and depth:11 parameters ensure the pattern is found starting at the third byte of the payload and within the first 11 bytes, which helps reduce false positives by targeting the exact protocol structure used by Turkojan.

Turkojan is a commercial remote access trojan (RAT) that provides attackers with extensive control over infected systems. The "Browse Drive" functionality allows attackers to remotely explore the file system of the compromised machine. When this command is executed, the malware responds with information about the drives and directories on the victim's system, using the specific protocol pattern identified in this rule. The string "metin" is a distinctive marker in Turkojan's protocol that indicates file system enumeration data is being transmitted.

This detection is significant because file system browsing represents an active intrusion where attackers are manually exploring a compromised system, typically as a precursor to data theft, lateral movement, or other malicious activities. The classification as "command-and-control" indicates this is part of the operational infrastructure used by attackers to maintain control over infected systems.

When this alert triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent data exfiltration
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures for forensic analysis
3. Examine the affected system for additional Turkojan artifacts, focusing on persistence mechanisms
4. Review network logs to identify the initial infection vector and any other compromised systems
5. Block the destination IP at the network perimeter to disrupt the C2 channel
6. Collect memory dumps from the affected system for malware analysis

2008029.msg: ET MALWARE Turkojan C&C nxt Command (nxt)
2008029.description:
This rule detects command and control (C2) traffic associated with the Turkojan remote access trojan. Specifically, it identifies the "nxt" command sent from an external server to a host on the internal network.

The rule targets TCP traffic from external networks using high ports (1024 and above) to internal network hosts on ports 1023 and above. It only triggers on established connections where data is flowing toward the client, and specifically looks for packets that are exactly 3 bytes in size containing the string "nxt" within the first 3 bytes of the payload.

Turkojan is a remote access trojan that provides attackers with comprehensive control over infected systems. The "nxt" command appears to be part of the trojan's command protocol, likely instructing the malware to perform a specific function or move to the next stage in its operation sequence.

The classification as "command-and-control" indicates this traffic represents communication between the malware and its control server. This type of traffic is particularly significant as it indicates an active infection where the attacker is issuing commands to compromised systems within the protected network.

Detection of this traffic pattern should trigger immediate incident response procedures as it indicates an active compromise with external control of internal systems.

2008030.msg: ET MALWARE Turkojan C&C nxt Command Response (nxt)
2008030.description:
This Suricata rule detects network traffic associated with the Turkojan remote access trojan's command and control (C&C) communications. Specifically, it identifies responses from a C&C server containing the "nxt" command.

The rule monitors TCP traffic from external networks on high ports (1024 and above) to any port on the internal network. It triggers when the following conditions are met:
- Established TCP connection with traffic flowing to the client (internal host)
- Packet size is exactly 16 bytes
- Content includes the string "nxt" followed by the hex values 09 00 00 00 within the first 7 bytes

Turkojan is a remote access trojan that provides attackers with complete control over infected systems. This particular rule identifies the "nxt" command response from the C&C server, which likely instructs the malware to execute the next command or move to the next stage in its operation.

The detection of C&C traffic is critical as it indicates an active malware infection where the attacker maintains persistent control over the compromised system. This type of communication enables data exfiltration, further system compromise, and potential lateral movement within a network.

Upon alert triggering, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected internal host immediately to prevent further command execution
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Examine the host for indicators of compromise, focusing on persistence mechanisms
4. Review network logs to identify the initial infection vector and any additional C&C communications
5. Block the external IP at the network perimeter and add it to threat intelligence feeds

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" highlights its significance in identifying malicious infrastructure communication rather than just initial infection vectors.

2008031.msg: ET MALWARE Dorf/Win32.Inject.adt C&C Communication Outbound
2008031.description:
This Suricata rule detects outbound command and control (C2) communications associated with the Dorf/Win32.Inject.adt malware variant.

The rule triggers when TCP traffic originating from any port on the internal network attempts to connect to any destination port 1024 or higher on external networks. The alert specifically looks for established connections with a packet size of exactly 16 bytes containing the specific byte pattern "1SCD|00 00|" within the first 6 bytes of the payload.

This detection identifies infected systems attempting to communicate with remote C2 servers. The Dorf/Win32.Inject.adt malware uses this distinctive network signature when "phoning home" to its operators. The fixed packet size (16 bytes) and specific command header pattern serve as reliable indicators of compromise.

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" indicates this traffic represents an active malware infection where the compromised system is receiving instructions from or sending data to its controllers. This type of communication typically enables remote access, data exfiltration, or further system compromise.

Organizations detecting this traffic should immediately isolate the affected system, as it indicates an active malware infection attempting to maintain persistence through external communication channels.

2008032.msg: ET MALWARE Dorf/Win32.Inject.adt C&C Communication Inbound
2008032.description:
This Suricata rule detects inbound command and control (C2) communications associated with the Dorf/Win32.Inject.adt malware variant. The rule specifically monitors established TCP connections from external networks (ports 1024 and above) to any port on the internal network.

The detection focuses on network traffic with exactly 16 bytes in size containing the specific byte pattern "1SCD|00 00|" within the first 6 bytes of the packet payload. This distinctive signature represents the communication protocol used by the malware's command and control infrastructure to issue instructions to infected systems.

The Dorf malware family (also known as Win32.Inject.adt) is a trojan that establishes persistent connections to remote servers, allowing attackers to control compromised systems. This particular rule identifies the inbound communication channel where the C2 server sends commands to infected hosts.

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" indicates its severity, as C2 traffic represents active control of compromised systems by threat actors. Detection of this traffic pattern strongly suggests an active malware infection requiring immediate remediation to prevent data exfiltration, lateral movement, or other malicious activities.

2008033.msg: ET DELETED Banker.maf SMTP Checkin (Not in the Control...)
2008033.et_name: Banker.maf SMTP Checkin (Not in the Control...)
2008033.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Banker.maf banking trojan's command and control communications.

The rule monitors outbound SMTP traffic (TCP port 25) from internal networks to external destinations. It specifically identifies when a compromised system attempts to communicate with command and control servers using distinctive email headers and message content. The rule requires an established TCP connection with traffic flowing to the server.

The detection focuses on two key patterns:
1. An X-Mailer header claiming to be "Microsoft CDO for Windows 2000"
2. A specific message body containing the text "_-=| Not in the Control System 6.0 |=-_" followed by a period, which must appear within a specific distance from the first pattern

This appears to be a check-in mechanism where infected systems report their status to remote operators through SMTP channels. The rule is classified as "trojan-activity" which accurately reflects its purpose in identifying malware command and control traffic.

Banking trojans like this typically steal financial credentials, online banking session data, and other sensitive information from compromised systems. The SMTP communication channel allows the malware to exfiltrate stolen data or receive commands while attempting to blend in with normal email traffic.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further data exfiltration
2. Capture full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Examine the affected system for additional indicators of compromise
4. Review email logs to identify when the infection occurred and potential lateral movement
5. Block the destination IP at network boundaries to prevent further communication

The specific string patterns in this rule represent unique signatures of the Banker.maf variant, making this a high-fidelity detection for this particular banking trojan's communications.

2008034.msg: ET MALWARE LDPinch SMTP Password Report

2008035.description:
This Suricata rule (SID 2008035) detects HTTP traffic associated with the System.Poser malware checking in with its command and control server. The rule has been marked as DELETED in the message field, indicating it has been deprecated or replaced by newer detection methods.

The rule triggers when an internal host makes an HTTP request to an external server with specific characteristics indicative of System.Poser malware communication. The detection focuses on three key elements:

1. The HTTP URI contains "/check.php?c=" (case insensitive)
2. The URI also contains the parameter "&v=" (case insensitive)
3. The User-Agent header is set to "Microsoft BITS"

System.Poser is a trojan that uses the Microsoft Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) as a disguise for its command and control communications. This technique helps the malware blend in with legitimate traffic while maintaining persistence on infected systems.

2008039.msg: ET MALWARE Egspy Infection Report Email
2008039.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the EgySpy keylogger malware sending infection reports via email.

The rule monitors outbound SMTP traffic (TCP port 25) from internal networks to external mail servers. It specifically looks for emails with distinctive characteristics of EgySpy infection reports, including:

- A recipient identified as "EgySpy User"
- A subject line containing "E g y S p y KeyLogger" with spaces between characters

EgySpy is a keylogger trojan that captures user keystrokes and sends the collected data to attackers via email. This rule identifies the exfiltration phase of the infection when the malware is attempting to transmit stolen information.

The detection is significant because:
- It indicates an active keylogger infection capturing sensitive user input
- The compromised system is successfully communicating with external servers
- Credentials and other sensitive information are likely being exfiltrated

Recommended response actions:
1. Immediately isolate the affected system from the network
2. Capture and preserve a forensic image of the system for analysis
3. Examine email logs to identify when the infection began and what data may have been exfiltrated
4. Scan the system with updated anti-malware tools to identify and remove the keylogger

2008040.description:

As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware / Spyware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware / Spyware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Spyware often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Spyware User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

Spyware is a grey area, and isn't necessarily "malicious" depending on the observer's opinion.

These signatures are a good indicator of a compromised client, server, phone, etc.

Empty User-Agent headers are anomalous in legitimate web traffic, as browsers and legitimate applications typically include identifying information. This pattern is commonly associated with adware and potentially unwanted programs (PUP) that attempt to hide their identity while communicating with command and control servers or tracking systems.

The absence of User-Agent information represents an attempt to evade detection or fingerprinting while maintaining HTTP communication channels. This technique helps malicious software remain undetected while exfiltrating data or receiving instructions.

When investigating alerts from this rule, analysts should:
1. Identify the internal host generating the empty User-Agent traffic and examine it for signs of adware infection

4. Correlate with endpoint security logs to identify the process generating the traffic
5. Consider isolating the host if multiple indicators of compromise are present

The rule's classification as "pup-activity" indicates it's targeting potentially unwanted programs that may not be explicitly malicious but are associated with privacy concerns, system performance degradation, or unwanted advertising.

Organizations should investigate any triggered alerts to determine if the traffic originates from legitimate legacy systems that require isolation or replacement, or from potentially compromised hosts running malware that manipulates User-Agent strings.

2008087.description:

- A parameter "s=" followed by hexadecimal characters (A-F, 0-9)
- A parameter "t=" containing date information in format "digit/digit/20xx"

This traffic pattern is characteristic of the Downloader.VB.CEJ malware's command and control communications. The malware likely uses these HTTP requests to check in with its controller, potentially to receive instructions, download additional payloads, or exfiltrate data.

The rule classifies this activity as "command-and-control" traffic, indicating it represents malware communicating with its operators. This type of traffic is significant as it indicates an active malware infection within the network that has established external communications channels.
