rule_metadata.affected_product: Web_Server_Applications, attack_target Web_Server, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Datacenter, confidence Medium, signature_severity Major, tag SQL_Injection, updated_at 2020_09_14, mitre_tactic_id TA0001, mitre_tactic_name Initial_Access, mitre_technique_id T1190, mitre_technique_name Exploit_Public_Facing_Application

2008362.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2008364.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Donkeyp2p malware attempting to communicate with command and control servers for updates.

The rule monitors HTTP GET requests from internal networks to external destinations, specifically targeting requests to "donkeyp2p.php" that contain multiple parameters including "kind", "args", "ver", "uniq", and "dllver". This pattern represents the update mechanism used by the Donkeyp2p malware.

Donkeyp2p is a trojan that masquerades as a legitimate peer-to-peer file sharing application but contains malicious functionality. When infected, the malware attempts to contact its command and control infrastructure to receive updates or additional instructions using the specific HTTP request pattern defined in the rule.

The update mechanism uses a structured query format with multiple parameters that likely provide the controller with system information, version details, and a unique identifier for the infected host. The "dllver" parameter suggests the malware may use DLL files as part of its infection or update process.

The rule specifically looks for established TCP connections from the infected host to the server (flow:established,to_server), ensuring it only captures outbound update requests rather than responses. The "nocase" modifiers ensure detection regardless of case sensitivity in the GET method and "dllver" parameter, preventing evasion through case manipulation.

When this rule triggers, security teams should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further communication
2. Capture full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Examine the host for additional indicators of compromise, particularly focusing on DLL files
4. Search network logs for historical communication with the same external endpoints
5. Analyze HTTP traffic for other suspicious parameters or patterns that may indicate variant communications

This type of communication represents a significant security risk as it indicates an active malware infection attempting to maintain persistence and potentially download additional malicious components. The rule classifies this activity as "trojan-activity" which accurately reflects the nature of the threat.

2008365.msg: ET MALWARE Playtech Downloader Online Gaming Checkin
2008365.description:
This rule detects potential command-and-control communication from Playtech gaming software. The alert triggers when a system on the internal network makes an HTTP request to an external server with the specific URI path "/client_update_urls.php" while using a User-Agent string that begins with "Playtech|20|" (where |20| represents the hexadecimal value for a space character).

The rule identifies a specific pattern associated with Playtech downloader software checking in with remote servers. This behavior could indicate:

- Legitimate gaming software updates from Playtech
- Potentially compromised or malicious versions of Playtech software
- Command-and-control traffic disguised as gaming software communication

The detection focuses on the combination of the specific URI path and User-Agent string, which together create a distinctive network traffic signature. The rule references a specific MD5 hash (00740d7d15862efb30629ab1fd7b8242) associated with this activity, which security analysts should investigate to determine the specific malware variant.

This alert is classified as "command-and-control" traffic, indicating the security community has observed this pattern being used for remote control of compromised systems. The classification suggests this may represent malicious activity rather than legitimate software behavior, potentially allowing attackers to maintain persistence and control over infected systems.

The rule specifically targets established connections flowing from internal to external networks, which is consistent with the behavior of infected hosts communicating with command-and-control infrastructure. When investigating this alert, analysts should examine the full HTTP session details, verify the User-Agent format with the hexadecimal space character, and correlate with other suspicious network activities from the same host.

The rule's revision number (12) indicates it has been updated multiple times, suggesting ongoing refinement based on observed threat activity.

2008367.et_name: Possible Windows executable sent when remote host claims to send Javascript
2008367.description:
This rule detects attempts to deliver Windows executable files disguised as JavaScript content. The alert triggers when an external server sends HTTP traffic to internal networks with content that claims to be JavaScript (via Content-Type header) but actually contains Windows executable code.

The rule identifies this deception by looking for:
- HTTP responses from external servers to internal networks
- Content-Type header indicating JavaScript application
- Presence of "MZ" and "PE" headers, which are distinctive markers of Windows executable files

This technique is a common malware delivery method where attackers attempt to bypass security controls by misrepresenting the true nature of the transmitted file. When users believe they are receiving JavaScript but actually download an executable, they may inadvertently execute malicious code. The rule classifies this activity as "trojan-activity" which indicates its potential to deliver malware.

The deception is particularly dangerous because:
- It exploits trust in legitimate web content types
- It may bypass content filtering systems that rely on declared content types
- Executable files have significantly higher risk potential than script files
- Users may not recognize the threat until after execution has occurred

The detection focuses on the fundamental mismatch between the declared content type and the actual file format, which is a strong indicator of malicious intent.

2008380.et_name: PoisonIvy Key Exchange with CnC Init
2008380.description:
PoisonIvy is a Remote Access Tool (RAT) that gives an attacker virtually full control over its victim. It first appeared as far back as 2005 where it was available for a free download on the website poisonivy-rat[.]com [1]. This RAT has been used in several noteworthy attacks over the years, many of which are believed to have been carried out by various APT actors with ties to China. Most PoisonIvy variants used today make use of a custom, Camellia encrypted TCP protocol for communication between client and the Command and Control (C2/CnC) server. 

Due to the nature of encrypted traffic, PoisonIvy is difficult to effectively detect with signature-based IDPS rules as the network traffic changes based on the hardcoded password in the RAT’s configuration. For this reason, each individual PoisonIvy signature is crafted for a password that has been observed being used by at least one PoisonIvy sample. The network traffic and its encryption method is described in detail by Conix Security [2]. PoisonIvy variants are still being used today in targeted attacks [3] making it a still relevant threat.

You can further validate a potential PoisonIvy RAT infection by looking for other indicators of compromise such malware, trojan, and C2 signatures which have also triggered on the client in question, along with looking at ET Intelligence to determine if the server is known to be a malicious PoisonIvy RAT system.


Documentation References:
https://www.fireeye.com/content/dam/fireeye-www/global/en/current-threats/pdfs/rpt-poison-ivy.pdf
http://blog.conixsecurity.fr/wp-content/uploads/2013/10/Poison-Ivy-RAT-conf-comms.pdf

2008381.et_name: PoisonIvy Key Exchange with CnC Response
2008381.description:
PoisonIvy is a Remote Access Tool (RAT) that gives an attacker virtually full control over its victim. It first appeared as far back as 2005 where it was available for a free download on the website poisonivy-rat[.]com [1]. This RAT has been used in several noteworthy attacks over the years, many of which are believed to have been carried out by various APT actors with ties to China. Most PoisonIvy variants used today make use of a custom, Camellia encrypted TCP protocol for communication between client and the Command and Control (C2/CnC) server. 

Due to the nature of encrypted traffic, PoisonIvy is difficult to effectively detect with signature-based IDPS rules as the network traffic changes based on the hardcoded password in the RAT’s configuration. For this reason, each individual PoisonIvy signature is crafted for a password that has been observed being used by at least one PoisonIvy sample. The network traffic and its encryption method is described in detail by Conix Security [2]. PoisonIvy variants are still being used today in targeted attacks [3] making it a still relevant threat.

You can further validate a potential PoisonIvy RAT infection by looking for other indicators of compromise such malware, trojan, and C2 signatures which have also triggered on the client in question, along with looking at ET Intelligence to determine if the server is known to be a malicious PoisonIvy RAT system.

2008387.msg: ET DELETED Possible ASPROX Hostile JS Being Served by a Local Webserver (/ngg.js)
2008387.et_name: Possible ASPROX Hostile JS Being Served by a Local Webserver (/ngg.js)
2008387.description:
This rule detects attempts by compromised web servers to distribute malicious JavaScript associated with the Asprox botnet. Specifically, it alerts when a local web server delivers HTTP content containing a script tag referencing an external "ngg.js" script, which is a known indicator of Asprox infection.

The rule examines established HTTP connections from internal servers to external clients and triggers when three content conditions are met: (1) the presence of "<script src=http://" (case insensitive), (2) the absence of "nextgen-gallery" within 15 bytes after the first match, and (3) the presence of "/ngg.js>" within 50 bytes after the first match. The negated content match for "nextgen-gallery" is critical - the rule will only trigger if this string is NOT present, helping to distinguish malicious Asprox activity from legitimate uses of similarly named scripts in the NextGEN Gallery WordPress plugin.

Asprox is a botnet that initially emerged as a spam botnet but evolved to include web server compromise capabilities. When web servers are infected, they're modified to serve malicious JavaScript to visitors, potentially leading to drive-by downloads or further system compromise.

When investigating alerts from this rule, analysts should:
1. Examine the full HTTP session to identify the complete script injection pattern
2. Verify if the referenced external domain hosting "ngg.js" is known malicious
3. Check the compromised web server for unauthorized modifications to web content
4. Look for additional indicators of compromise such as unexpected outbound connections
5. Consider isolating the affected server until remediation is complete

False positives may occur with custom applications using similar script naming conventions. The reference URL provides additional context about Asprox payload evolution and can assist with investigation and attribution.

2008388.msg: ET DELETED Possible ASPROX Hostile JS Being Served by a Local Webserver (/b.js)
2008388.et_name: Possible ASPROX Hostile JS Being Served by a Local Webserver (/b.js)
2008388.description:
This rule detects potential ASPROX botnet activity by identifying JavaScript injection patterns served from local web servers.

The rule monitors HTTP traffic from internal web servers to external clients, specifically looking for script tags that reference external JavaScript files named "b.js". The detection pattern involves two key elements: first, the presence of "<script src=http://" (case insensitive) followed by "/b.js>" within 50 characters.

ASPROX is a known botnet that compromises web servers and injects malicious JavaScript into legitimate web pages. When visitors access these compromised pages, the injected script tags load the external "b.js" file, which typically contains exploit code or malware delivery mechanisms.

This detection is significant because it identifies when an internal web server may have been compromised and is actively serving malicious content to visitors. The classification as "trojan-activity" indicates the rule is targeting malware distribution behavior. The rule specifically focuses on the server-side of the attack, detecting when compromised servers are distributing the malicious code rather than when clients are being infected.

The rule's revision history (rev:6) suggests it has been updated multiple times to improve detection accuracy or address evasion techniques.

2008391.description:
Trojan User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Trojan User-Agent strings that are leveraged by compromised machines.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Trojan often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Trojan User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

2008402.msg: ET ADWARE_PUP Realtimegaming.com Online Casino Spyware Gaming Checkin
2008402.et_name: Realtimegaming.com Online Casino Spyware Gaming Checkin
2008402.description:
This Suricata rule (SID 2008402) detects network traffic associated with Realtimegaming[.]com online casino software communicating with external servers.

The rule triggers when TCP traffic originates from any port on the internal network and connects to port 20000 on external networks. It specifically looks for established connections with a small payload size (less than 30 bytes) containing the binary sequence "|43 01 00|" within the first 4 bytes and the string "Casino" anywhere in the packet (case-insensitive).

This detection identifies check-in or heartbeat communications from potentially unwanted adware/spyware components related to online casino gaming software. The classification as "pup-activity" (Potentially Unwanted Program) indicates this software may engage in tracking or monitoring behaviors without explicit user consent.

The technical indicators suggest a specific protocol pattern used by this software to communicate with its control servers. The small packet size and distinctive binary header pattern (|43 01 00|) are characteristic of a proprietary protocol or identification mechanism.

Organizations should monitor for this traffic as it may indicate unauthorized software operating within the network environment, potentially collecting user data or introducing additional security risks.

2008405.msg: ET MALWARE Obitel trojan calling home
2008405.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Obitel trojan's command and control (C2) communication pattern. The rule specifically monitors HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations, focusing on established connections where requests contain "/gate.php?hash=" in the URI path.

The detection targets the Obitel trojan, a malware variant that communicates with its C2 server using a specific URL pattern. When infected systems attempt to contact their control servers, they send HTTP requests to a path containing "/gate.php?hash=" followed by an alphanumeric hash value that must strictly conform to 8-16 lowercase letters and numbers.

The rule employs several detection techniques:
- Monitors established HTTP connections from internal to external networks, specifically targeting outbound requests (to_server flow direction)
- Uses fast pattern matching for the "/gate.php?hash=" string to optimize performance
- Implements a PCRE regular expression that specifically validates the hash parameter value follows the expected format (8-16 lowercase alphanumeric characters)

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further C2 communication
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Examine the specific hash value being transmitted for potential host identification or campaign correlation
4. Investigate the affected system for additional indicators of compromise, focusing on persistence mechanisms
5. Check for data exfiltration evidence or secondary payload downloads

This detection is classified as "trojan-activity" and identifies active malware infections attempting to communicate with remote control infrastructure. Such communications typically indicate a compromised system that may be receiving commands, exfiltrating data, or downloading additional malicious payloads.

The rule references www[.]abuse[.]ch as a source of additional information about this threat, which is a reputable security resource that tracks malware and botnet activities.

2008407.et_name: Snapshot Viewer for Microsoft Access ActiveX Control Arbitrary File Download (1)
2008407.description:
ActiveX controls are Microsoft Internet Explorer’s native version of plug-ins and can be leveraged by non browse applications as well..  ActiveX provides web application developers a facility to execute code on a client machine through the web browser.  Unfortunately, ActiveX controls have been a significant source of security problems both due to vulnerabilities in the ActiveX control itself, in the browser which can allow the activeX control to bypass security, as well as the fact that it has extensive capabilities to attacker drive code.
ActiveX controls are very powerful and can be used for legitimate and nefarious purposes including monitoring your personal browsing habits, install malware, generate pop-ups, log your keystrokes and passwords, and do other malicious things. ActiveX controls are actually not Internet Explorer-only. They also work in other Microsoft applications, such as Microsoft Office. Other browsers, such as Firefox, Chrome, Safari, and Opera, all use other types of browser plug-ins. ActiveX controls only function in Internet Explorer. A website that requires an ActiveX control is an Internet Explorer-only website.
If you see these ActiveX controls alerts firing, they are unlikely to succeed in exploiting all but legacy windows systems running older versions of IE.  To help validate whether the signature is triggering a valid compromise you should look for other malicious signatures related to the client endpoint which is triggering.  This includes Exploit Kit, Malware, and Command and Control signatures, along with looking to see if the web server is known to be malicious in ET Intelligence.

2008412.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Trojan-Dropper.Win32.Small.avu malware, specifically its HTTP command and control (C2) communication patterns.

The rule monitors outbound HTTP requests from internal networks to external destinations, focusing on specific URL parameter patterns characteristic of this trojan dropper's check-in behavior. The malware uses HTTP requests with multiple required parameters including "m=", "a=", "r=", "os=", and "00000" in the communication.

Additionally, the rule employs regular expressions to identify two specific patterns: URLs containing "/s_" followed by two digits, an underscore, and one or more digits, followed by a question mark, and an "os" parameter containing a 40-character alphanumeric string.

This detection is significant because trojan droppers are designed to download and install additional malicious payloads onto infected systems. The Small.avu variant appears to use HTTP for command and control communications, allowing it to blend in with normal web traffic while reporting system information and potentially receiving instructions from its operators.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should immediately isolate the affected system from the network to prevent further C2 communication and potential payload downloads. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the detected traffic for forensic analysis. Investigate the compromised host by examining running processes, scheduled tasks, startup items, and recently modified files. Collect and analyze memory dumps to identify persistence mechanisms. Scan the system with updated anti-malware tools focusing on trojan droppers. Document all observed C2 infrastructure including domains and IP addresses for threat intelligence sharing and network defense updates. After remediation, monitor the affected system for at least 30 days for signs of reinfection or dormant components.

2008414.msg: ET SCAN Cisco Torch TFTP Scan

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, confidence High, signature_severity Informational, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2019_07_26

2008414.description:
This rule detects reconnaissance activity targeting TFTP services using the Cisco Torch scanning tool.

The alert triggers when external hosts send UDP traffic to port 69 (TFTP) on internal networks containing a specific hex-encoded content pattern "|52 61 6E 64 30 6D 53 54 52 49 4E 47 00 6E 65 74 61 73 63 69 69|" which translates to "Rand0mSTRING" followed by a null byte and "netascii". This pattern is a signature of the Cisco Torch security assessment tool when it performs TFTP scanning operations. The rule uses offset:2 and depth:21 parameters to efficiently search for this pattern starting 2 bytes into the packet and examining only the next 21 bytes.

Cisco Torch is a network reconnaissance tool specifically designed to identify vulnerabilities in Cisco devices. When used for TFTP scanning, it attempts to connect to TFTP servers and probe for configuration files or other sensitive information that might be accessible. The tool sends specially crafted packets with this distinctive signature to identify potential targets.

The rule is classified as "attempted-recon" which indicates its purpose is to detect reconnaissance activities that precede potential attacks. TFTP servers running on port 69 can be vulnerable to unauthorized access if improperly configured, potentially exposing sensitive configuration files containing credentials or network information.

When this alert triggers, security analysts should:
1. Verify the source IP address and determine if it belongs to authorized security testing
2. Check if the targeted TFTP server is properly secured with access controls
3. Review logs for subsequent connection attempts from the same source
4. Consider blocking the source IP if unauthorized scanning is confirmed
5. Examine the targeted TFTP server for any signs of compromise or data exfiltration

Detection of this activity is significant as it indicates an attacker is actively mapping the network infrastructure with a focus on Cisco devices, which is typically an early phase in the attack chain before attempting exploitation. This rule has been revised twice (rev:2) since its initial creation, indicating ongoing maintenance to ensure detection effectiveness.

2008415.msg: ET SCAN Cisco Torch IOS HTTP Scan

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, confidence Medium, signature_severity Informational, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2020_04_23

2008415.description:
This Suricata rule detects reconnaissance attempts using the Cisco-Torch scanning tool targeting Cisco IOS devices via HTTP.

The rule triggers when established HTTP connections from external networks to internal networks contain the specific user agent string "Cisco-torch" in HTTP requests. The flow direction requirement (established,to_server) ensures the rule only matches complete connection attempts directed toward internal systems. Cisco-Torch is a network reconnaissance tool specifically designed to identify and probe Cisco devices for vulnerabilities.

The detection focuses on the initial scanning phase of an attack lifecycle, where attackers attempt to discover Cisco infrastructure within a network. This represents a critical early warning sign of potential targeted attacks against network infrastructure.

The rule references documentation about the tool from hackingexposedcisco[.]com and securiteam[.]com, confirming its purpose as a specialized scanner for Cisco devices. The classification as "attempted-recon" accurately reflects its function in identifying reconnaissance activities.

Network defenders should monitor these alerts as they indicate deliberate attempts to map Cisco infrastructure, which often precedes more targeted exploitation attempts against network devices. Cisco infrastructure compromise can lead to network monitoring, traffic interception, or serve as a persistent access point for attackers.

2008417.msg: ET SCAN Wapiti Web Server Vulnerability Scan

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, confidence Medium, signature_severity Informational, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2019_09_27

2008417.description:
This rule detects reconnaissance activity from the Wapiti web vulnerability scanner targeting HTTP servers. The alert triggers when an external host sends a GET request to an HTTP server with specific characteristics of Wapiti scanning patterns.

The rule identifies Wapiti scans by looking for:
- GET requests starting with "GET /"
- Requests containing the string "?http://www.google." (defanged: ?http://www[.]google[.]) within the first 100 bytes
- User-Agent header containing "Python-httplib2"

Wapiti is an open-source web application vulnerability scanner that performs automated black-box testing to identify security issues in web applications. It checks for vulnerabilities such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), file inclusion, and other common web application security flaws.

This type of scanning activity represents reconnaissance, where attackers or security professionals gather information about potential vulnerabilities in web servers. The rule classifies this activity as "attempted-recon" which indicates it's detecting early-stage attack preparation rather than an actual exploitation attempt.

Organizations should investigate these alerts to determine if the scanning is authorized security testing or potentially malicious reconnaissance. Unauthorized scanning may indicate that an attacker is preparing for a more targeted attack by identifying vulnerabilities in the web infrastructure.

rule_metadata.affected_product: Any, attack_target Client_and_Server, created_at 2010_07_30, deployment Perimeter, deployment Internet, deployment Internal, deployment Datacenter, signature_severity Critical, tag Metasploit, updated_at 2019_07_26

2008418.description:
The Metasploit Project is a computer security project that provides information about security vulnerabilities and aids in penetration testing and IDS signature development.
Its best-known project is the open source Metasploit Framework, a tool for developing and executing exploit code against a remote target machine. Other important sub-projects include the Opcode Database, shellcode archive and related research.
The Metasploit Project is well known for its anti-forensic and evasion tools, some of which are built into the Metasploit Framework (MSF).
Shellcode is a small piece of code used as the payload in the exploitation of a software vulnerability. It is called "shellcode" because it typically starts a command shell from which the attacker can control the compromised machine, but any piece of code that performs a similar task can be called shellcode. Shellcode is commonly written in machine code.

These alerts will fire when shellcode known to be part of Metasploit Project is detected traversing the network. This indicates active use of Metasploit Framework, and it will fire very frequently during a penetration test. If you see only one or two alerts, it may indicate the attacker has copied the shellcode from Metasploit. There have been a few examples of its use in APT campaigns for persistence and lateral movement. 1,2

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, confidence High, signature_severity Major, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2019_07_26

2008426.description:
This rule detects exploitation attempts targeting a buffer overflow vulnerability in Alt-N Technologies SecurityGateway 1.0.1.

The rule monitors TCP traffic from external networks to port 4000 on internal networks, specifically looking for POST requests to "/SecurityGateway.dll" containing "logon" and "username" parameters. The critical detection mechanism is the PCRE regex that identifies when a username parameter exceeds 720 characters, which triggers the buffer overflow condition.

CVE-2008-4193 describes a stack-based buffer overflow in SecurityGateway.dll that allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a long username parameter. This vulnerability was publicly disclosed in 2008, with exploit code available on security websites.

The attack is particularly dangerous as successful exploitation could lead to remote code execution with the privileges of the SecurityGateway application. Since the vulnerable service runs on a standard port (4000) and requires minimal authentication to exploit, attackers can easily target internet-facing SecurityGateway installations.

Organizations running SecurityGateway 1.0.1 should immediately update to a patched version or implement network-level protections to block exploitation attempts.

2008427.description:
Trojan User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Trojan User-Agent strings that are leveraged by compromised machines.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Trojan often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Trojan User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

2008435.et_name: Win32.Testlink Trojan Speed Test Start port 8888
2008435.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Win32.Testlink Trojan's speed test functionality.

The rule monitors TCP traffic from internal networks to external destinations specifically on port 8888. It triggers when an established connection from client to server contains a 25-byte payload with the specific HTTP request "GET /test_link HTTP/1.0" followed by a carriage return and line feed (0d 0a in hexadecimal).

Win32.Testlink is a trojan that appears to use HTTP requests to port 8888 as part of its command and control (C2) infrastructure or functionality testing. The specific pattern suggests the malware is initiating a speed or connectivity test to assess the victim's network capabilities.

The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this is malicious behavior associated with a known trojan. The communication pattern represents an attempt by the infected host to communicate with its C2 server using a specific HTTP request format on an uncommon port, which helps the malware operator measure connection quality or verify successful infection.

This detection is significant as it identifies active malware communication from compromised systems, allowing security teams to identify infected hosts within their network perimeter. The rule (SID:2008435, revision 3) specifically monitors established connections flowing from internal clients to external servers, which is consistent with the expected C2 communication pattern of this malware.

2008436.msg: ET DELETED Win32.Testlink Trojan Speed Test port 8888
2008436.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Win32.Testlink Trojan's speed test functionality operating on port 8888.

The rule monitors established TCP connections from internal networks to external destinations specifically on port 8888. It triggers when the data size exceeds 1000 bytes and contains a specific byte pattern starting with "Data:" followed by a sequence of null bytes. This pattern is characteristic of the Win32.Testlink Trojan's communication protocol when performing speed tests. The rule examines only the first 35 bytes of the payload (as specified by the depth parameter) to efficiently identify this signature.

The "DELETED" status in the rule message indicates this rule has been deprecated or removed from active use in newer rule sets, possibly due to false positives or because the threat has evolved. However, the rule remains documented for reference or for environments that may still encounter this specific variant.

The Trojan appears to use port 8888 for command and control (C2) communications, specifically for testing connection speeds between the infected host and its control server. This functionality helps the malware operator assess the bandwidth capabilities of compromised systems, which could be useful for determining which infected machines are suitable for specific malicious activities such as data exfiltration or participating in distributed denial of service attacks.

The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this is malware designed to provide unauthorized access to the affected system. The presence of this traffic on a network strongly suggests an active malware infection that has established external communications.

Network defenders should investigate any systems triggering this alert as they likely require immediate remediation to address the trojan infection.

2008437.msg: ET DELETED Win32.Testlink Trojan Checkin port 8888
2008437.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Win32.Testlink Trojan communicating with command and control servers.

The rule monitors outbound TCP connections from internal networks to external servers on port 8888, specifically targeting established connections flowing to the server. It looks for HTTP-like requests containing four distinct patterns in sequence: "/stat?uptime=", followed immediately by "&downlink=" (distance:0), then "&uplink=" (distance:0), and finally "&id=" (distance:0). The distance:0 modifiers ensure these parameters appear consecutively without interruption, matching the Trojan's precise communication protocol.

Win32.Testlink is a Trojan that establishes persistent connections to remote servers, allowing attackers to maintain control over infected systems. The specific communication pattern indicates the malware is reporting operational metrics to its command infrastructure.

The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" confirms this is malicious software designed to provide unauthorized access to compromised systems. The communication on port 8888 represents the command and control channel through which the attacker can monitor infected hosts and potentially issue commands.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further command and control communication
2. Capture full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Examine the identified host for additional indicators of compromise, focusing on persistence mechanisms
4. Check for lateral movement attempts from the compromised system
5. Block the destination IP at network boundaries and add to threat intelligence feeds
6. Collect and preserve the malware sample for further analysis if possible

This detection is significant as it identifies active malware infections attempting to communicate with external control servers, indicating a system compromise that requires immediate remediation.

2008439.et_name: AlstraSoft Affiliate Network Pro (pgm) Parameter SQL Injection
2008439.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2008444.et_name: PWDump4 Password dumping exe copied to victim
2008444.description:
# Suricata Rule Analysis: PWDump4 Password Dumping Detection

This rule detects attempts to copy the PWDump4 password extraction utility to a target system over SMB protocols. The alert triggers when the PWDump4.exe filename is transferred to ports 139 or 445 on internal networks.

## Technical Details

- **Protocol/Ports**: TCP traffic directed to ports 139 and 445 (SMB/CIFS services)
- **Target**: Internal networks ($HOME_NET)
- **Detection Method**: Pattern matching for the Unicode string "OriginalFilename" followed by "PWDUMP4.exe"
- **Classification**: suspicious-filename-detect
- **SID**: 2008444

## Threat Analysis

PWDump4 is a legitimate security testing tool that extracts password hashes from Windows systems. When deployed by unauthorized actors, it enables credential theft by:

1. Extracting NTLM password hashes from the Security Account Manager (SAM)
2. Accessing cached credentials
3. Facilitating lateral movement within networks

This rule specifically identifies the file transfer phase of an attack, where the executable is being copied to a victim machine prior to execution.

## Security Context

This detection is significant because:

- Password hash extraction is a critical step in the attack chain
- The presence of PWDump4 on systems where it's not authorized indicates potential compromise
- The tool's transfer over SMB suggests deliberate targeting of Windows authentication mechanisms
- Post-exploitation credential harvesting typically precedes privilege escalation or lateral movement

Network defenders should investigate any triggers of this rule as they likely indicate active credential theft attempts against Windows systems.

2008445.description:
This rule detects attempts to use the Pwdump6 password extraction tool against Windows systems. The alert triggers when a TCP connection to ports 139 or 445 (SMB/CIFS services) on internal networks contains a specific byte sequence representing the Unicode string "\test.pwd", which is a test file created during Pwdump6 operations.

Pwdump6 is a credential harvesting tool designed to extract password hashes from Windows systems. When executed, it creates a test file on the victim machine as part of its operation. This rule specifically identifies the established session where this test file creation occurs. The byte sequence "|5c 00 74 00 65 00 73 00 74 00 2e 00 70 00 77 00 64|" represents the Unicode-encoded filename "\test.pwd" with null bytes between each character, typical of SMB/CIFS protocol communications.

The detection focuses on the SMB/CIFS protocol (ports 139 and 445), which is commonly used for file sharing on Windows networks. The "flow:established,to_server" parameter ensures the rule only triggers on established connections flowing toward the server.

This activity indicates an attacker has gained access to the target system and is actively attempting to extract password hashes. Password hash extraction is a critical security event as it allows attackers to perform offline password cracking attempts, potentially leading to further system compromise or lateral movement within a network.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent potential lateral movement
2. Examine the source IP address to identify the attack origin
3. Review authentication logs and network traffic for signs of initial compromise
4. Collect memory dumps and system artifacts for forensic analysis
5. Initiate password resets for potentially compromised accounts
6. Check for additional indicators of compromise related to Pwdump6 usage

The rule has undergone four revisions (rev:4) to improve detection accuracy and reduce false positives. For additional technical context, refer to the documentation at xinn[.]org/Snort-pwdump6.html.

The "established,to_server" flow directive ensures that the rule only triggers on active connections initiated from the infected host to the command and control server, reducing false positives.

This rule detects command and control (C&C) traffic associated with a backdoor identified as "Backdoor.Cow Variant" or "Backdoor.Win32.Agent.lam". The rule monitors UDP traffic from internal networks to external networks on high ports (1024 and above).

The detection focuses on specific patterns in the network traffic that are characteristic of this backdoor's communication protocol. The rule looks for UDP packets containing the hexadecimal sequence "|6C 3C|" at the beginning of the payload, followed by "|3E 20|" within the next 3 bytes. Additionally, it searches for several parameter identifiers typical of this backdoor's C&C protocol: "bid=" (likely bot ID), "bver=" (likely bot version), "bip=" (likely bot IP address), and "bn=" (possibly bot name).

This backdoor represents a significant security threat as it establishes persistent unauthorized access to compromised systems. The communication pattern suggests a structured reporting mechanism where infected hosts send system information to remote command servers. The "command-and-control" classification indicates this traffic is part of an established malicious infrastructure used to control compromised systems remotely.

The detection of such traffic on a network strongly indicates an active malware infection that requires immediate remediation to prevent data exfiltration, lateral movement, or other malicious activities.

2008467.et_name: Possible SQL Injection Attempt Danmec related (declare) in HTTP URI
2008467.description:
SQL injection (SQLi) attacks are a type of injection attack, in which SQL commands are injected into data-plane input in order to effect the execution of predefined SQL commands. A successful SQL injection exploit can read sensitive data from the database, modify database data, execute administration operations on the database, recover the content of a given file present on the DBMS file system and in some cases issue commands to the operating system. Common actions taken by successful attackers are to spoof identity, tamper with existing data, cause repudiation issues such as voiding transactions or changing balances, allow the complete disclosure of all data on the system, destroy the data or make it otherwise unavailable, and become administrators of the database server.

SQLi vulnerabilities are common, and have enjoyed the top ranks of the OWASP top 10 for a number of years. Furthermore, it is very common with PHP and ASP applications due to the prevalence of older functional interfaces. Due to the nature of programmatic interfaces available, J2EE and ASP.NET applications are less likely to have easily exploited SQL injections.

When these signatures generate alerts, it indicates an attacker is probing for a web application that is vulnerable to SQLi. It is a common practice for attackers to scan en masse for these vulnerabilities and then return with more sophisticated attacks when the web application returns a SQL error message that indicates it is vulnerable. A typical next step for an attacker would be to inject malicious redirects, or reset an administrative password.

To aid in validating whether or not an SQL Injection alert is a valid hit, you can take the following steps:
Is the signature triggering on a web application in your datacenter?  These signatures are not typically deployed for inspecting outbound client traffic to the internet. 
Does the alert match the web application deployed (if not generic SQL detection?) Sometimes due to broad vulnerabilities that might be perfectly fine behavior in certain apps they can impact other applications if misapplied.
Is the attack source known in ET Intelligence?  Often times well known scanners, brute forcers, and other malicious actors will have reputation in ET Intelligence which can help to determine if the behavior is previously known to be malicious.

2008476.description:
This Suricata rule detects attempts to inject password dumping DLLs into systems, specifically targeting Windows SMB services.

The rule monitors TCP traffic directed to ports 139 and 445 on internal networks, which are standard ports for Windows file sharing and SMB services. It triggers when specific byte sequences are detected in established connections to these services. The hexadecimal content pattern "|6c 00 73 00 72 00 65 00 6d 00 6f 00 72 00 61|" translates to "lsremora" in Unicode format, which is associated with password dumping tools.

This detection is linked to tools developed by Foofus.net, particularly those designed to extract password hashes from Windows systems. The rule specifically identifies techniques used by password dumping utilities that inject DLLs into system processes to extract credentials from memory.

The threat is classified as "suspicious-filename-detect" indicating it's monitoring for suspicious filenames or patterns associated with known attack tools. This type of activity typically represents an active attempt to compromise credentials on a target system, often occurring after an attacker has already gained initial access.

The reference URL points to documentation about detecting fgdump, a well-known credential harvesting tool used to extract password hashes from Windows systems. This tool is frequently used during the post-exploitation phase of attacks to obtain credentials for lateral movement within networks.

Organizations should treat alerts from this rule as high priority, as they indicate potential credential theft activities in progress.

2008477.description:
This Suricata rule (SID 2008477) detects network traffic associated with the Banload banking trojan, specifically identifying POST request check-ins from infected systems.

The rule monitors HTTP POST requests from internal networks to external destinations, looking for specific patterns in the HTTP request body. It triggers when all of the following parameters are found in the same request: "PC=", "&USER=", "&HASH=", and "&DADOS=". These parameters represent a structured data exfiltration format used by Banload malware when communicating with its command and control infrastructure.

Banload is a banking trojan primarily targeting Brazilian financial institutions. This particular rule identifies the data exfiltration phase where the malware sends system information, user credentials, and potentially harvested banking details to its operators. The "DADOS" parameter (Portuguese for "data") typically contains the encrypted or encoded payload of stolen information.

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" indicates this traffic represents malware maintaining communication with its control servers. This type of traffic is a critical indicator of compromise, as it signals an active infection where sensitive data may be exfiltrated from the network.

Detection of this traffic pattern should trigger immediate incident response procedures, as it indicates an active Banload infection with potential financial data theft in progress.

2008481.description:
This Suricata rule detects network traffic associated with the Trojan-PSW.Win32.Nilage.crg malware's command and control communications.

The rule monitors TCP traffic from internal networks to external destinations specifically on port 2227. It triggers only on established connections where traffic is flowing from the client to the server. The rule identifies packets with an exact size of 32 bytes containing two distinct binary patterns: the first pattern "|00 c0 a8 01 f4 6f 00 00 00|" must appear within the first 12 bytes of the packet (enforced by the depth:12 parameter), while the second pattern "|00 00 00 05 01 28 0a|" can appear anywhere in the packet.

The detected malware is a password-stealing Trojan that targets Windows systems. When infected, the malware attempts to communicate with its command and control server using these specific binary patterns as part of its check-in process. The first pattern includes what appears to be an internal IP address reference (c0 a8 01 f4 corresponds to 192.168.1.244), while the second pattern likely represents a command code or protocol identifier.

This detection is significant because password-stealing Trojans can lead to credential theft, data exfiltration, and further system compromise. The communication with external servers on port 2227 represents the malware's attempt to receive commands or exfiltrate stolen information.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further data exfiltration
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the communication for forensic analysis
3. Scan the originating system with updated anti-malware tools focusing on Trojan-PSW variants
4. Investigate for signs of credential compromise and unauthorized access
5. Block the destination IP at the network perimeter
6. Implement memory forensics to identify persistence mechanisms used by the malware

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" indicates this is part of the malware's infrastructure communication rather than the initial infection vector.

2008484.msg: ET ADWARE_PUP Cleancop.co.kr Fake AV User-Agent (CleancopUpdate)

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, confidence High, signature_severity Minor, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2024_03_02

2008484.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with a potentially unwanted program (PUP) or adware from Cleancop.co[.]kr, which appears to be a fake antivirus application.

The rule triggers when any internal network host makes an HTTP request to an external destination with a User-Agent string that begins with "Cleancop". Specifically, it's looking for update-related communications from the application "CleancopUpdate" as indicated in the rule message.

The rule monitors established HTTP connections flowing from internal networks to external destinations. It inspects the HTTP User-Agent field for strings starting with "Cleancop" using the "startswith" modifier, which ensures the detection focuses on the beginning of the User-Agent string. The "flow:established,to_server" parameter ensures that only established connections from internal clients to external servers are evaluated.

Fake antivirus programs like this typically attempt to deceive users by falsely reporting security issues on their systems and then offering to fix these non-existent problems, usually after payment. These applications may:

- Display false positive detections to create urgency
- Attempt to convince users to purchase premium versions
- Collect user information
- Deliver additional unwanted software
- Generate revenue through deceptive advertising

The classification "pup-activity" indicates this is considered a potentially unwanted program rather than a critical security threat, but such software can degrade system performance, compromise privacy, and potentially lead to more serious security issues if users provide payment information.

Recommended response actions:
1. Identify and isolate affected systems showing this traffic
2. Block the domain cleancop.co[.]kr at the network perimeter
3. Scan affected systems with legitimate security software to remove the PUP
4. Review HTTP logs to identify when the infection occurred and potential lateral movement
5. Implement application control policies to prevent unauthorized software installation

2008488.description:
Trojan User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Trojan User-Agent strings that are leveraged by compromised machines.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Trojan often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Trojan User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.

2008491.description:
This Suricata rule detects network traffic associated with the Banker.OT banking trojan's command and control (C2) communication pattern. Note that this is a deleted rule as indicated by the "ET DELETED" prefix in the message field, suggesting it has been deprecated or replaced by newer detection methods.

The rule monitors HTTP traffic from internal networks to external web servers, specifically looking for established connections with traffic flowing to the server. It identifies HTTP requests containing three distinct parameters: "praquem=", "&titulo=", and "&texto=". These parameters form a distinctive pattern used by the Banker.OT malware during its check-in process with command and control servers.

The "depth:8" parameter restricts the search for "praquem=" to the first 8 bytes of the HTTP request payload, which optimizes performance by limiting where this initial pattern must be found. The rule message includes "(2 packet)" as part of the alert text, which is likely a reference to this being a variant of the malware's communication pattern.

The "flow:established,to_server" directive ensures that the rule only inspects established TCP connections with traffic flowing from the client to the server, which helps reduce false positives by focusing on actual request traffic rather than connection setup packets.

Banking trojans like Banker.OT typically steal financial credentials, hijack banking sessions, or manipulate transactions. This detection identifies the malware's communication with its control infrastructure, which is a critical point for identifying infected systems before financial theft occurs.

When this rule triggers, security teams should isolate the affected system, capture full packet captures for forensic analysis, scan the system for malware, and investigate other network connections from the same host for additional malicious activity. Since banking trojans often operate as part of larger campaigns, correlation with other security events is recommended.

The rule is classified as "trojan-activity" indicating its focus on malicious software behavior rather than exploitation of a specific vulnerability.

2008492.description:
This Suricata rule detects network traffic associated with the Win32.Downloader.pgp malware family. The rule specifically identifies HTTP communication patterns used during the malware's check-in process to command and control servers.

The rule monitors outbound HTTP requests from internal networks to external destinations, looking for specific URL parameter patterns in the HTTP URI. It triggers when all of the following parameters appear in a single HTTP request: "?id=", "&e=", "&err=", and "&c=". These parameters likely represent a structured communication protocol where the malware reports its identifier, execution status, error codes, and possibly command acknowledgments.

This detection focuses on the command and control (C2) communication phase of the malware infection lifecycle. The Win32.Downloader.pgp malware, as indicated by its classification, functions primarily as a downloader - malware designed to retrieve and install additional malicious payloads onto the infected system.

The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" indicates this is malicious software that disguises its true intent. The established flow requirement ensures the rule only triggers on active connections, reducing false positives.

Detection of this traffic pattern is significant as it indicates an active malware infection on the network that is attempting to communicate with its operators, potentially leading to further compromise through additional malware downloads or data exfiltration.

2008502.msg: ET MALWARE Antispywareexpert.com Fake AS Install Checkin
2008502.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with fake anti-spyware software communicating with command and control infrastructure.

The alert triggers when an HTTP request is made from an internal network to an external destination with specific URL patterns that match the communication protocol of a malicious application known as "Antispywareexpert[.]com". The rule specifically looks for HTTP requests containing multiple parameters in the URL structure: "/?action=", "&pc_id=", "&abbr=", "&a=", "&l=", and "&addt".

This traffic pattern represents check-in communications from infected systems to the command and control server. The fake anti-spyware application is a type of scareware or potentially unwanted application (PUA) that falsely claims to detect spyware on a victim's computer, then attempts to convince users to purchase a "full version" to remove non-existent threats.

The rule's classification as "command-and-control" indicates this is part of a botnet infrastructure where compromised machines report back to a central server. This type of malware typically aims to:

1. Extract payment information from victims
2. Collect system information for further exploitation
3. Download additional malicious payloads
4. Maintain persistence on infected systems

The structured URL parameters likely contain encoded information about the infected system, potentially including unique identifiers, system information, and status updates to the controller.

2008507.msg: ET MALWARE Backdoor.Win32.VB.fdi Bot Reporting to Controller
2008507.description:
This Suricata rule detects network traffic associated with the Backdoor.Win32.VB.fdi malware variant, specifically when an infected system communicates with its command and control (C2) server.

The rule monitors outbound TCP connections from any port on the internal network to external destinations using ports 1024 and above. It triggers when an established connection contains the specific string "state: 0 - zombie is ready for control" within the first 38 bytes of the payload.

This particular communication pattern represents the initial check-in or "beaconing" behavior of the malware, where the compromised host (referred to as a "zombie" in the malware's terminology) signals its availability to receive commands from the controller. The message content indicates the bot is in a ready state and awaiting instructions.

The rule classifies this activity as "trojan-activity," which accurately reflects the backdoor nature of this threat. Backdoor.Win32.VB.fdi is a Visual Basic-based malware that establishes persistent remote access to infected systems, allowing threat actors to maintain control over compromised hosts.

Detection of this traffic pattern indicates an active malware infection in the environment that has already established outbound communication with its control infrastructure, representing a significant security incident requiring immediate investigation and remediation.

2008510.description:
A Trojan-Downloader is a type of malware that is responsible for loading and facilitating the continued proliferation of further payloads upon the victim machine. Typically, Trojan-Downloaders will ensure further infection is successful but reporting a successful install, modifying system settings to ensure future malware can be installed/executed without issue, and enable persistency mechanisms for long term infection. Windows is the most commonly observed platform for this type of infection, however, it is not limited-- Macintosh OS X and Linux are also potential targets for compromise.
Valid Trojan-Downloader activity can include network connectivity to a command and control server to report successful infection on a victim machine. Typically, machines impacted with a Trojan-Downloader will have several system settings modified, such as modifications to the Registry where malicious entries may be made. Additionally, the download of a second-stage payload may occur once the original malware has ran. Trojan-Downloaders have been observed with the ability to exfiltrate sensitive data. Confirmation of hostile IP addresses or domains observed with Trojan-Downloader activity may take place in the ET Intelligence portal.
From a network perspective, malware that falls under the Trojan-Downloader has been observed performing activity that would trigger several Emerging Threats INFO, POLICY, and TROJAN style alerts, such as checking an external IP address, the presence of a downloaded executable, or a suspicious HTTP POST to a server. This combination of Trojan-Downloader alerts, as well as complimentary INFO, POLICY, or TROJAN alerts, would warrant an immediate follow up for a compromised workstation.

rule_metadata.created_at: 2010_07_30, malware_family Win32_Antivirus2008, signature_severity Major, tag Description_Generated_By_Proofpoint_Nexus, updated_at 2019_07_26

2008511.description:
This rule detects network traffic associated with the Win32/Antivirus2008 fake antivirus software. The rule monitors HTTP traffic from internal networks to external destinations, specifically looking for HTTP URI patterns that indicate communication from this malware.

The rule identifies HTTP requests containing the pattern "?type=scanner&pin=" followed by "&lnd=" in the URI, which represents the fake antivirus software's installation reporting mechanism. These parameters are likely used by the malware to communicate with command and control servers, confirming successful installation on victim systems. The rule specifically monitors established connections from internal hosts to external servers (flow:established,to_server), focusing on outbound HTTP traffic.

Win32/Antivirus2008 is a well-documented fake antivirus program that tricks users into believing their system is infected with malware, then prompts them to purchase the "full version" to remove non-existent threats. This social engineering technique aims to extract payment information from victims.

The rule's classification as "trojan-activity" indicates that this traffic represents malicious software that masquerades as legitimate security software. The detection is significant because fake antivirus programs can lead to financial fraud, additional malware installation, and data theft. These programs typically display false security alerts to create urgency and manipulate users into making hasty decisions.

The fast_pattern modifier optimizes the detection process by prioritizing the search for the "?type=scanner&pin=" pattern, improving performance when processing large volumes of network traffic.

When this rule triggers, security analysts should:
1. Isolate the affected system immediately to prevent further communication with command and control servers
2. Capture and preserve full packet captures of the detected traffic for forensic analysis
3. Examine the host for additional indicators of compromise, particularly focusing on browser extensions, scheduled tasks, and registry modifications
4. Scan the system with legitimate anti-malware tools to identify and remove the fake antivirus software
5. Investigate whether payment information or credentials were compromised and initiate appropriate remediation steps

This rule has undergone multiple revisions (currently at revision 6), suggesting ongoing refinement to improve detection accuracy and reduce false positives as the malware's communication patterns evolve.

2008512.description:
Trojan User-Agent signatures are a class of alerts that specifically look for known Trojan User-Agent strings that are leveraged by compromised machines.  As part of HTTP, the web client must identify what software it is running by leveraging the user agent string.  Malware often specifies it’s own user agent string using either explicit user agent names, or more subtly tries to disguise itself as legitimate software by using strings that look like standard software like Internet Explorer, Mozilla, Chrome &c.  Malware authors often use a unique user agent string to help differentiate compromised clients from legitimate web traffic.  The Trojan often leverages this traffic is used to fetch additional payloads, configurations, and instructions--or to report back to command and control infrastructure.  

When reviewing a Trojan User Agent signature to determine if it is a legitimate hit, it is worth reviewing the IDS logs to determine if other alerts for related malware have triggered on this given client, as well as reviewing ET Intelligence to determine if the client is speaking to known malware infrastructure such as command and control systems.  If possible, reviewing a packet capture of the offending traffic can be helpful to identify if this is a legitimate hit or if there is a potential false positive due to obscure user agent headers.
